optionD: Django caches the product and serves the stale row
correctAnswerText: Both read 5 before either saved, so one update is lost
explanation: A read-modify-write race. Use update(stock=F('stock') - 1), or select_for_update inside atomic() when the logic needs the row in Python.

prompt: An orders page shows each order's customer name and all of its line items. Which loading plan is best?
optionA: select_related('customer', 'items') in a single join
optionB: No hints; cache the page so the queries rarely matter
optionC: select_related('customer') plus prefetch_related('items')
optionD: prefetch_related('customer', 'items') for everything
correctAnswerText: select_related('customer') plus prefetch_related('items')
explanation: Join the single-valued customer, prefetch the many-valued items. select_related cannot follow a reverse or many relation, and caching hides the problem until the cache misses.

prompt: Order has a ForeignKey to Customer, and orders are invoices kept for tax audits. Which on_delete is the sound choice?
optionA: DO_NOTHING, and let the database sort out the rest
optionB: CASCADE, so no order is ever left without a customer
optionC: SET_NULL, so deleting a customer is always allowed
optionD: PROTECT, and deactivate customers instead of deleting
correctAnswerText: PROTECT, and deactivate customers instead of deleting
explanation: CASCADE would silently destroy financial records. PROTECT turns a careless delete into an error; a soft-delete flag handles the "remove this customer" need.

prompt: A view only needs to know whether the user has placed any order. Which check is best?
optionA: Order.objects.filter(user=u).count() > 0
optionB: len(Order.objects.filter(user=u)) > 0
optionC: Order.objects.filter(user=u).exists()
optionD: list(Order.objects.filter(user=u)) != []
correctAnswerText: Order.objects.filter(user=u).exists()
explanation: exists() asks the database for at most one row. count() scans all matches, and len() or list() load every order into Python just to throw them away.

prompt: Signup creates a user in an atomic block and must send a welcome email. Where should the send happen?
optionA: In a model save() override so it can never be missed
optionB: Before the atomic block, so the email is never late
optionC: Inside the atomic block, right after the create call
optionD: In transaction.on_commit, after the commit succeeds
correctAnswerText: In transaction.on_commit, after the commit succeeds
explanation: An email cannot be rolled back. Sending inside the block emails people whose signup then fails; on_commit runs only once the row really exists.

prompt: A migration already applied in production added a wrong default. What is the right fix?
optionA: Edit the applied migration file and redeploy it
optionB: Delete all migrations and run makemigrations again
optionC: Change the column by hand in the production database
optionD: Write a new migration that corrects the default
correctAnswerText: Write a new migration that corrects the default
explanation: Applied migrations are recorded by name and never rerun, so edits do nothing in production and diverge from new databases. A forward migration keeps every database in step.

prompt: A home page shows each course with its enrolment count. When is a stored counter column better than annotate(Count(...))?
optionA: When counting on every request is measured to be too slow
optionB: Whenever the course table has more than twenty columns
optionC: Always, because annotate cannot be used on a home page
optionD: Never, because a stored counter can never be kept right
correctAnswerText: When counting on every request is measured to be too slow
explanation: annotate is always correct; a counter is faster but must be maintained (F() updates, signals) and can drift. Pay that cost only when the count is a measured hot spot.

prompt: A team proposes giving customers is_staff so they can edit their own profiles in the Django admin. Your judgement?
optionA: Accept it: the admin already checks object ownership itself
optionB: Accept it, as long as the admin URL is renamed to hide it
optionC: Reject it only because the admin cannot be styled to match
optionD: Reject it: the admin is a trusted staff tool, not a user UI
correctAnswerText: Reject it: the admin is a trusted staff tool, not a user UI
explanation: Admin permissions are per model, not per row, so a customer could see or edit others' data. Build normal views with ownership checks for end users.

prompt: Three report views need a login, and every request needs a request-id header logged. Which split is sound?
optionA: Decorators for both, added to every view in the whole project
optionB: Decorators on the three views; middleware for the request id
optionC: Middleware for both, checking URLs for the three report views
optionD: Settings flags for both, read inside each view at the start
correctAnswerText: Decorators on the three views; middleware for the request id
explanation: Middleware suits concerns that apply to every request; a decorator suits a few named views. URL matching inside middleware is fragile and easy to bypass by adding a route.

prompt: Which approach to development and production settings holds up best as a team grows?
optionA: One settings module reading environment values, with safe defaults
optionB: A settings file per developer, each committed with real passwords
optionC: One settings file edited by hand on the server after each deploy
optionD: Production values hard-coded and switched off with comment marks
correctAnswerText: One settings module reading environment values, with safe defaults
explanation: The code stays identical across environments and only configuration changes. Hand edits on the server are lost on redeploy, and committed passwords leak.

prompt: Stock must never go negative, even under concurrent checkouts. Which design gives that guarantee?
optionA: A form validator that rejects quantities above stock
optionB: A nightly job that resets any negative stock to zero
optionC: An if stock > 0 check in the view before calling save()
optionD: A filtered F() update plus a database check constraint
correctAnswerText: A filtered F() update plus a database check constraint
explanation: update(stock=F('stock') - 1) filtered on stock__gt=0 is atomic, and a CheckConstraint makes the database refuse the impossible. Python checks race; nightly fixes are too late.

prompt: In DRF, which class turns model instances into JSON-ready data and validates incoming data?
optionA: A Serializer
optionB: A Renderer
optionC: A Throttle
optionD: A Router
correctAnswerText: A Serializer
explanation: A serializer converts objects to primitive data for output and validates input into validated_data. The renderer only turns that data into JSON bytes.

prompt: Besides model, what must a ModelSerializer's Meta declare?
optionA: renderer or parser
optionB: fields or exclude
optionC: queryset or manager
optionD: lookup_field or pk
correctAnswerText: fields or exclude
explanation: Leaving both out raises an AssertionError (checked); DRF disallowed the implicit "all fields" years ago so that new model columns are never exposed by accident.

prompt: What generates the list and detail URL patterns for a registered ModelViewSet?
optionA: A router such as DefaultRouter
optionB: An APIView subclass's as_view
optionC: The serializer's Meta class
optionD: The INSTALLED_APPS setting
correctAnswerText: A router such as DefaultRouter
explanation: router.register('books', BookViewSet) followed by router.urls produces /books/ and /books/{pk}/ with the right method mapping.

prompt: Which status code does a ModelViewSet return after successfully creating a resource?
optionA: 201 Created
optionB: 200 OK
optionC: 204 No Content
optionD: 202 Accepted
correctAnswerText: 201 Created
explanation: CreateModelMixin returns 201 with the new object in the body (measured). 204 is what destroy returns.

prompt: Which two REST_FRAMEWORK settings turn on page-number pagination for every list view?
optionA: PAGINATE_BY and DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES
optionB: DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS and PAGE_SIZE
optionC: DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS and MAX_ROWS
optionD: DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS and PAGE_SIZE
correctAnswerText: DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS and PAGE_SIZE
explanation: Set DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS to PageNumberPagination and PAGE_SIZE to the page length; either one alone does nothing.

prompt: Which built-in permission class lets only logged-in users reach a view?
optionA: DjangoModelPermissions
optionB: IsAdminUser
optionC: IsAuthenticated
optionD: AllowAny
correctAnswerText: IsAuthenticated
explanation: IsAuthenticated denies anonymous requests. IsAdminUser additionally needs is_staff, and DjangoModelPermissions checks per-model add/change/delete permissions.

prompt: What does Simple JWT's TokenObtainPairView return for a correct username and password?
optionA: An access token and a refresh token
optionB: A single token that never expires
optionC: The user object with a hashed password
optionD: A session cookie and a CSRF token
correctAnswerText: An access token and a refresh token
explanation: Measured: the response body has the keys access and refresh. The access token is short-lived; the refresh token is exchanged for new access tokens.

prompt: Which APIClient method makes later test requests run as a given user without real credentials?
optionA: force_authenticate(user=u)
optionB: credentials(user=u)
optionC: login_as(user=u)
optionD: set_user(user=u)
correctAnswerText: force_authenticate(user=u)
explanation: force_authenticate skips the authentication classes entirely. credentials() sets headers such as Authorization, which is how you test the real token path.

prompt: What is the name of the serializer method that validates only the title field?
optionA: validate_title(self, value)
optionB: title_validator(self, value)
optionC: clean_title(self, value)
optionD: check_title(self, value)
correctAnswerText: validate_title(self, value)
explanation: DRF calls validate_<field_name> with that field's value and uses what it returns. clean_<field> is the Django forms convention, not DRF's.

prompt: With django-cors-headers, which setting lists the frontend origins allowed to call the API?
optionA: CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS
optionB: CORS_EXPOSE_HEADERS
optionC: ALLOWED_HOSTS
optionD: CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS
correctAnswerText: CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS
explanation: CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS names browser origins such as http://localhost:5173. ALLOWED_HOSTS is about the Host header the server answers to, a different check.

prompt: After serializer.is_valid() returns True, what is serializer.validated_data?
optionA: The saved model instance with its new primary key
optionB: A list of the error messages that were suppressed
optionC: The input converted to Python types, after all checks
optionD: The raw request body exactly as the client sent it
correctAnswerText: The input converted to Python types, after all checks
explanation: validated_data is the cleaned input that save() passes to create() or update(). The raw body is request.data, and the instance exists only after save().

prompt: How does a ViewSet differ from an APIView?
optionA: It handles a single HTTP method and needs one class per verb
optionB: It skips serializers and returns model instances to the client
optionC: It names actions like list and create, and a router maps methods
optionD: It runs without authentication, unlike an APIView subclass
correctAnswerText: It names actions like list and create, and a router maps methods
explanation: An APIView has get, post, put methods for one URL. A ViewSet groups actions for a resource across the list and detail URLs, and the router binds verbs to them.

prompt: What separates a 401 from a 403 in a well-behaved API?
optionA: 401: who you are is unknown. 403: known, but not allowed
optionB: 401: the URL is wrong. 403: the HTTP method is wrong
optionC: 401: the token expired. 403: the password is wrong
optionD: 401: the server crashed. 403: the client sent bad JSON
correctAnswerText: 401: who you are is unknown. 403: known, but not allowed
explanation: 401 means credentials are missing or invalid, and invites the client to authenticate. 403 means the identity is accepted but lacks permission for this action.

prompt: When does DRF call a permission class's has_object_permission?
optionA: When the view calls get_object(), as on a detail route
optionB: Only when the user is a staff member or a superuser
optionC: On every request, before the view method runs at all
optionD: Once per row while the list endpoint is serializing
correctAnswerText: When the view calls get_object(), as on a detail route
explanation: Object checks run inside get_object(), used by retrieve, update and destroy. A list never calls it, which is why ownership filtering belongs in get_queryset.

prompt: Why does Simple JWT issue a refresh token alongside a short-lived access token?
optionA: So the access token can be sent without any HTTPS at all
optionB: So a stolen access token expires soon without forcing logins
optionC: So the client can choose which user it wants to act as next
optionD: So the server can store every access token in its database
correctAnswerText: So a stolen access token expires soon without forcing logins
explanation: Access tokens are checked without a database lookup and cannot be revoked cheaply, so they are kept short. The refresh token renews them quietly.

prompt: Why does SessionAuthentication enforce CSRF while a Bearer-token header does not need it?
optionA: CSRF only applies to GET requests, which tokens never make
optionB: Bearer tokens are encrypted, so forged requests cannot read them
optionC: Browsers attach cookies automatically, but not custom headers
optionD: SessionAuthentication is older and kept CSRF for compatibility
correctAnswerText: Browsers attach cookies automatically, but not custom headers
explanation: CSRF exploits credentials the browser sends on its own, which cookies are. A page on another site cannot make the browser add an Authorization header it does not know.

prompt: What does listing owner in read_only_fields do to that field?
optionA: It appears in responses and is ignored in request input
optionB: It is hidden from responses but still accepted as input
optionC: It is stored encrypted and decrypted on every response
optionD: It is required on create and may not change on update
correctAnswerText: It appears in responses and is ignored in request input
explanation: Measured: posting owner=another user to a read-only owner field was ignored and the view's save(owner=request.user) won.

prompt: What is a custom EXCEPTION_HANDLER in DRF typically for?
optionA: Logging successful responses for later analysis
optionB: Hiding all 4xx errors from the client as 200s
optionC: Giving every API error the same JSON body shape
optionD: Retrying failed database queries a second time
correctAnswerText: Giving every API error the same JSON body shape
explanation: It wraps the default exception_handler and reshapes its response, so validation, auth and not-found errors share one format a frontend can rely on.

prompt: Once PageNumberPagination is on, how does a list response body change?
optionA: It stays a plain list and the page goes in a response header
optionB: It returns only ids, and each item is fetched one at a time
optionC: It becomes an object with count, next, previous and results
optionD: It becomes a list of lists, one inner list for each page
correctAnswerText: It becomes an object with count, next, previous and results
explanation: The array moves under results, with count and next/previous links. Frontends that expected a bare array break the day pagination is switched on.

prompt: Your API sends no CORS headers. A curl request to it still succeeds. Why?
optionA: The server allows any origin when no list is configured
optionB: CORS is enforced by browsers, not by the server or curl
optionC: CORS is only checked for requests that carry cookies
optionD: curl sends an Origin header that every server accepts
correctAnswerText: CORS is enforced by browsers, not by the server or curl
explanation: The server merely sends headers; the browser decides whether page scripts may read the response. CORS is not an access control against non-browser clients.

prompt: A booking serializer must reject an end_date earlier than start_date. Where does that rule go?
optionA: In validate_end_date(self, value) on its own
optionB: In validate(self, attrs), comparing both fields
optionC: In to_representation(), when building output
optionD: In the view, after serializer.save() returns
correctAnswerText: In validate(self, attrs), comparing both fields
explanation: A rule involving two fields belongs in object-level validate(attrs). validate_end_date sees only its own value, and after save() the bad row already exists.

prompt: A TaskViewSet must show each user only their own tasks, on list and detail routes alike. What do you override?
optionA: list only, filtering the tasks before they are serialized
optionB: get_serializer_class, choosing a serializer per user
optionC: get_queryset, returning tasks filtered by owner=request.user
optionD: perform_create, saving the owner as the current user
correctAnswerText: get_queryset, returning tasks filtered by owner=request.user
explanation: Every action reads from get_queryset, so filtering there covers list, retrieve, update and delete at once; another user's id simply returns 404.

prompt: New tasks must be owned by the logged-in user, never by whoever the client names. Which code sets that?
optionA: def create(self, request): request.data['owner'] = request.user
optionB: def perform_create(self, s): s.save(owner=self.request.user)
optionC: def get_queryset(self): return Task.objects.filter(owner=None)
optionD: class Meta: fields = '__all__'; extra_kwargs = {'owner': {}}
correctAnswerText: def perform_create(self, s): s.save(owner=self.request.user)
explanation: perform_create is the hook between validation and saving; keyword arguments to save() are merged into validated_data. Pair it with owner as read-only.

prompt: GET /api/books/?search=django should match book titles. What goes on the viewset?
optionA: queryset = Book.objects.filter(title=request.GET['search'])
optionB: filterset_fields = ['search'] and ordering = ['title']
optionC: filter_backends = [SearchFilter] and search_fields = ['title']
optionD: pagination_class = SearchFilter and search_fields = ['title']
correctAnswerText: filter_backends = [SearchFilter] and search_fields = ['title']
explanation: SearchFilter reads the search parameter and applies icontains over search_fields. The request is not available at class level, so the last option cannot run.

prompt: With OrderingFilter enabled and created allowed, how does a client ask for newest first?
optionA: ?sort=created&dir=desc
optionB: ?ordering=-created
optionC: ?order_by=created desc
optionD: ?ordering=created:desc
correctAnswerText: ?ordering=-created
explanation: OrderingFilter reads the ordering parameter with Django's minus-sign convention for descending order; list fields allowed in ordering_fields.

prompt: router.register('books', BookViewSet). Which request deletes the book with id 7?
optionA: DELETE /books/?id=7
optionB: POST /books/7/delete/
optionC: DELETE /books/7/
optionD: GET /books/delete/7/
correctAnswerText: DELETE /books/7/
explanation: The router maps DELETE on the detail URL to destroy. Measured: the delete returned 204.

prompt: You need POST /books/7/publish/ on an existing BookViewSet. What do you add?
optionA: An @action(detail=False, methods=['get']) method named publish
optionB: A second router.register('books/publish', BookViewSet) line
optionC: A publish field on the serializer marked as write_only=True
optionD: An @action(detail=True, methods=['post']) method named publish
correctAnswerText: An @action(detail=True, methods=['post']) method named publish
explanation: detail=True puts the route under /books/{pk}/, the method name becomes the path segment, and methods limits the verbs. Reproduced: it returned 200.

prompt: A React app holds a Simple JWT access token. How should it send it on each API call (default settings)?
optionA: Query string ?access=<access> on the URL
optionB: Header Authorization: Token <access>
optionC: Header Authorization: Bearer <access>
optionD: Header X-CSRFToken: <access> on each call
correctAnswerText: Header Authorization: Bearer <access>
explanation: AUTH_HEADER_TYPES defaults to Bearer. Measured: the same token with the word Token in front got 401; with Bearer it got 200.

prompt: A test should POST {"title": "x"} as JSON and expect 201. Which call fits?
optionA: client.get('/tasks/', {'title': 'x'}, format='json')
optionB: client.post('/tasks/', json.loads('{"title": "x"}'))
optionC: client.post('/tasks/', data='title=x', format='text')
optionD: client.post('/tasks/', {'title': 'x'}, format='json')
correctAnswerText: client.post('/tasks/', {'title': 'x'}, format='json')
explanation: format='json' encodes the dict and sets the JSON content type. Without it APIClient falls back to multipart, which hides problems with nested or typed JSON.

prompt: Write the core of an IsOwner permission so only a task's owner may update or delete it.
optionA: has_permission returns obj.owner == request.user
optionB: has_object_permission returns obj.owner == request.user
optionC: has_permission returns request.user.is_authenticated
optionD: has_object_permission returns request.user.is_staff
correctAnswerText: has_object_permission returns obj.owner == request.user
explanation: Ownership is about one object, so it lives in has_object_permission. has_permission runs before any object is loaded and has no obj argument.

prompt: fields = ['id', 'title', 'owner'] and perform_create calls save(owner=request.user). POST {"title": "x"} returns 400 "owner: This field is required". Why?
optionA: Validation runs before perform_create; owner must be read-only
optionB: perform_create is never called by a ModelViewSet on create
optionC: owner must also be passed in the URL as a query parameter
optionD: The client is anonymous, so request.user is set to None
correctAnswerText: Validation runs before perform_create; owner must be read-only
explanation: Reproduced. is_valid() fails first, so perform_create never runs. Mark owner read_only (read_only_fields) and the save(owner=...) supplies it.

prompt: permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated, IsOwner] and queryset = Task.objects.all(). GET /tasks/5/ for another user's task is refused, yet GET /tasks/ lists every user's tasks. Why?
optionA: Permissions are cached after the first successful request
optionB: The router registers the list URL without the viewset's classes
optionC: IsAuthenticated overrides IsOwner whenever both are listed
optionD: IsOwner is an object check, and list never calls get_object
correctAnswerText: IsOwner is an object check, and list never calls get_object
explanation: Reproduced: the detail route returned 403 while the list returned all rows. Filter by owner in get_queryset; object permissions are a second line, not the first.

prompt: With DRF's default authentication classes, an anonymous GET to an IsAuthenticated view returns 403, not 401. Why?
optionA: DRF always returns 403 for every unauthenticated request
optionB: The first class, SessionAuthentication, sends no challenge
optionC: A 401 needs DEBUG=False, so development servers send 403
optionD: IsAuthenticated is coded to raise PermissionDenied only
correctAnswerText: The first class, SessionAuthentication, sends no challenge
explanation: DRF sends 401 only if the first authentication class provides a WWW-Authenticate header. Measured: defaults gave 403, JWTAuthentication first gave 401.

optionA: A call to s.is_valid() before reading s.data
optionB: A many=True argument when building the serializer
optionC: A call to s.save() before Response is created
optionD: An instance= argument holding the existing task
correctAnswerText: A call to s.is_valid() before reading s.data
explanation: Reproduced: DRF asserts that is_valid() runs before .data when the serializer was given data. Save is optional; validation is not.

prompt: REST_FRAMEWORK = {'PAGE_SIZE': 10}, yet list endpoints still return every row. Why?
optionA: Clients must send ?page=1 before pagination turns on
optionB: PAGE_SIZE must be a string such as '10' to be read
optionC: Pagination only applies to APIView, never to viewsets
optionD: No DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS is set, so nothing paginates
correctAnswerText: No DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS is set, so nothing paginates
explanation: PAGE_SIZE alone does nothing; DRF even emits system check rest_framework.W001 for it (reproduced). Set the class too, or pagination_class on the view.

A ZeroDivisionError in a view now gives AttributeError. Why?
optionA: ZeroDivisionError responses have no data attribute set
optionB: The default handler returns None for non-API exceptions
optionC: Custom handlers must not call the default handler at all
optionD: status_code is read-only on every DRF Response object
correctAnswerText: The default handler returns None for non-API exceptions
explanation: Reproduced. exception_handler only handles APIException, Http404 and PermissionDenied; anything else returns None so Django can produce a 500. Check r is not None.

prompt: Tests using force_authenticate pass, but the mobile app sends "Authorization: Token <jwt>" and always gets 401. Likely cause?
optionA: The access token must be sent in the request body instead
optionB: force_authenticate tokens differ from production tokens
optionC: The SECRET_KEY on the phone differs from the server's key
optionD: Simple JWT expects the Bearer prefix, so no auth happens
correctAnswerText: Simple JWT expects the Bearer prefix, so no auth happens
explanation: An unrecognised prefix makes JWTAuthentication skip the header (reproduced: 401 with Token, 200 with Bearer). force_authenticate bypasses that path entirely.

prompt: API tests with a logged-in session POST fine, but the browser's POST gets 403 "CSRF Failed". Why do the tests miss it?
optionA: APIClient skips CSRF unless enforce_csrf_checks=True
optionB: Tests use JWT behind the scenes instead of sessions
optionC: The test database turns off all middleware by default
optionD: CSRF is only checked when DEBUG is set to False
correctAnswerText: APIClient skips CSRF unless enforce_csrf_checks=True
explanation: Reproduced: the same POST gave 201 by default and 403 with enforce_csrf_checks=True. The browser must send the X-CSRFToken header from the csrftoken cookie.

prompt: CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS = ['http://localhost:5173/']. Django now refuses to start with error corsheaders.E014. What is wrong?
optionA: localhost is never allowed as an origin by the package
optionB: Origins must use https, even for local development
optionC: An origin has no path, so the trailing slash is invalid
optionD: Port numbers must go in a separate CORS_PORTS setting
correctAnswerText: An origin has no path, so the trailing slash is invalid
explanation: An origin is scheme, host and port only. The check reports that the origin "should not have path" (reproduced); write 'http://localhost:5173'.

prompt: BookSerializer declares author = AuthorSerializer(). POSTing a book with a nested author validates, then save() raises an AssertionError. Why?
optionA: AuthorSerializer needs read_only=False to be saved at all
optionB: ModelSerializer.create does not write nested objects by default
optionC: The author dict must be sent as a JSON string, not an object
optionD: Nested serializers must always be declared with many=True
correctAnswerText: ModelSerializer.create does not write nested objects by default
explanation: Reproduced: "The .create() method does not support writable nested fields by default." Write create() yourself, or accept author as a primary key instead.

prompt: For another user's invoice, one design returns 404 (filtered queryset) and another 403 (object permission). Which is better and why?
optionA: 404, because a 403 makes the database lookup much slower
optionB: 403, because a 404 would break the client's retry logic
optionC: 404, because it does not reveal that the invoice exists
optionD: 403, because it tells attackers exactly what is protected
correctAnswerText: 404, because it does not reveal that the invoice exists
explanation: A 403 confirms the id is real, which helps anyone enumerating ids. Filtering in get_queryset hides it and also covers the list endpoint.

prompt: A student sets ACCESS_TOKEN_LIFETIME to 30 days "so users stay logged in". Your verdict?
optionA: Fine, since a JWT is signed and so cannot be misused
optionB: Better to remove expiry entirely and rotate the key
optionC: Keep access short and let a refresh token keep the login
optionD: Fine, as long as the token is saved in localStorage
correctAnswerText: Keep access short and let a refresh token keep the login
explanation: A stolen access token works until it expires, and without a blacklist it cannot be revoked. Short access plus refresh (with rotation and blacklisting) keeps the login without that exposure.

prompt: A busy activity feed gets new rows every second, and users scroll endlessly. Which pagination suits it best?
optionA: CursorPagination, stable while new rows arrive
optionB: LimitOffsetPagination, with a large offset limit
optionC: PageNumberPagination, with page numbers to jump
optionD: No pagination, letting the client trim the list
correctAnswerText: CursorPagination, stable while new rows arrive
explanation: Page and offset positions shift as rows are inserted, so users see duplicates or gaps, and large offsets get slow. A cursor resumes after the last item seen.

prompt: Payments must be listable and viewable but never edited or deleted through the API. Which viewset base fits?
optionA: ModelViewSet, returning 200 with no change on writes
optionB: ModelViewSet, telling the frontend not to call delete
optionC: ReadOnlyModelViewSet, so the write routes never exist
optionD: ModelViewSet, with IsAdminUser on the delete action
correctAnswerText: ReadOnlyModelViewSet, so the write routes never exist
explanation: Routes that do not exist cannot be misused. Relying on the frontend or on one permission leaves update and partial_update open or quietly lying.

prompt: One API serves a same-domain web app and an Android app. Which authentication plan is sound?
optionA: Basic auth for both, sending the password on every request
optionB: JWT in localStorage for both, with CSRF turned off globally
optionC: Session cookies for both, with CSRF exempted for Android
optionD: Session plus CSRF for the web app, JWT for the Android app
correctAnswerText: Session plus CSRF for the web app, JWT for the Android app
explanation: DRF can list several authentication classes. Sessions with CSRF fit the browser, and tokens fit a native client that has no cookie jar or CSRF problem.

prompt: To "fix CORS errors" a teammate sets CORS_ALLOW_ALL_ORIGINS = True on an API that uses session cookies. Your judgement?
optionA: Keep it, because CSRF protection alone covers every risk
optionB: Replace it with the exact frontend origins that are needed
optionC: Keep it, since CORS only matters for public read-only APIs
optionD: Replace it by turning CORS middleware off on the server
correctAnswerText: Replace it with the exact frontend origins that are needed
explanation: Allowing every origin lets any site's scripts read responses the browser makes for your users. List the real origins; removing the middleware just breaks the frontend.

prompt: Emails must be unique. A serializer checks for an existing email before saving. Is that enough?
optionA: Yes: DRF locks the table while validation is running
optionB: No: the check should move to the frontend form instead
optionC: No: add a unique constraint, since two requests can race
optionD: Yes: serializer validation runs inside one transaction
correctAnswerText: No: add a unique constraint, since two requests can race
explanation: Two signups can both pass the check before either saves. The database constraint is the guarantee; the serializer check gives the friendly message.

prompt: Each view wraps its body in try/except and returns its own error JSON. What is the better design?
optionA: Raise DRF exceptions and shape them in one handler
optionB: Let every error become a 500 and log it on the server
optionC: Keep per-view handling, since each view knows best
optionD: Return 200 with an error flag so clients never fail
correctAnswerText: Raise DRF exceptions and shape them in one handler
explanation: Raising ValidationError, NotFound or PermissionDenied keeps status codes right, and one EXCEPTION_HANDLER gives every endpoint the same error shape.

prompt: A suite tests serializers directly but never calls an endpoint. What important bugs can it not catch?
optionA: Permission, routing and status-code mistakes in the views
optionB: Errors in validate() methods that compare two fields
optionC: Field validation errors such as a missing required title
optionD: Type conversion of the input into Python data types
correctAnswerText: Permission, routing and status-code mistakes in the views
explanation: Ownership leaks, wrong status codes and missing routes live in views, permissions and routers. APIClient requests through the URLs exercise all of that.

prompt: A list endpoint nests AuthorSerializer inside BookSerializer and has slowed down as data grew. Which fix is best?
optionA: Cache the whole response for a day regardless of changes
optionB: Raise PAGE_SIZE so fewer requests are needed for the list
optionC: select_related('author') in get_queryset, keeping the shape
optionD: Drop the nested author and make clients fetch each one later
correctAnswerText: select_related('author') in get_queryset, keeping the shape
explanation: Each nested author is a lazy query per row. Loading it in the queryset fixes the N+1 at the source; the other options move or hide the cost.

optionA: The query string, as ?limit=
optionB: A request header named limit
optionC: A path segment after /items
optionD: The JSON request body
correctAnswerText: The query string, as ?limit=
explanation: A simple-typed parameter that is not in the path is a query parameter. A Pydantic model parameter would be read from the body.

prompt: What makes FastAPI read a POST endpoint's parameter from the JSON body?
optionA: Giving the parameter a default value of None
optionB: Declaring the route with @app.post instead of get
optionC: Annotating it with a Pydantic BaseModel subclass
optionD: Naming the parameter body or data in the signature
correctAnswerText: Annotating it with a Pydantic BaseModel subclass
explanation: A BaseModel-typed parameter is a body parameter. The HTTP method alone does not decide it; a plain str on a POST route is still a query parameter.

prompt: Which status code does FastAPI return when request data fails validation?
optionA: 422 Unprocessable Content
optionB: 500 Internal Server Error
optionC: 400 Bad Request
optionD: 409 Conflict
correctAnswerText: 422 Unprocessable Content
explanation: Measured: a non-integer path id returned 422 with a detail list. You can change that with a custom exception handler, but 422 is the default.

prompt: What does response_model=UserOut on a route decorator do?
optionA: Validates and filters the output to UserOut's fields
optionB: Validates the request body against UserOut's fields
optionC: Stores the returned object in a database table
optionD: Sets the response status code to match UserOut
correctAnswerText: Validates and filters the output to UserOut's fields
explanation: The return value is validated against UserOut and serialized with only its fields, and the schema appears in the OpenAPI docs.

prompt: Which FastAPI function declares that a parameter is supplied by another callable, such as get_db?
optionA: Provide
optionB: Depends
optionC: Resolve
optionD: Inject
correctAnswerText: Depends
explanation: db = Depends(get_db) tells FastAPI to call get_db for each request (with its own parameters resolved the same way) and pass the result in.

prompt: In current FastAPI, what is the recommended way to run startup and shutdown code?
optionA: Code placed at the top of the first route
optionB: An async context manager passed as lifespan=
optionC: A middleware that checks for the first request
optionD: Functions decorated with @app.on_event only
correctAnswerText: An async context manager passed as lifespan=
explanation: Code before the yield runs at startup and code after it at shutdown. on_event handlers still work but are deprecated in favour of lifespan.

prompt: Which class lets a pytest test call a FastAPI app without starting a server?
optionA: uvicorn.TestRunner
optionB: fastapi.testing.MockServer
optionC: pytest.HttpClient
optionD: fastapi.testclient.TestClient
correctAnswerText: fastapi.testclient.TestClient
explanation: TestClient wraps the ASGI app with an httpx-style interface, so client.get('/items') runs the app in-process.

prompt: Which app attribute lets a test swap a dependency for a fake one?
optionA: app.dependency_overrides
optionB: app.state.dependencies
optionC: app.extra_dependencies
optionD: app.router.mocks
correctAnswerText: app.dependency_overrides
explanation: It is a dict from the original dependency callable to its replacement; clear it after the test.

prompt: Which response class sends a body built from a generator, piece by piece, as it is produced?
optionA: StreamingResponse
optionB: FileResponse
optionC: RedirectResponse
optionD: JSONResponse
correctAnswerText: StreamingResponse
explanation: StreamingResponse iterates a sync or async generator and writes each chunk to the client as it arrives, which is how token streaming works.

prompt: In Pydantic v2, which method turns a model instance into a plain dict?
optionA: dict()
optionB: model_dump()
optionC: to_dict()
optionD: as_json()
correctAnswerText: model_dump()
explanation: v2 renamed .dict() to model_dump() and .json() to model_dump_json(); the old names are deprecated.

prompt: How does FastAPI run a route written with plain def rather than async def?
optionA: It refuses plain def routes and raises at startup
optionB: On the event loop, exactly like an async def route
optionC: In a thread pool, so blocking calls do not stall the loop
optionD: In a new process that is started for each request
correctAnswerText: In a thread pool, so blocking calls do not stall the loop
explanation: Sync routes are sent to a worker thread. async def routes run on the event loop itself, so they must only await, never block.

prompt: In a dependency that does db = Session(); yield db; db.close(), when does db.close() run?
optionA: After the route finishes handling the request
optionB: Before the route function is ever called
optionC: Never, since code after yield is skipped
optionD: Only when the application shuts down
correctAnswerText: After the route finishes handling the request
explanation: FastAPI injects the yielded value, runs the route, then resumes the generator for cleanup, which makes yield dependencies the place for per-request resources.

prompt: Why do FastAPI projects usually define UserIn and UserOut instead of a single User model?
optionA: Pydantic cannot reuse a single model for two routes
optionB: Input needs a password that output must never include
optionC: FastAPI requires the two names to build its docs
optionD: Output models are faster because they skip checks
correctAnswerText: Input needs a password that output must never include
explanation: Input and output differ: a password goes in, an id and created time come out. Separate models make leaking a field a type error rather than a habit.

prompt: A 422 response body contains "loc": ["path", "item_id"]. What does that tell the client?
optionA: The item_id route was not found, so the path is wrong
optionB: The client must resend item_id in the JSON body instead
optionC: The item_id path parameter is where validation failed
optionD: The server failed while loading the item from the path
correctAnswerText: The item_id path parameter is where validation failed
explanation: loc names the source (path, query, body, header) and the field. Measured: /items/abc gave loc [path, item_id] with type int_parsing.

prompt: Why should every outbound HTTP call from an API route carry a timeout?
optionA: So the response is cached for the length of the timeout
optionB: So a slow upstream cannot hold your request open indefinitely
optionC: So the upstream server knows how fast to send its response
optionD: So FastAPI can retry the call automatically when it fails
correctAnswerText: So a slow upstream cannot hold your request open indefinitely
explanation: Without a bound, a hung dependency ties up your workers and connections until your own service stops answering. The timeout is how your API fails fast instead.

prompt: Two sub-dependencies of one route both use Depends(get_current_user). How many times is get_current_user called per request?
optionA: It depends on the order the routes were declared
optionB: Once; the result is cached for that request
optionC: Twice; once for each sub-dependency that uses it
optionD: Once per application, then reused for every request
correctAnswerText: Once; the result is cached for that request
explanation: Measured: a counter in a shared dependency moved by 1. Pass use_cache=False to Depends if a dependency truly must run each time.

prompt: What does auto_error=True (the default) on HTTPBearer do when the Authorization header is missing?
optionA: Calls the route with the credentials set to None
optionB: Rejects the request before the route runs, with 401
optionC: Logs a warning and lets the request through as is
optionD: Redirects the client to the OpenAPI login page
correctAnswerText: Rejects the request before the route runs, with 401
explanation: Measured on current FastAPI: 401 "Not authenticated" with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer. Older versions sent 403. auto_error=False hands you None instead.

prompt: For Server-Sent Events, how must each event be framed in the response body?
optionA: A data: line ending in a blank line, as text/event-stream
optionB: One JSON object per chunk, sent as application/json
optionC: A length prefix and then the bytes, as octet-stream
optionD: An HTML script tag per event, sent as text/html
correctAnswerText: A data: line ending in a blank line, as text/event-stream
explanation:
The browser's EventSource splits events on a blank line and reads data: fields. Measured: the stream body was "data: Hel

data: lo

".

prompt: Why must /users/me be declared before /users/{user_id} in a FastAPI app?
optionA: FastAPI sorts routes by length and longer ones match last
optionB: Routes are matched in declaration order, first match wins
optionC: Path parameters are ignored when a fixed path is declared
optionD: Fixed paths only work when declared before the app starts
correctAnswerText: Routes are matched in declaration order, first match wins
explanation: The first matching route handles the request. With {user_id} first, "me" goes to it and fails int validation.

prompt: Compared with Django, what does FastAPI deliberately leave for you to choose and wire up?
optionA: Request validation and the OpenAPI documentation
optionB: Serialization of return values into JSON
optionC: The ORM, migrations, admin and user management
optionD: Routing of HTTP methods and paths to functions
correctAnswerText: The ORM, migrations, admin and user management
explanation: FastAPI is a thin, typed API layer: validation and docs are built in, while database, migrations, admin and auth are libraries you add.

optionA: {"skip": 0, "limit": 5}
optionB: {"skip": 5, "limit": 10}
optionC: {"skip": 0, "limit": 10}
optionD: 422, since skip is missing
correctAnswerText: {"skip": 0, "limit": 5}
explanation: Measured. Parameters with defaults are optional query parameters; limit is converted from the string "5" to an int.

prompt: A product's price must be greater than zero, rejected with 422 otherwise. How do you declare it?
optionA: price: float = Field(min=0)
optionB: price: PositiveOnly[float]
optionC: price: float = Field(gt=0)
optionD: price: float = 0 if price > 0
correctAnswerText: price: float = Field(gt=0)
explanation: Field(gt=0) adds a greater-than constraint; measured, price 0 returned 422. ge=0 would allow zero. There is no min keyword.

prompt: A create endpoint should answer 201 instead of FastAPI's default 200. What is the simplest way?
optionA: return {'status': 201, 'item': item}
optionB: raise HTTPException(status_code=201)
optionC: @app.post('/items', status_code=201)
optionD: @app.post('/items', response_code=201)
correctAnswerText: @app.post('/items', status_code=201)
explanation: status_code on the decorator sets the success code and documents it. A status key inside the body leaves the actual status at 200.

prompt: get_item looks up an id that does not exist. How should the route respond with 404?
optionA: return HTTPException(status_code=404, detail='Not found')
optionB: raise ValueError('404 Not found') and let it bubble up
optionC: raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail='Not found')
optionD: return {'error': 'Not found', 'status_code': 404}
correctAnswerText: raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail='Not found')
explanation: HTTPException must be raised, not returned. Returning a dict gives 200, and an unhandled ValueError becomes a 500.

prompt: Internal services must send an X-API-Key header on every call to an endpoint. Which declaration reads it?
optionA: key = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl='X-API-Key')
optionB: key = APIKeyHeader(name='X-API-Key'), then Depends(key)
optionC: key = HTTPBearer(name='X-API-Key'), then Depends(key)
optionD: def route(x_api_key: str): with no other declaration
correctAnswerText: key = APIKeyHeader(name='X-API-Key'), then Depends(key)
explanation: APIKeyHeader reads the named header and documents it in OpenAPI. A bare str parameter is a query parameter, and HTTPBearer reads Authorization only.

prompt: An async def route must call a weather API without blocking the event loop. Which code fits?
optionA: r = httpx.get(url, timeout=5) inside the async def route body
optionB: r = asyncio.run(httpx.AsyncClient().get(url)) inside the route
optionC: async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5) as c: r = await c.get(url)
optionD: r = requests.get(url, timeout=5) inside the async def route
correctAnswerText: async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5) as c: r = await c.get(url)
explanation: AsyncClient awaits the network, letting the loop serve others. httpx.get and requests.get block, and asyncio.run cannot start inside a running loop.

prompt: Routes use Depends(get_db). A test should give them a fake database. Which line does that?
optionA: app.state.db = fake_db before creating TestClient
optionB: app.dependency_overrides['get_db'] = fake_db
optionC: get_db = lambda: fake_db at the top of the test
optionD: app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = lambda: fake_db
correctAnswerText: app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = lambda: fake_db
explanation: The key is the dependency function object and the value is a callable returning the replacement (measured). Rebinding the name in the test module changes nothing the app holds.

prompt: A 2 GB embedding model should load once when the server starts and be shared by all requests. Where does the load go?
optionA: Inside each route, so every request gets a fresh copy
optionB: In a background task started by the first request only
optionC: In a yield dependency, loaded and released per request
optionD: Before the yield in a lifespan handler, kept on app.state
correctAnswerText: Before the yield in a lifespan handler, kept on app.state
explanation: Lifespan runs once per process before traffic; app.state makes the object reachable from routes. Loading per request would repeat the 2 GB load every time.

prompt: An async generator gen() yields "data: <token>\n\n" strings from an LLM. How does the route stream them as SSE?
optionA: return JSONResponse(list(gen()), media_type='text/event-stream')
optionB: return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type='text/event-stream')
optionC: return [t async for t in gen()] with response_model=list[str]
optionD: return StreamingResponse(gen, media_type='application/json')
correctAnswerText: return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type='text/event-stream')
explanation: StreamingResponse takes the generator object and the SSE media type (measured: text/event-stream). Collecting into a list waits for the whole answer first.

prompt: A route only calls a synchronous PDF library that takes two seconds. How should the route be written?
optionA: As a plain def route, so it runs in the thread pool
optionB: As async def, calling the library directly inside it
optionC: As async def, wrapping the call in asyncio.run(...)
optionD: As async def, with await placed before the library call
correctAnswerText: As a plain def route, so it runs in the thread pool
explanation: A plain def route keeps the blocking work off the event loop. You cannot await a sync function, and calling it inside async def stalls every other request.

optionA: The four requests share one TCP connection that is serialised
optionB: time.sleep blocks the event loop, so requests run one by one
optionC: async routes always run slower than sync routes in FastAPI
optionD: Uvicorn allows only one async route to run at any one time
correctAnswerText: time.sleep blocks the event loop, so requests run one by one
explanation: Measured: 2.01 s for the async def with time.sleep, 0.54 s as plain def, 0.51 s with await asyncio.sleep. Blocking inside async def stalls everyone.

optionA: 200 from me(), the more specific route
optionB: 422, because "me" is not a valid int
optionC: 405, because two routes share one path
optionD: 404, because no route matched exactly
correctAnswerText: 422, because "me" is not a valid int
explanation: Measured: 422. The parameter route matches first and then fails validation; FastAPI does not go on to try later routes. Declare /users/me first.

optionA: A plain str is read from the query, not the JSON body
optionB: The JSON must be sent as form data for a str field
optionC: POST routes cannot take parameters of type str at all
optionD: FastAPI needs the field to be named body to read it
correctAnswerText: A plain str is read from the query, not the JSON body
explanation: Measured: the error loc was [query, name]. Use a Pydantic model, or name: str = Body(embed=True), to read it from the body.

optionA: {"name": "...", "password": "..."} unchanged
optionB: A 422 error, since password is not in UserOut
optionC: A 500 error, since the dict has an extra key
optionD: {"name": "..."}, the password filtered out
correctAnswerText: {"name": "..."}, the password filtered out
explanation: Measured: only name came back. response_model filters output to its fields, which is exactly why it is the safety net against leaking secrets.

prompt: Code copied from an old tutorial has class Config: orm_mode = True. Under Pydantic v2 it warns, and reading from ORM objects fails. What is the fix?
optionA: model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)
optionB: Install pydantic[orm] to restore the old option
optionC: class Config: orm_mode = 'enabled' as a string
optionD: Call model.dict() on the ORM object before use
correctAnswerText: model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)
explanation: Reproduced: v2 warns that orm_mode was renamed to from_attributes and that class-based Config is deprecated. Then use Model.model_validate(obj).

prompt: A test writes app.dependency_overrides[get_db()] = lambda: fake_db, but routes still receive the real database. Why?
optionA: Overrides do not apply to dependencies that use yield
optionB: The lambda must be an async function to be accepted
optionC: Overrides only take effect after the app is restarted
optionD: The key must be get_db itself, not the result of calling it
correctAnswerText: The key must be get_db itself, not the result of calling it
explanation: Reproduced: keyed by get_db() (a generator object) the real value came back; keyed by get_db the fake did. The dict is looked up by the function.

prompt:
def get_db():
    db = Session()
    yield db
    db.close()
Connections leak, but only on requests where the route raised HTTPException. Why?
optionA: HTTPException closes the session before the dependency does
optionB: Yield dependencies are not resumed for any non-200 response
optionC: The exception is thrown in at yield, so close() is skipped
optionD: close() runs, but only after the server process has exited
correctAnswerText: The exception is thrown in at yield, so close() is skipped
explanation: Reproduced: cleanup ran after a normal request but not after one that raised. Put the cleanup in try: yield db / finally: db.close().

prompt: A route depends on HTTPBearer(). A client calls it with no Authorization header. On current FastAPI, what does it get?
optionA: 403 Forbidden, with a body of Not authenticated
optionB: 200, with the credentials argument set to None
optionC: 401 Not authenticated, with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer
optionD: 422, with a validation error for the header field
correctAnswerText: 401 Not authenticated, with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer
explanation: Measured on FastAPI 0.143: 401 plus the challenge header. Older releases returned 403, so tutorials disagree. None arrives only with auto_error=False.

prompt: A route calls an upstream report API with httpx.AsyncClient() and no timeout argument. The report takes 8 seconds and the route fails with httpx.ReadTimeout. Why?
optionA: The upstream closed the socket because no timeout was sent
optionB: AsyncClient waits forever, so the server killed the route
optionC: Uvicorn cancels any outbound request after 5 seconds
optionD: httpx has a 5-second default timeout unless you set one
correctAnswerText: httpx has a 5-second default timeout unless you set one
explanation: Checked: httpx.Client().timeout is Timeout(5.0). Unlike requests, httpx is bounded by default; pass a timeout that fits the upstream, deliberately.

prompt: The lifespan handler sets app.state.model. A test does client = TestClient(app) and the route finds no model. What is wrong?
optionA: app.state is cleared before each request made in tests
optionB: Lifespan runs only when TestClient is used in a with block
optionC: The test must call app.startup() before every request
optionD: Lifespan only runs under Uvicorn, never in any test
correctAnswerText: Lifespan runs only when TestClient is used in a with block
explanation: Reproduced: without with the model was None; inside with TestClient(app) as client it was loaded. The context manager drives startup and shutdown.

prompt: A college needs a staff portal (admin screens, roles, reports) and a separate service that serves an ML model. Which pairing fits?
optionA: Django for the portal, FastAPI for the model service
optionB: Django for both, with the model loaded inside each view
optionC: FastAPI for both, building an admin panel from scratch
optionD: FastAPI for the portal, Django for the model service
correctAnswerText: Django for the portal, FastAPI for the model service
explanation: Django ships the admin, auth and ORM the portal needs. A small async FastAPI service with lifespan-loaded models suits inference.

prompt: A team uses a synchronous database driver and writes every route as async def "because async is faster". Your verdict?
optionA: Wrong: FastAPI only supports async drivers anyway
optionB: Right, as long as the server runs four Uvicorn workers
optionC: Wrong: use def routes, or switch to an async driver
optionD: Right: async def makes any database driver faster
correctAnswerText: Wrong: use def routes, or switch to an async driver
explanation: Blocking calls inside async def serialize the worker. Either let FastAPI thread-pool them with def, or go async end to end with an async driver.

prompt: A service is called by another backend and by thousands of end users. How should the two be authenticated?
optionA: One shared API key, embedded in the users' mobile apps
optionB: Per-user bearer tokens for both, with no key for servers
optionC: No auth for the backend, since it sits inside the network
optionD: API key for the backend, per-user bearer tokens for users
correctAnswerText: API key for the backend, per-user bearer tokens for users
explanation: A key identifies a trusted service and can be rotated; users need their own expiring identity. A key shipped in an app is public the day it is released.

prompt: A chat page streams an LLM answer to the browser; the user's question is sent once per turn. SSE or WebSocket?
optionA: SSE: one-way over plain HTTP is all that is needed
optionB: Neither: poll the server every 100 ms for new tokens
optionC: WebSocket: SSE cannot send text to a browser at all
optionD: WebSocket: SSE responses must fit in one TCP packet
correctAnswerText: SSE: one-way over plain HTTP is all that is needed
explanation: The server-to-client stream is one direction and each question is an ordinary POST. SSE works through proxies and auth as plain HTTP; WebSockets earn their place with two-way traffic.

prompt: A busy route calls the same upstream on every request. Where should the httpx.AsyncClient live?
optionA: A module-level client that is never closed or cleaned up
optionB: One client created in lifespan and reused by requests
optionC: A new client per request, closed at the end of each one
optionD: A new client per call, so retries never share a socket
correctAnswerText: One client created in lifespan and reused by requests
explanation: A shared client reuses pooled connections and TLS sessions; creating one per request pays the handshake every time. Lifespan also closes it cleanly.

prompt: To test routes without the real payment gateway, which approach holds up best?
optionA: Inject the gateway via Depends and override it in tests
optionB: Patch the gateway module's internals with monkeypatch
optionC: Skip route tests and only test the helper functions
optionD: Call the real gateway and refund each charge afterwards
correctAnswerText: Inject the gateway via Depends and override it in tests
explanation: A dependency is a declared seam: overriding it survives refactors inside the gateway code. Patching internals breaks when names move, and live calls are slow and risky.

prompt: A teammate wants one User model for input, database and output to "avoid duplication". What is the main risk?
optionA: The OpenAPI docs will list every endpoint under one model
optionB: Pydantic will refuse to validate one model for two purposes
optionC: Responses get slower because the model is larger than needed
optionD: Fields like password_hash or is_admin leak or become writable
correctAnswerText: Fields like password_hash or is_admin leak or become writable
explanation: One model means clients can send is_admin and receive the hash. Small duplication between UserIn and UserOut buys a hard boundary.

prompt: An LLM provider sometimes times out. Which retry policy for the route's outbound call is sound?
optionA: No timeout and unlimited retries until the call succeeds
optionB: Immediate retries in a tight loop for up to one minute
optionC: Retry every failed call, including 400 and 401 responses
optionD: A timeout, a few retries with backoff, then a clear error
correctAnswerText: A timeout, a few retries with backoff, then a clear error
explanation: Bounded retries with backoff ride out blips without hammering a struggling provider. 4xx errors will not fix themselves, and unbounded retries hang your own users.

prompt: A route takes a dict and checks keys and types by hand with if statements. Why move that into a Pydantic model?
optionA: Pydantic stores the request so it can be replayed
optionB: Uniform 422 errors, typed data and documented schemas
optionC: Pydantic checks run on the client before the request
optionD: Manual checks are not allowed inside FastAPI routes
correctAnswerText: Uniform 422 errors, typed data and documented schemas
explanation: Declaring the shape once gives consistent error bodies, converted types and an OpenAPI schema. Hand checks drift and miss cases.

prompt: Opening the database pool at module import instead of in lifespan. What is the main drawback?
optionA: Python forbids network calls while a module is importing
optionB: Module-level code runs again before every single request
optionC: Connections opened at import can never be used by routes
optionD: Merely importing the app, as tests do, opens connections
correctAnswerText: Merely importing the app, as tests do, opens connections
explanation: Import-time side effects fire in tests, tooling and every worker with no clean shutdown. Lifespan ties opening and closing to the server's actual start and stop.

prompt: Which suffix turns the numeric literal 19.99 into a decimal value in C#?
optionA: L, as in 19.99L
optionB: d, as in 19.99d
optionC: f, as in 19.99f
optionD: m, as in 19.99m
correctAnswerText: m, as in 19.99m
explanation: The m suffix marks a decimal literal. d marks a double (the default for a literal with a point), f marks a float, and L marks a long and is not valid on a literal with a fraction.

prompt: The C# keyword int is an alias for which .NET type?
optionA: System.Int32
optionB: System.Number
optionC: System.Integer
optionD: System.Int64
correctAnswerText: System.Int32
explanation: int is always the 32-bit System.Int32, whatever the platform; long is System.Int64. .NET has no System.Integer or System.Number type.

prompt: Which C# operator gives a fallback value when the expression on its left is null?
optionA: ?. — the null-conditional operator
optionB: ?: — the conditional (ternary) operator
optionC: ?? — the null-coalescing operator
optionD: ! — the null-forgiving operator
correctAnswerText: ?? — the null-coalescing operator
explanation: a ?? b returns a when it is not null and b otherwise. ?. skips a member access on null, ?: chooses on a bool, and ! only silences a nullable warning.

prompt: Which keyword declares a local value that is fixed at compile time and can never be reassigned?
optionA: static
optionB: sealed
optionC: fixed
optionD: const
correctAnswerText: const
explanation: const declares a compile-time constant, such as const double Gst = 0.18;. static means "belongs to the type", sealed stops inheritance, and fixed pins memory in unsafe code.

prompt: Which method turns a string into an int and reports bad input with a bool instead of throwing?
optionA: Int32.Format
optionB: int.Parse
optionC: Convert.ToInt32
optionD: int.TryParse
correctAnswerText: int.TryParse
explanation: int.TryParse returns false and sets its out value to 0 when the text is not a number. int.Parse and Convert.ToInt32 throw FormatException; Int32.Format does not exist.

prompt: Which class, in the System.Text namespace, builds up text in a mutable buffer?
optionA: StringBuilder
optionB: StringWriter
optionC: StringReader
optionD: StringBuffer
correctAnswerText: StringBuilder
explanation: System.Text.StringBuilder appends into a growable buffer. StringWriter and StringReader live in System.IO, and StringBuffer is the Java class of that name.

prompt: Which parameter modifier passes a variable by reference and requires it to be assigned before the call?
optionA: ref
optionB: this
optionC: params
optionD: out
correctAnswerText: ref
explanation: ref passes the variable itself and the caller must initialise it first. out also passes by reference but the method must assign it; params gathers arguments into an array.

prompt: Which C# loop always runs its body at least once, even when its condition is false from the start?
optionA: while (condition) { ... }
optionB: foreach (var item in items) { ... }
optionC: for (init; condition; step) { ... }
optionD: do { ... } while (condition);
correctAnswerText: do { ... } while (condition);
explanation: do-while tests its condition after the body, so the body runs once before the first test. while, for and foreach all test (or check for an element) before each pass.

prompt: After bool[] flags = new bool[4]; what does each element hold?
optionA: false
optionB: true
optionC: null
optionD: Nothing — reading one is a compile error
correctAnswerText: false
explanation: Array elements start at their type's default value: 0 for numbers, false for bool and null for references. Only local variables must be assigned before they are read.

prompt: Which member gives the number of elements in a C# array such as int[] marks?
optionA: marks.Size
optionB: marks.Count
optionC: marks.Length
optionD: marks.length()
correctAnswerText: marks.Length
explanation: Arrays expose a Length property. Count is the property on List<T>, Size does not exist, and C# member names are PascalCase, so length() is not a member at all.

prompt: Why is a variable declared with var still statically typed in C#?
optionA: var is only allowed for string and int variables
optionB: The runtime checks its type again on every assignment
optionC: var variables may only ever hold the type object
optionD: The compiler fixes its type from the initialiser, once
correctAnswerText: The compiler fixes its type from the initialiser, once
explanation: var asks the compiler to infer the type from the right-hand side at compile time. From then on the variable has that type exactly as if it had been written out.

prompt: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 false for double operands yet true when all three are decimal?
optionA: The compiler folds decimal constants but not double ones
optionB: double stores binary fractions; decimal stores base-10 digits
optionC: double comparison checks references instead of the values
optionD: decimal has fewer digits, so it rounds both sides the same
correctAnswerText: double stores binary fractions; decimal stores base-10 digits
explanation: 0.1 has no exact binary representation, so each double is a close approximation and the sum misses 0.3 slightly. decimal stores base-10 digits, so 0.1m, 0.2m and 0.3m are exact.

prompt: What does assignment copy for a value type such as double, compared with a reference type such as an array?
optionA: The value itself, versus a reference to one shared object
optionB: A reference to the value, versus a full copy of the array
optionC: A deep copy for both, so the two never affect each other
optionD: Nothing for either — both keep pointing at the original
correctAnswerText: The value itself, versus a reference to one shared object
explanation: A value-type variable holds its value, so assignment copies it. An array variable holds a reference, so after b = a both names reach the same array object.

prompt: Why is if (s != null && s.Length > 0) safe to run when s is null?
optionA: && skips its right side once the left side is false
optionB: && evaluates both sides but ignores any exception
optionC: Length returns 0 on a null string rather than throwing
optionD: The compiler removes s.Length when s could be null
correctAnswerText: && skips its right side once the left side is false
explanation: && short-circuits: when s != null is false the whole condition must be false, so s.Length is never evaluated and no NullReferenceException can occur.

prompt: What actually happens in memory when code runs report += line; on a string variable?
optionA: A new string is built and report now refers to it
optionB: The old string is resized to make room for line
optionC: line is appended into the existing string in place
optionD: report becomes a StringBuilder behind the scenes
correctAnswerText: A new string is built and report now refers to it
explanation: Strings are immutable, so += allocates a new string holding both parts and repoints the variable. In a long loop that copying is what makes StringBuilder worthwhile.

prompt: How does an out parameter differ from a ref parameter in what the compiler enforces?
optionA: out must be assigned by the method; ref must be set by the caller
optionB: out is read-only inside the method; ref may be changed by it
optionC: out may only be used for strings; ref works for any type at all
optionD: out is passed by value; ref is passed by reference to the method
correctAnswerText: out must be assigned by the method; ref must be set by the caller
explanation: Both pass the variable by reference. For ref the caller must initialise it before the call; for out the method must assign it on every path before returning.

prompt: What does declaring a variable as double? rather than double let it represent?
optionA: A double that can never be changed once it is set
optionB: A double that is checked for overflow on arithmetic
optionC: Values larger than a plain double is able to hold
optionD: The absence of a value, alongside every normal double
correctAnswerText: The absence of a value, alongside every normal double
explanation: double? is Nullable<double>: it holds any double or null. That lets "no reading yet" be told apart from a real 0.0 without a magic sentinel value.

prompt: Why does adding 1 to int.MaxValue at run time produce a negative number instead of an error?
optionA: Integer arithmetic is unchecked by default, so it wraps
optionB: int silently widens to long whenever a sum grows too big
optionC: The runtime clamps the result to the int.MinValue limit
optionD: Overflow is only detected when compiling in Debug mode
correctAnswerText: Integer arithmetic is unchecked by default, so it wraps
explanation: C# integer arithmetic runs unchecked unless you use checked(...), a checked block or the CheckForOverflowUnderflow project setting. Unchecked overflow wraps around to int.MinValue.

prompt: A Java developer asks what == compares when both operands are C# strings. What is the right answer?
optionA: The hash codes, which can collide for different text
optionB: The references, so equal text built twice gives false
optionC: Only the lengths, unless the strings were interned
optionD: The characters — string overloads == to compare content
correctAnswerText: The characters — string overloads == to compare content
explanation: System.String overloads == to call String.Equals, an ordinal comparison of the characters. Unlike Java, two separately built strings with the same text are == in C#.

prompt: static int Sum(params int[] xs) can be called as Sum(4, 5, 6). How does that work?
optionA: The method is overloaded once per number of arguments
optionB: The compiler packs the arguments into a new int array
optionC: params turns the three arguments into a List<int> instead
optionD: The runtime splits a single argument into three values
correctAnswerText: The compiler packs the arguments into a new int array
explanation: params is a compile-time convenience: the call site builds new int[] { 4, 5, 6 } and passes it. Inside the method xs is an ordinary array, empty when no arguments are given.

prompt: What does Console.WriteLine(10 / 4 * 4.0); print?
explanation: Evaluation is left to right: 10 / 4 is int division and gives 2, then 2 * 4.0 is 8.0, which Console prints as 8. The fraction was lost before the double ever appeared.

optionD: It throws, because a[2] was never assigned
explanation: A new int array is filled with zeros, so a[2] is 0, and Length is 5. 0 + 5 prints 5.
Indexes start at 0: the first e is at 4 and the last at 6. Both methods return int, so + adds them to 10 rather than joining text.

prompt: What does Console.WriteLine(Math.Round(2.5) + Math.Round(3.5)); print?
explanation: Math.Round uses MidpointRounding.ToEven by default: 2.5 rounds to 2 and 3.5 rounds to 4, giving 6. Pass MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero for school-style rounding.
i takes 10, 7, 4 and 1, then becomes -2 and the loop stops. 10 + 7 + 4 + 1 is 22.
ref passes n itself, so each call doubles the caller's variable: 3 becomes 6, then 12. Without ref, n would still be 3.

optionB: cba
optionD: abc
correctAnswerText: cba
explanation: Each character is put in front of what has been built so far: "a", then "ba", then "cba". char + string is string concatenation, not numeric addition, because one operand is a string.
