optionC: It throws InvalidOperationException
explanation: Arithmetic on nullable values is lifted: if either operand is null the result is null. p + q is null, so ?? supplies 0.

prompt: What does Console.WriteLine('5' - '0' + 1); print?
explanation: chars are promoted to int for arithmetic: '5' is 53 and '0' is 48, so the difference is 5 and adding 1 gives 6. This is the usual way to turn a digit character into its value.

prompt: What does Console.WriteLine(int.Parse("2024-10-21".Split('-')[1]) + 1); print?
explanation: Split('-') gives { "2024", "10", "21" }; index 1 is "10". int.Parse makes it the number 10, so + 1 is arithmetic and prints 11.

optionA: count must be declared as long for a division to be exact
optionB: double cannot hold 3.5 exactly, so it is rounded down
optionC: Console.WriteLine drops the fraction of any double value
optionD: sum / count is int division; it is widened only afterwards
correctAnswerText: sum / count is int division; it is widened only afterwards
explanation: Both operands are int, so the division happens in int and gives 3; only then is 3 converted to double. Cast one operand first: (double)sum / count gives 3.5.

optionA: Length throws on any string that has no characters
optionB: A null string cannot be compared with == at all
optionC: name == null is false, so the right side must run
optionD: | always evaluates both sides; only || stops early
correctAnswerText: | always evaluates both sides; only || stops early
explanation: On bools, | is the non-short-circuit OR: it evaluates name.Length even though name == null is already true. With || the right side would be skipped and "empty" printed.

prompt: A menu checks if (choice == "Exit") and users who type exit stay in the loop. What is wrong, and what fixes it?
optionA: Strings need .Equals; == never works on string variables
optionB: ReadLine adds a newline; compare against "Exit\n" instead
optionC: == is case-sensitive; use OrdinalIgnoreCase in string.Equals
optionD: == compares references; call choice.CompareTo("Exit") instead
correctAnswerText: == is case-sensitive; use OrdinalIgnoreCase in string.Equals
explanation: String == compares characters exactly, so "exit" is not "Exit". string.Equals(choice, "Exit", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ignores case. ReadLine already strips the line ending.

prompt:
for (byte b = 0; b < 256; b++) { ... }
The compiler warns and the loop never ends. Why?
optionA: byte loop counters are read-only inside a for statement
optionB: A byte is always below 256; b++ at 255 wraps back to 0
optionC: b++ on a byte throws OverflowException at 255 each time
optionD: The condition b < 256 is converted to false at compile time
correctAnswerText: A byte is always below 256; b++ at 255 wraps back to 0
explanation: byte holds 0 to 255, so b < 256 is always true (warning CS0652 says the comparison is useless). Unchecked b++ at 255 wraps to 0 and the loop starts over.

optionA: Replace is case-insensitive, so it found nothing to change
optionB: Replace changes msg only once the next statement has run
optionC: Replace returns a new string, and the result was thrown away
optionD: Replace only changes text when called with char arguments
correctAnswerText: Replace returns a new string, and the result was thrown away
explanation: Strings are immutable: Replace builds and returns a new string and leaves msg untouched. Write msg = msg.Replace("STUDENT", "Asha"); to keep the result.

prompt:
for (double d = 0; d != 1.0; d += 0.1) { ... }
This loop runs forever. What is going on?
optionA: d += 0.1 is integer arithmetic, so d stays at zero forever
optionB: Ten additions of 0.1 give 0.9999999999999999, never 1.0
optionC: A double loop variable is reset to 0 on each iteration
optionD: != is not defined for double, so the test is always true
correctAnswerText: Ten additions of 0.1 give 0.9999999999999999, never 1.0
explanation: 0.1 is approximate in binary, and summing it ten times lands just below 1.0, so d != 1.0 stays true as d moves past 1. Loop on an int counter, or test d < 1.0.

optionA: ArgumentException — Split needs a count for three fields
optionB: city is an empty string, because Split pads the array
optionC: IndexOutOfRangeException — the array has only 2 elements
optionD: city is null, since a missing field is filled with null
correctAnswerText: IndexOutOfRangeException — the array has only 2 elements
explanation: Split returns exactly as many parts as the text has fields: { "Asha", "21" }. Index 2 is past the end of an array, which throws IndexOutOfRangeException. Check parts.Length first.

prompt: A fee import calls int.Parse("1,200") and fails. What is thrown, and why?
optionA: FormatException — the default style rejects thousands commas
optionB: InvalidCastException — a comma makes the text a decimal
optionC: ArgumentNullException — the comma splits it into two parts
optionD: OverflowException — 1,200 is read as a value too large
correctAnswerText: FormatException — the default style rejects thousands commas
explanation: int.Parse(string) uses NumberStyles.Integer: optional whitespace and sign only. A thousands separator is not allowed, so it throws FormatException. NumberStyles.AllowThousands accepts it.

prompt: A factorial method keeps its running product in an int. Factorial(15) returns 2004310016, which is not 15!. Why?
optionA: The method returned an uninitialised local variable value
optionB: 15! exceeds int.MaxValue and the int product wrapped silently
optionC: The loop stopped early, because i <= n should be i < n
optionD: int multiplication rounds large results to the nearest even
correctAnswerText: 15! exceeds int.MaxValue and the int product wrapped silently
explanation: An int product overflows after 12!; the result keeps wrapping without an error, giving a plausible-looking wrong number. Use long (good to 20!) and checked arithmetic to make overflow loud.

optionA: b is formatted first and then a, so the digits are reversed
optionB: Console.WriteLine joins all of its arguments without spaces
optionC: + runs left to right; once a string appears, each + concatenates
optionD: int values are always converted to text before any addition
correctAnswerText: + runs left to right; once a string appears, each + concatenates
explanation: "Total: " + a is a string, so adding b appends "3" rather than adding 3. Write "Total: " + (a + b), or use interpolation $"Total: {a + b}" (C# 6).

prompt: At startup an app reads the port number from its own settings file, and it cannot run without a valid port. Which parsing choice fits best?
optionA: Convert.ToInt32, since it turns a missing value into 0
optionB: int.TryParse, quietly falling back to port 0 when it fails
optionC: int.Parse — a bad value is a defect, so failing at once is right
optionD: A try/catch around int.Parse that logs and keeps running
correctAnswerText: int.Parse — a bad value is a defect, so failing at once is right
explanation: TryParse is for input that is expected to be wrong sometimes, like user typing. A required setting that does not parse is a configuration bug; failing fast at startup surfaces it before any request is served.

prompt: A lab simulation processes millions of sensor temperatures and computes averages and square roots. Which type should hold the readings?
optionA: double — fast hardware maths for approximate measurements
optionB: string — store the raw text so that no precision is ever lost
optionC: decimal — exact base-10 digits are always the safest choice
optionD: int — whole degrees avoid every floating-point rounding issue
correctAnswerText: double — fast hardware maths for approximate measurements
explanation: Measurements are already approximate, and double is fast and has Math functions such as Math.Sqrt. decimal is the right call for money, where base-10 exactness matters, but it is slower here for no gain.

prompt: In code review, which use of var most hurts readability?
optionA: var names = new List<string>();
optionB: var result = processor.Run(input);
optionC: var price = 499.00m;
optionD: var count = 10;
correctAnswerText: var result = processor.Run(input);
explanation: var is clearest when the type is obvious from the right-hand side, as with new List<string>() or a suffixed literal. Run(input) says nothing about what it returns, so a reader must go and look.

prompt: A method builds one greeting from a first name, a last name and a city. A reviewer insists on StringBuilder. Which response is best?
optionA: Disagree — StringBuilder cannot hold more than two pieces
optionB: Agree — StringBuilder is faster for any number of pieces
optionC: Interpolation is fine here; StringBuilder pays off in long loops
optionD: Agree — + on strings is deprecated in .NET 8 code
correctAnswerText: Interpolation is fine here; StringBuilder pays off in long loops
explanation: A handful of fixed pieces is compiled into a single concatenation, so there is nothing to gain. StringBuilder earns its place when text is appended many times, typically in a loop.

prompt: A loop sums order amounts in rupees into an int, and the yearly total now passes 2.1 billion. Which fix is best?
optionA: Use double, since a double total can never overflow
optionB: Make the total a decimal: it is money and has the range
optionC: Cast the final int total to long just before printing
optionD: Wrap the sum in checked so it throws when it overflows
correctAnswerText: Make the total a decimal: it is money and has the range
explanation: The type should fit the domain: money belongs in decimal, which is exact and holds far larger totals. checked only turns a wrong number into a crash, a late cast widens an already wrong value, and double drifts.

prompt: A method must return both the lowest and the highest mark in an array. In C# 7 or later, which design reads best at the call site?
optionA: Return a named tuple such as (int Min, int Max)
optionB: Use two out parameters and return nothing at all
optionC: Store the two results in static fields of the class
optionD: Return an int[] where index 0 is min and 1 is max
correctAnswerText: Return a named tuple such as (int Min, int Max)
explanation: A named tuple (C# 7) returns both values with names: var (min, max) = Range(marks);. out parameters work but read awkwardly, an array hides which slot is which, and static fields add shared state.

prompt: A hospital form records a baby's age in months, and the age may not be known yet. How should the field be typed?
optionA: int with -1 meaning unknown, checked wherever it is read
optionB: int? — null means unknown and 0 stays a real age
optionC: string, so that "unknown" can be stored as plain text
optionD: int with 0 meaning unknown, to keep the type simple
correctAnswerText: int? — null means unknown and 0 stays a real age
explanation: For a newborn, 0 months is a genuine value, so it cannot also mean "unknown". int? makes absence explicit and the compiler forces .HasValue or ?? before use, unlike a -1 sentinel that is easy to forget.

prompt: Coupon codes must match regardless of case. Which comparison is the best choice?
optionA: string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)
optionB: a.ToLower() == b.ToLower(), using the current culture
optionC: a.ToUpper().CompareTo(b.ToUpper()) == 0 in a helper
optionD: a.Length == b.Length && a[0] == b[0] as a fast check
correctAnswerText: string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)
explanation: OrdinalIgnoreCase compares without allocating new strings and without culture surprises (the Turkish dotless i is the famous one). ToLower and ToUpper allocate two strings per comparison and use culture rules.

prompt: A validation method nests five if blocks, one per rule, before doing its real work at the deepest level. Which restructuring is best?
optionA: Move each rule into a separate static field that is checked first
optionB: Merge all five rules into one long && condition on one line
optionC: Guard clauses: return early on each failed rule, then do the work
optionD: Wrap the whole method in try/catch and throw for each rule
correctAnswerText: Guard clauses: return early on each failed rule, then do the work
explanation: Returning early when a rule fails keeps the main path unindented and each rule readable on its own. Exceptions for ordinary validation are costly, and one giant condition hides which rule failed.

prompt: A billing app uses an 18% GST rate in many places, and the government can revise it. How should the rate be held?
optionA: Read it from configuration so a change needs no rebuild
optionB: Declare const double Gst = 0.18; and rebuild on change
optionC: Type the literal 0.18 at each place it is used in code
optionD: Keep it in a local variable inside the Main method only
correctAnswerText: Read it from configuration so a change needs no rebuild
explanation: const suits values that never change, such as the number of months in a year. A tax rate set by policy belongs in configuration, read once at startup, so a revision is an edit rather than a release.

prompt: In C#, how does a derived class constructor pass arguments to its parent class constructor?
optionA: With this.base(args) inside the constructor body
optionB: With super(args) as its first statement
optionC: With : parent(args) after the parameter list
optionD: With : base(args) after the parameter list
correctAnswerText: With : base(args) after the parameter list
explanation: C# writes the call as an initializer: public Manager(string n) : base(n) { }. super is Java's keyword; : this(...) would call another constructor of the same class.

prompt: Which keyword must a base class method carry before a derived class is allowed to override it?
optionA: sealed (to lock it)
optionB: new (to hide it)
optionC: virtual (or abstract)
optionD: static (to share it)
correctAnswerText: virtual (or abstract)
explanation: C# methods are non-virtual by default. The base marks a method virtual (or abstract) and the derived class writes override; overriding a plain method is a compile error, and new only hides it.

prompt: Which modifier stops any other class from inheriting from a C# class?
optionA: sealed
optionB: static
optionC: readonly
optionD: final
correctAnswerText: sealed
explanation: A sealed class cannot be a base class. final is the Java word, static makes a class that cannot be instantiated at all, and readonly applies to fields and structs.

prompt: Which access modifier makes a class visible to all code in the same assembly but to nothing outside it?
optionA: internal
optionB: public
optionC: protected
optionD: private
correctAnswerText: internal
explanation: internal limits access to the assembly (the compiled project). It is also the default for a top-level class that declares no modifier.

prompt: A member must be reachable inside its class and in derived classes, but not from unrelated code. Which modifier gives that?
optionA: private
optionB: internal
optionC: protected
optionD: static
correctAnswerText: protected
explanation: protected members are visible to the declaring class and every class that derives from it. private stops at the class itself; internal opens the member to the whole assembly.

prompt: In a C# class declaration, how many base classes and how many interfaces may follow the colon?
optionA: Either a single class or interfaces, never both
optionB: Any number of classes, but only one interface
optionC: One class at most, plus any number of interfaces
optionD: Two classes at most, plus up to two interfaces
correctAnswerText: One class at most, plus any number of interfaces
explanation: C# has single class inheritance and multiple interface implementation: class Clerk : Employee, IAuditable, IComparable<Clerk>. The class, if any, comes first.

prompt: What does declaring a type with record (C# 9) give you automatically that a plain class does not?
optionA: Value-based equality across all of its members

optionC: Storage on the stack instead of on the heap
optionD: Automatic saving of the object to a database
correctAnswerText: Value-based equality across all of its members
explanation: The compiler generates Equals, GetHashCode, == and != that compare member values, plus a readable ToString and support for with. A record class is still a reference type on the heap.

prompt: What is public int Age { get; set; } called in C#?
optionA: A public field with accessors
optionB: An indexer over an int value
optionC: An auto-implemented property
optionD: A read-only computed property
correctAnswerText: An auto-implemented property
explanation: An auto-implemented property: the compiler creates a hidden backing field and the get and set accessors. Callers use it like a field but it remains a property.

prompt: What kind of type does the C# keyword struct declare?
optionA: A value type
optionB: A reference type
optionC: An abstract type
optionD: An interface type
correctAnswerText: A value type
explanation: A struct is a value type: a variable holds the data itself and assignment copies it. int, double and DateTime are all structs.

prompt: A field is declared static in a C# class. Who owns it?
optionA: The type itself — one copy shared by every instance
optionB: The calling method, for the length of that call
optionC: Each object — a separate copy per new instance made
optionD: The first object created, until it is collected
correctAnswerText: The type itself — one copy shared by every instance
explanation: Static members belong to the type. There is one copy no matter how many objects exist, and it is reached through the class name, as in Ticket.Count.

prompt: Why do C# guidelines expose public state through properties rather than public fields?
optionA: Only properties may be used with the + and - operators in C#
optionB: Properties are stored more compactly in memory than fields are
optionC: Fields cannot be read by code outside the class that owns them
optionD: Accessors can validate and change later without breaking callers
correctAnswerText: Accessors can validate and change later without breaking callers
explanation: A property is a pair of methods behind field-like syntax. You can add validation, logging or a computed value later, and switching a public field to a property is a binary-breaking change.

prompt: What is the difference between a derived method marked override and one marked new?
optionA: override is checked at run time; new is checked once at compile time
optionB: override replaces it for base references; new hides it for derived ones
optionC: override copies the base body; new starts from an empty method body
optionD: override needs a public method; new works for private methods only
correctAnswerText: override replaces it for base references; new hides it for derived ones
explanation: override takes over the virtual slot, so a call through a base-typed reference reaches the derived method. new declares an unrelated method that only code using the derived type sees.

prompt: Why does C# refuse new Shape() when Shape is declared abstract?
optionA: It may have abstract members with no body to run
optionB: Abstract classes have no constructors of any kind
optionC: Abstract classes can only hold static members
optionD: Only the runtime may create abstract objects
correctAnswerText: It may have abstract members with no body to run
explanation: An abstract class is an incomplete type: members like Area() may have no implementation. Only a concrete subclass that supplies them can be created, though the abstract constructor still runs as part of it.

prompt: What can an abstract class give its subclasses that an interface cannot?
optionA: Instance fields and constructors that hold shared state
optionB: Methods that a subclass is forced to implement itself
optionC: Support for being implemented by more than one class
optionD: The ability to be used as the type of a variable
correctAnswerText: Instance fields and constructors that hold shared state
explanation: Interfaces define a contract and, since C# 8, may carry default method bodies, but they cannot hold instance fields or constructors. Shared state and initialisation need an abstract base class.

prompt: How does a readonly field differ from a const field in C#?
optionA: readonly works only for strings; const works for any type
optionB: readonly may be changed by any method of its own class
optionC: readonly is set at run time, in a constructor or initializer
optionD: readonly is copied into callers' code exactly as const is
correctAnswerText: readonly is set at run time, in a constructor or initializer
explanation: const is a compile-time value baked into every caller. readonly is assigned once at run time, in its initializer or a constructor, so it can hold DateTime.Now or a new List.

prompt: Why does changing a struct received as a method parameter leave the caller's variable unchanged?
optionA: The method got its own copy of every field in the struct
optionB: Struct fields are read-only once the constructor finishes
optionC: Structs are passed by reference but locked during calls
optionD: The runtime undoes changes when the method call returns
correctAnswerText: The method got its own copy of every field in the struct
explanation: Passing a struct by value copies all of its fields into the parameter. The method edits that copy; the caller sees changes only if the struct is passed with ref or the new value is returned.

prompt: Payment p = new UpiPayment(); p.Process(); runs UpiPayment's override. What decides that?
optionA: The run-time type of the object, since Process is virtual
optionB: The declared type of the variable p, which is Payment
optionC: The order in which the two classes appear in the file
optionD: Whichever of the two classes was compiled most recently
correctAnswerText: The run-time type of the object, since Process is virtual
explanation: For a virtual method the call is dispatched on the object actually referenced, so the UpiPayment override runs. The variable's declared type only decides which members you may call.

prompt: Why is overriding ToString on a domain class such as Invoice worth the few lines it takes?
optionA: Logs, debuggers and string joins then show useful text
optionB: Objects without it cannot be added to a List<T>
optionC: It makes the object comparable with == by its text
optionD: The compiler requires it for every public class
correctAnswerText: Logs, debuggers and string joins then show useful text
explanation: Without an override, ToString returns the full type name. Concatenation, string.Join, interpolation, log messages and the debugger all call ToString, so an override makes them meaningful.

prompt: Why does the base class constructor body run before the derived class constructor body?
optionA: The derived body runs first, then the base body is skipped
optionB: The derived part may rely on base state already being set up
optionC: C# runs constructors in alphabetical order of the class name
optionD: Base classes are always compiled before their derived classes
correctAnswerText: The derived part may rely on base state already being set up
explanation: An object is built from the base outwards so that, when the derived constructor body runs, every inherited member it might use has been initialised by its own class.

prompt: For a class that does not override Equals, when do two variables count as equal?
optionA: Only when both refer to the very same object
optionB: When both objects were made by the same constructor
optionC: When their ToString results produce the same text
optionD: When every public field holds the same value
correctAnswerText: Only when both refer to the very same object
explanation: object.Equals for classes is reference equality. Two separately created objects with identical data are not equal unless the class overrides Equals (and GetHashCode) or is a record.
The : this(5) initializer runs the other constructor completely before the calling constructor's body, so 2 is written first and then 1.

prompt: class Pt adds public bool Equals(Pt o) comparing X and Y, and nothing else. new Pt(1,1).Equals(new Pt(1,1)) is True, yet list.Contains(new Pt(1,1)) is False. Why?
optionA: Equals(Pt) is an overload; Contains calls Equals(object)

correctAnswerText: Equals(Pt) is an overload; Contains calls Equals(object)
explanation: Without IEquatable<Pt> or an override of Equals(object), the collection's default comparer calls object.Equals, which is reference equality. Override Equals(object) and GetHashCode, or implement IEquatable<Pt>.

prompt:

correctAnswerText: value is static, so both objects share a single field
explanation: A static field has one copy for the whole type, so all four increments land in it. Remove static to give each Counter its own value.

correctAnswerText: B — the copy of the reference was repointed after the edit

prompt: Key overrides Equals and GetHashCode using its Id. A key is added to a HashSet<Key>, then its Id is changed from 1 to 99. Now set.Contains(key) is False. Why?
optionA: HashSet removes any element automatically once its fields change

optionD: The set filed it under the old hash and now looks in another bucket
correctAnswerText: The set filed it under the old hash and now looks in another bucket
explanation: A hash set places an item by its hash code at insertion. After Id changes, the new hash leads the lookup to a different bucket, so the item is lost while Count still says 1. Keep key fields immutable.

prompt: record Order(int Id, List<string> Items); (C# 9) — var copy = order with { Id = 2 }; copy.Items.Add("pen"); and the original order now lists pen too. Why?
optionA: with returns the same object with its Id changed in place

correctAnswerText: with copies member values, so both share one List object
explanation: A with expression makes a shallow copy: each member value is copied, and for a List that value is a reference. Both records point at one list; use an immutable collection or copy the list.

optionA: The literal 5 is a double in C# unless it has an int suffix
optionB: Methods newly declared in PD win before overrides are considered

prompt: A developer writes class Car : Engine so that Car can reuse Start() and Stop(). Which design is better, and why?
optionA: Car holds an Engine field: a car has an engine, it is not one
optionB: Copy the Start and Stop bodies into Car to avoid any coupling
optionC: Keep Car : Engine, since inheritance is the way to reuse code
optionD: Make Engine a static class so that Car can call it directly
correctAnswerText: Car holds an Engine field: a car has an engine, it is not one
explanation: Inheritance claims that a Car can be used anywhere an Engine is expected, which is false. Composition reuses the behaviour, keeps Car's public surface its own and lets the engine be swapped.

prompt: Three report exporters share the same validate-format-save steps and differ only in formatting. Which shape fits best?
optionA: An abstract base runs the steps; subclasses override Format
optionB: Three unrelated classes, each copying the shared steps
optionC: An interface each exporter implements fully, steps and all
optionD: One class with a switch on a string that names the format
correctAnswerText: An abstract base runs the steps; subclasses override Format
explanation: When subclasses share a fixed sequence and real code, an abstract base with an abstract Format step (the template method) keeps the steps in one place. An interface alone would duplicate them three times.

prompt: Which of these types is the best candidate to be a struct rather than a class?
optionA: A Customer with a dozen fields that many services update
optionB: A Course whose list of enrolled students keeps on growing
optionC: An OrderService that holds a database connection and a logger
optionD: A small immutable GeoPoint holding a latitude and a longitude
correctAnswerText: A small immutable GeoPoint holding a latitude and a longitude
explanation: Structs suit small, immutable values that are copied cheaply and compared by value. Large, mutable or identity-bearing objects should be classes, or every assignment copies them and edits get lost.

prompt: A Student entity is loaded, tracked and updated by EF Core 8, and identified by its key. Record or class?
optionA: A record — with copies are how EF Core saves updates
optionB: A class — its identity is the key, not its current values
optionC: A struct — entities are best copied on every assignment
optionD: A record — value equality makes change tracking faster
correctAnswerText: A class — its identity is the key, not its current values
explanation: An entity is the same student even after its fields change, and EF Core tracks that one instance. Records compare by value and encourage with copies, which suits DTOs and value objects rather than tracked entities.

prompt: A team ships a NuGet package whose Settings type exposes public int Timeout; as a field. Later they need validation. What should they have done?
optionA: Marked the field const so that consumers cannot set a bad value
optionB: Made the field static so that one shared value is easy to check
optionC: Kept the field and validated Timeout in every method that uses it
optionD: Exposed a property from the start, so adding rules breaks no one
correctAnswerText: Exposed a property from the start, so adding rules breaks no one
explanation: Turning a public field into a property changes the compiled member, so every consumer must recompile. Starting with a property lets validation be added inside the setter later with no breaking change.

prompt: A notification hierarchy has grown to UrgentEmailWithAttachmentNotification five levels deep. What is the best direction?
optionA: Merge every level into one class with many bool flags
optionB: Compose small parts such as channel and priority objects
optionC: Seal the deepest class so the hierarchy stops growing
optionD: Add a sixth level for each new combination that appears
correctAnswerText: Compose small parts such as channel and priority objects
explanation: Each independent variation (channel, urgency, attachments) multiplies the subclasses. Composing objects lets combinations be assembled at run time without a class per combination.

prompt: A fee calculator reads DateTime.Now inside a static helper to apply late fees, and tests cannot fake the date. Which redesign is best?
optionA: Inject an IClock interface and pass a fake one in tests
optionB: Store the date in a public static field the tests set
optionC: Copy the helper into each test with a fixed date in it
optionD: Keep it static and run the tests on the right dates
correctAnswerText: Inject an IClock interface and pass a fake one in tests
explanation: Depending on an abstraction (an IClock, or TimeProvider in .NET 8) lets production pass the real clock and tests pass a fixed one. A public static field shares mutable state between tests.

prompt: Square : Rectangle overrides the Width setter to set Height too. A method doubles a Rectangle's width and expects its area to double. Verdict?
optionA: The design is wrong: a Square cannot stand in for a Rectangle
optionB: The design is fine: a square is a rectangle in mathematics
optionC: The design is fine as long as both setters are marked virtual
optionD: The method is wrong: it must check for Square before acting
correctAnswerText: The design is wrong: a Square cannot stand in for a Rectangle
explanation: Substitutability is the test for inheritance: code written for Rectangle breaks when handed a Square, because the area quadruples. Model them as separate shapes rather than adding type checks.

prompt: An InvoiceCalculator class was never designed to be extended. Should it be marked sealed?
optionA: Yes — sealed classes are the only ones the GC can collect
optionB: No — sealed classes cannot implement any interfaces at all
optionC: No — sealed classes cannot be created with the new keyword
optionD: Yes — it blocks subclasses that rely on internals it may change
correctAnswerText: Yes — it blocks subclasses that rely on internals it may change
explanation: Sealing a class that was not built for inheritance stops others depending on behaviour you never promised, and lets the JIT devirtualise calls. It can still implement interfaces and be instantiated normally.

prompt: A Money type is shared by carts, invoices and refunds. Settable Amount property, or get-only properties with methods returning new Money?
optionA: Settable: it saves memory, since no new objects are created
optionB: Immutable: the GC never collects objects without any setters
optionC: Immutable: one holder can never change another holder's value
optionD: Settable: immutable types cannot be used as Dictionary keys
correctAnswerText: Immutable: one holder can never change another holder's value
explanation: When one instance is referenced from many places, a setter lets one caller silently change everyone's amount. Immutable values, like string and DateTime, are safe to share and to use as keys.

prompt: Which class is the base of every exception type in .NET?
optionA: System.Fault
optionB: System.Error
optionC: System.Throwable
optionD: System.Exception
correctAnswerText: System.Exception
explanation: Every exception derives from System.Exception, directly or through types such as SystemException. Throwable is the Java root; .NET has no System.Error or System.Fault.

prompt: Which block runs whether the try block finishes normally, returns early or throws?
optionA: else
optionB: finally
optionC: ensure
optionD: catch
correctAnswerText: finally
explanation: finally runs on every exit from the try, which is why cleanup goes there. catch runs only for a matching exception; C# has no else or ensure clause on try.

prompt: A type can appear in a using statement because it implements which interface?
optionA: IDisposable
optionB: IComparable
optionC: IEnumerable
optionD: ICloneable
correctAnswerText: IDisposable
explanation: using calls Dispose() when the block ends, and Dispose is the single method of IDisposable. StreamReader, SqlConnection and HttpResponseMessage all implement it.

prompt: Calling a method on a variable that holds null throws which exception?
optionA: ArgumentNullException
optionB: InvalidCastException
optionC: NullReferenceException
optionD: NullPointerException
correctAnswerText: NullReferenceException
explanation: The runtime throws NullReferenceException when a member is used through null. ArgumentNullException is thrown deliberately by a method that rejects a null argument; NullPointerException is Java.

prompt: Reading marks[10] from an int array of length 10 throws which exception?
optionA: IndexOutOfRangeException
optionB: ArgumentOutOfRangeException
optionC: OverflowException
optionD: KeyNotFoundException
correctAnswerText: IndexOutOfRangeException
explanation: Valid array indexes are 0 to Length - 1, and the runtime throws IndexOutOfRangeException past them. A List<T> indexer throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException instead; dictionaries throw KeyNotFoundException.

prompt: Your public method receives null for a parameter that must not be null. Which exception should it throw?
optionA: NotSupportedException
optionB: NullReferenceException
optionC: InvalidOperationException
optionD: ArgumentNullException
correctAnswerText: ArgumentNullException
explanation: ArgumentNullException names the parameter the caller got wrong. NullReferenceException is reserved for the runtime, and InvalidOperationException means the object is in the wrong state.

prompt: Which Exception property holds the original exception that a new one was thrown to wrap?
optionA: Source
optionB: InnerException
optionC: BaseException
optionD: Data
correctAnswerText: InnerException
explanation: Passing the caught exception to the constructor, new X("msg", ex), stores it in InnerException. GetBaseException() is a method that walks that chain; Source names the assembly.

prompt: Which keyword adds a condition to a catch clause, so it handles the exception only when the condition is true (C# 6)?
optionA: if
optionB: case
optionC: when
optionD: where
correctAnswerText: when
explanation: An exception filter is written catch (IOException ex) when (condition). When the condition is false the clause is skipped as if it did not match.

prompt: Which System.IO call writes a whole string to a file, creating it or replacing its contents?
optionA: File.AppendAllText(path, text)
optionB: File.Create(path, text)
optionC: File.WriteAllText(path, text)
optionD: File.Open(path, text)
correctAnswerText: File.WriteAllText(path, text)
explanation: File.WriteAllText opens, writes, flushes and closes in one call, overwriting any existing file. AppendAllText adds to the end, and File.Create and File.Open return streams rather than taking text.

prompt: Ship() is called on an order that has already been cancelled. Which built-in exception fits?
optionA: NotImplementedException
optionB: FormatException
optionC: InvalidOperationException
optionD: ArgumentException
correctAnswerText: InvalidOperationException
explanation: InvalidOperationException means the call is not valid for the object's current state, even though the arguments are fine. ArgumentException is for a bad argument value.

prompt: In an exception's stack trace, what does the top "at ..." line show?
optionA: The Main method, where the program first started
optionB: The catch block that finally handled the exception
optionC: The last method that completed without any error
optionD: The method and line where the exception was thrown
correctAnswerText: The method and line where the exception was thrown
explanation: A stack trace lists frames from the throw point outwards: the top line is where it was raised, and each line below is a caller. Read from the top to find the fault, then down for how you got there.

prompt: Why does a using block release its resource even when an exception is thrown inside it?
optionA: The garbage collector runs as soon as an exception occurs
optionB: using catches and discards every exception from its body
optionC: Dispose is called by the constructor if anything fails
optionD: The compiler expands it to try/finally that calls Dispose
correctAnswerText: The compiler expands it to try/finally that calls Dispose
explanation: using (var r = ...) { } compiles to a try whose finally calls r.Dispose() when r is not null. The exception still propagates; using does not catch it.

prompt: Why should exceptions not be used for ordinary control flow, such as ending a loop?
optionA: Each exception thrown leaks memory until the app restarts
optionB: The compiler removes throw statements that occur in loops
optionC: A loop body is not allowed to contain a try/catch at all
optionD: Throwing captures a stack trace and unwinds; it is costly
correctAnswerText: Throwing captures a stack trace and unwinds; it is costly
explanation: Creating and throwing an exception records a stack trace and unwinds frames, which is far slower than a branch, and it hides the normal path. Exceptions are for exceptional conditions.

prompt: Why is catch (Exception) acceptable in a top-level handler but a warning sign deep inside a method?
optionA: Deep inside, it is slower because the stack is larger there
optionB: At the top it can only log and respond; deeper it hides bugs
optionC: The compiler only allows catch (Exception) inside Main
optionD: At the top level, exceptions no longer carry stack traces
correctAnswerText: At the top it can only log and respond; deeper it hides bugs
explanation: A last-resort handler (Main, ASP.NET Core exception middleware) should catch everything to log it and fail cleanly. Inside business code, a catch-all swallows bugs it cannot actually recover from.

prompt: An exception in a console app is never caught by any catch block. What happens?
optionA: Main restarts from the beginning with the same arguments
optionB: The process terminates and the exception details are reported
optionC: The runtime skips that line and continues with the next one
optionD: The exception is written to a log file and ignored silently
correctAnswerText: The process terminates and the exception details are reported
explanation: An unhandled exception ends the process; the runtime writes the type, message and stack trace to the console (standard error). No code after the throw point in that call chain runs.

prompt: The garbage collector frees memory, so why must a FileStream still be disposed?
optionA: The GC runs at unpredictable times; the file handle stays held
optionB: A FileStream that is not disposed deletes its file on collection
optionC: The GC never collects objects whose type implements IDisposable
optionD: Disposing is only needed when running the Debug configuration
correctAnswerText: The GC runs at unpredictable times; the file handle stays held
explanation: The GC manages memory, not OS resources, and it runs whenever it decides. Until then a file stays locked or a pooled connection stays checked out. Dispose releases the resource at a known moment.

prompt: A method three calls deep throws, and only Main has a matching catch. What happens on the way up?
optionA: Each frame is unwound, running its finally blocks, until Main
optionB: The two middle methods are skipped and their finally blocks too
optionC: The runtime asks each method in turn to retry the failed call
optionD: Each method in between returns its default value to its caller
correctAnswerText: Each frame is unwound, running its finally blocks, until Main
explanation: The runtime searches up the call stack for a matching catch, then unwinds the frames in between, running each finally block on the way. None of the intermediate methods returns normally.

prompt: How does catch (X ex) when (cond) differ from catching X and calling throw; when cond is false?
optionA: Rethrowing with throw; erases the stack trace; filters keep it
optionB: A filter runs after every finally block, rethrowing does not
optionC: Filters can only test the Message property of the exception
optionD: A false filter never enters the catch, so the stack stays intact
correctAnswerText: A false filter never enters the catch, so the stack stays intact

prompt: Why build a file path with Path.Combine(folder, "marks.csv") instead of folder + "\\marks.csv"?

explanation: Path.Combine adds a separator only when one is missing and uses the platform's separator, which matters when the same .NET 8 app runs on Linux in a container. It does not touch the disk.

prompt: What is the shape of the .NET Try pattern, as in int.TryParse or Dictionary.TryGetValue?

explanation: A TryX method returns true with the value in an out parameter, or false with the out set to default. Expected failure is handled with an if instead of the cost of a throw.

prompt: One catch (ArithmeticException ex) must handle both checked(int.MaxValue + n) and 10 / zero for ints. Which types will it actually see?

The try is inside the loop, so each bad item is counted and the loop moves on. "x" and the empty string both throw FormatException; 4 + 5 = 9.

prompt: A catch block does throw new Exception(e.Message);. The logs now show only a plain Exception pointing at that catch. What was lost?

prompt:

prompt: An import wraps its whole foreach over 10,000 rows in one try/catch that logs. One bad row at position 12 means only 11 rows are saved. What is the cause?

prompt:

correctAnswerText: It hides a null bug; user?.Address?.City ?? "?" states intent

prompt: catch (Exception ex) when (Log(ex)) { ... } — Log writes the error and returns false. The log has the entry, yet the catch body never runs. Why?

prompt: File.ReadAllText("settings.json") works from the IDE but throws FileNotFoundException when the app is started from another folder. Why?
optionA: A relative path resolves against the current working directory

correctAnswerText: A relative path resolves against the current working directory
explanation: Relative paths are resolved from the process's current directory, which depends on how it was launched. Build the path from AppContext.BaseDirectory with Path.Combine to find files beside the app.

prompt: An order form posts no quantity at all, and the code saves an order of 0 items instead of failing. The line is qty = Convert.ToInt32(form["qty"]);. Why?
optionA: Convert.ToInt32 retries the parse until a number comes back
optionB: Convert.ToInt32(null) returns 0, where int.Parse(null) throws

correctAnswerText: Convert.ToInt32(null) returns 0, where int.Parse(null) throws
explanation: Convert.ToInt32(string) treats null as zero, so a missing field becomes a valid-looking 0. int.Parse(null) throws ArgumentNullException. Check for a missing value explicitly before converting.

prompt: Every layer — repository, service, controller — catches, logs and does throw;. Each failure appears in the log three times. What is the fix?
optionA: Log once, at the boundary that handles it; let lower layers pass it on
optionB: Catch Exception in the repository only and return null from there
optionC: Turn logging off in the service so only two copies are recorded
optionD: Replace throw; with throw ex; so each layer logs a different trace
correctAnswerText: Log once, at the boundary that handles it; let lower layers pass it on
explanation: Log-and-rethrow at every layer multiplies entries without adding information, since the one stack trace already shows every layer. Let it propagate and log it once where it is finally handled.

prompt: A runaway recursion crashes the process with a stack overflow, and the finally block that should log "shutting down" never writes. Why?
optionA: finally blocks are skipped for every exception thrown in Release
optionB: StackOverflowException cannot be caught; the process just ends
optionC: Recursive methods are not allowed to contain a finally block
optionD: The finally ran, but Console output is lost when a stack is full
correctAnswerText: StackOverflowException cannot be caught; the process just ends
explanation: Since .NET 2.0 a stack overflow terminates the process immediately; no catch or finally runs. The only fix is to prevent it: bound the recursion depth or use a loop.

prompt: A registration form has eight fields, and users should see every problem at once. How should the validator report them?
optionA: Log each failure and return true so the form can proceed
optionB: Return a result that lists every failed rule with its field
optionC: Throw an exception at the first failed rule it runs into
optionD: Throw one exception per failed rule, one after another
correctAnswerText: Return a result that lists every failed rule with its field
explanation: Invalid user input is expected, and a throw can report only the first problem. A result object with all errors lets the UI show them together, which is what ASP.NET Core validation does.

prompt: In an ASP.NET Core 8 API, where should unexpected exceptions such as a failed database call be turned into a 500 response?
optionA: In a try/catch inside every controller action separately
optionB: In one exception-handling middleware that logs and responds
optionC: In each repository method, which returns null on failure
optionD: Nowhere — the raw stack trace is useful to API clients
correctAnswerText: In one exception-handling middleware that logs and responds
explanation: A single handler (UseExceptionHandler with ProblemDetails) gives every endpoint the same logging and safe response. Per-action catches duplicate code, and stack traces must never reach clients.

prompt: When is defining a custom exception type better than reusing a built-in one such as ArgumentException?
optionA: Never — custom exceptions are not supported by ASP.NET Core
optionB: When callers must catch and handle that condition specifically
optionC: Always — every method should throw its own exception type
optionD: Whenever the message text needs to differ from the default
correctAnswerText: When callers must catch and handle that condition specifically
explanation: A custom type such as InsufficientStockException earns its place when a caller will catch it and act differently. For a bad argument, the built-in ArgumentException family already says it precisely.

prompt: A call to a payment gateway sometimes times out. Which retry design is sound?
optionA: Retry forever inside catch (Exception) until the call works
optionB: Never retry; show the raw exception message to the customer
optionC: Retry a few times with a delay, only on transient exceptions

correctAnswerText: Retry a few times with a delay, only on transient exceptions
explanation: Only transient failures (timeouts, 503s) can succeed on a retry, and a bounded count with backoff avoids hammering the gateway. Retrying a validation error or a bug can never succeed; for payments the call must also be idempotent.

prompt: A tool loads a 2 KB template file once at startup. A reviewer asks for a StreamReader loop instead of File.ReadAllText. Verdict?

prompt: Code checks File.Exists(path) and then opens the file, assuming it cannot fail. Why is that weaker than opening it and handling FileNotFoundException?

prompt: A payment exception message is being written. Which one is best?

prompt: An AuditLog class creates a StreamWriter in its constructor and writes to it from several methods. How should the writer be released?

prompt: A public SendInvoice(Customer c) uses c only after four other steps. Should it check c for null at the start?

prompt: A method writes report.csv and then moves it to an archive folder. Which form of using should hold the writer?

prompt: What does a List<T> keep its elements in?

prompt: Which Dictionary<TKey,TValue> member reads a key that may be absent without throwing?

prompt: Which .NET collection hands back the most recently added item first?

prompt: What does HashSet<T>.Add do when an equal element is already in the set?

prompt: Which type, added in .NET 6, dequeues the element with the smallest priority value first?

prompt: Which statement lets a method produce an IEnumerable<T> one element at a time?

prompt: Which constraint requires a type argument to have a public parameterless constructor?

prompt: Which interface gives a type a natural order, so list.Sort() with no arguments can sort it?

prompt: Which interface adds index access, as in items[i], on top of ICollection<T>?

prompt: Which collection holds each value once and enumerates them in ascending order?

correctAnswerText: SortedSet<T>

prompt: Why is looking a key up in a Dictionary O(1) on average?

prompt: Why would a method that only loops over orders take IEnumerable<Order> rather than List<Order>?

prompt: Why must two equal keys always return the same GetHashCode?

explanation: If equal keys hashed differently they would land in different buckets, and a lookup would search the wrong bucket and miss a key that is really there.

prompt: Why is Insert(0, item) slow on a List<T> holding a million elements?
optionA: The list doubles its capacity whenever index 0 is used

optionD: Every existing element shifts one slot to make room
correctAnswerText: Every existing element shifts one slot to make room
explanation: A List<T> is a contiguous array, so inserting at the front moves all n elements up one place: O(n). Appending at the end is amortised O(1).

prompt: Why does calling Remove on a List<T> inside a foreach over that list throw?
optionA: foreach holds a lock that Remove is not able to take
optionB: The loop variable is read-only, so removing it fails
optionC: Remove is not allowed on a list holding value types
optionD: The enumerator sees the list's version change and stops
correctAnswerText: The enumerator sees the list's version change and stops
explanation: List<T> keeps a version number that every Add or Remove bumps. Its enumerator checks it on MoveNext and throws InvalidOperationException rather than walk a changed list.

prompt: Why may an IEnumerable<string> be used as an IEnumerable<object>, while a List<string> cannot be used as a List<object>?
optionA: IEnumerable<T> copies every element into a new object sequence
optionB: List<T> is a class, and a class is never converted to anything

optionD: string and object differ in size, so one list cannot hold the other

explanation: IEnumerable<out T> is covariant because it only returns T. A List<object> view of a List<string> would accept Add(42), so List<T> must stay invariant.

prompt: What does Dictionary<TKey,TValue> promise about the order foreach visits its entries in?

optionB: Insertion order, kept even after removals

correctAnswerText: Nothing; the order is unspecified and may change
explanation: The order often looks like insertion order, but it is not documented and a removal followed by an Add reuses a freed slot. Sort for output, or use SortedDictionary.

prompt: Why is List<int> preferred to the old non-generic ArrayList for a list of numbers?
optionA: ArrayList cannot grow past its initial capacity at all
optionB: The ints are stored unboxed and type-checked at compile time
optionC: ArrayList stores each number as a string, wasting memory
optionD: List<int> is thread-safe for writes and ArrayList is not
correctAnswerText: The ints are stored unboxed and type-checked at compile time
explanation: ArrayList holds object, so each int is boxed on the heap and every read needs a cast that can fail at run time. List<int> stores the ints directly and the compiler checks types.

prompt: How do List<T>.Sort and LINQ OrderBy differ when two elements compare as equal?
optionA: Sort keeps equal items in input order; OrderBy may not
optionB: Both keep the order, but OrderBy sorts the list in place
optionC: OrderBy keeps equal items in input order; Sort may not

correctAnswerText: OrderBy keeps equal items in input order; Sort may not
explanation: OrderBy is documented as a stable sort. List<T>.Sort uses an introspective sort that is unstable, so equal elements may swap places.

prompt: Why does Queue<T> suit print jobs that must be handled in the order they arrived?
optionA: Dequeue always returns the oldest job still waiting
optionB: It sorts jobs by size before handing any of them out
optionC: Any job can be read by index without being removed
optionD: Dequeue returns whichever job was added most recently
correctAnswerText: Dequeue always returns the oldest job still waiting
explanation: A queue is first in, first out: Enqueue adds at the back and Dequeue takes from the front, so jobs come out in arrival order. Both operations are O(1).

prompt: A service must check, for each of a million incoming order ids, whether that id was already seen. Which collection should hold the seen ids?
optionA: HashSet<long>, for O(1) Add and Contains

explanation: HashSet<T>.Contains is O(1) on average, so the whole run is O(n). List.Contains scans the list, making the run O(n²) — minutes instead of milliseconds at this size.

prompt: City names arrive as "Pune", "PUNE" and "pune" and must count as one key. How should the dictionary be created?
optionA: new Dictionary<string, int>(3), one slot for each casing

explanation: Passing an IEqualityComparer<string> changes what counts as the same key: OrdinalIgnoreCase hashes and compares without case, so the three spellings share one entry.

optionA: True: Equals reports the two Sku objects match

optionA: 1 7 HYD

prompt: A Student class overrides Equals and GetHashCode from RollNo. A student is added to a HashSet<Student>, then its RollNo is corrected. Why does set.Contains(student) now return false?
optionA: HashSet<T> checks reference equality, not Equals

correctAnswerText: It is still filed in the bucket its old hash chose
explanation: The element sits in the bucket picked by the hash it had when added. The new hash points the lookup at a different bucket. Never mutate a key in place; remove, change and add again.

optionA: The list must be declared as an IList<Point> first
optionB: Struct fields cannot be assigned outside a constructor
optionC: The indexer returns a copy, and the change would be lost
optionD: A List<T> cannot hold value types such as a struct
correctAnswerText: The indexer returns a copy, and the change would be lost
explanation: The List indexer returns the struct by value, so assigning to the copy's field could never reach the list; the compiler rejects it (CS1612). Copy, change, and assign the copy back.

prompt: A list of balances is sorted with list.Sort((a, b) => a.Paise - b.Paise), where Paise is an int. It sorts small test data correctly but misorders some very large and very negative balances. Why?
optionA: The lambda must return a bool, not a difference
optionB: The subtraction can overflow and return the wrong sign

optionD: Sort ignores the lambda when the list is very large
correctAnswerText: The subtraction can overflow and return the wrong sign
explanation: Comparison<T> only needs the sign, but a - b overflows when the values are far apart (say int.MaxValue and -1), flipping the sign. a.Paise.CompareTo(b.Paise) cannot overflow.

optionA: foreach over an array boxes every single int id
optionB: Contains sorts the list before every search
optionC: Each Contains scans the list, so the loop is O(n²)
optionD: Add copies the whole list each time it is called
correctAnswerText: Each Contains scans the list, so the loop is O(n²)
explanation: List.Contains is a linear scan, and it runs once per id over a growing list. A HashSet<int> makes each check O(1) on average, and its Add already reports duplicates.

prompt: A repository returns a page of orders that callers will count and index but must not change. Which return type fits best?
optionA: object[] so that callers have to cast every item
optionB: IReadOnlyList<Order>: Count and an indexer, no Add
optionC: IEnumerable<Order> built lazily over the open query
optionD: List<Order>: callers get every method they may want
correctAnswerText: IReadOnlyList<Order>: Count and an indexer, no Add
explanation: IReadOnlyList<T> promises exactly what callers need — Count and indexing — and nothing that mutates. A List<T> invites edits; a lazy IEnumerable may run the query again each time.

prompt: A feature appends readings at the end and often reads reading number i. A teammate proposes LinkedList<T> "because inserts are O(1)". Which judgement is sound?
optionA: Either: the two have the same cost for every operation
optionB: LinkedList<T>: its nodes sit together, so reads are fast
optionC: LinkedList<T>: O(1) insert outweighs everything else
optionD: List<T>: appends are amortised O(1) and index reads O(1)
correctAnswerText: List<T>: appends are amortised O(1) and index reads O(1)
explanation: The workload is append-and-index, which List<T> does in O(1). LinkedList<T> has no indexer (reaching item i is O(n)) and scatters nodes across the heap; its O(1) insert needs a node in hand.

prompt: Scores for 50,000 players are updated all day; the sorted leaderboard is printed once, at midnight. Which design is better?
optionA: A SortedDictionary keyed by score, kept sorted all day
optionB: A SortedSet of players rebuilt on every update
optionC: A Dictionary for updates, sorted once when printing
optionD: A List re-sorted after every single score update
correctAnswerText: A Dictionary for updates, sorted once when printing
explanation: Keeping order costs on every update (O(log n), or O(n log n) for re-sorting) while order is needed once. O(1) updates plus a single O(n log n) sort at midnight is cheaper and simpler.

prompt: Attendance must be looked up by (classCode, date). Which dictionary key is the best design?
optionA: A mutable class with public fields and no Equals override
optionB: A value tuple (string Class, DateTime Date): both parts hashed
optionC: A string like classCode + date, parsed back where needed
optionD: The date alone, with the class code kept in each value
correctAnswerText: A value tuple (string Class, DateTime Date): both parts hashed
explanation: A value tuple (C# 7) already has value equality and a hash combining both parts, with no parsing. Concatenated strings need a separator to avoid clashes, and a class without Equals compares references.

prompt: A scheduler repeatedly takes the most urgent task while new tasks keep arriving. Which approach should it use?
optionA: A List re-sorted by urgency before every single take
optionB: A Queue, since tasks are taken in the order they come
optionC: A HashSet, scanned in full for the most urgent task
optionD: PriorityQueue: O(log n) to add and to take the next task
correctAnswerText: PriorityQueue: O(log n) to add and to take the next task
explanation: A heap keeps only enough order to find the minimum, so both Enqueue and Dequeue are O(log n). Re-sorting is O(n log n) per take, a scan O(n), and a plain Queue ignores urgency.

prompt: A loader knows it will read exactly 2,000,000 rows into a List<Row>. Is new List<Row>(2_000_000) worth writing?
optionA: No: List<T> ignores the capacity it is given
optionB: No: a preset capacity makes Add O(n) each time
optionC: Yes: it skips about twenty grow-and-copy steps
optionD: Yes: it makes the list safe for parallel writes
correctAnswerText: Yes: it skips about twenty grow-and-copy steps
explanation: Without it the backing array starts small and doubles about twenty times, copying each time and leaving garbage. Presizing when the count is known avoids that; it does nothing for thread safety.

prompt: Cart exposes public List<CartItem> Items { get; } and code elsewhere calls cart.Items.Add(...) without any stock check. Which change is best?
optionA: Expose the list as IEnumerable but keep casting it back
optionB: Make the property a public field so its intent is clearer
optionC: Keep a private list; expose IReadOnlyList and an AddItem method
optionD: Copy the list in the getter so that callers edit a copy
correctAnswerText: Keep a private list; expose IReadOnlyList and an AddItem method
explanation: The class owns its invariants, so adding goes through a method that validates. IReadOnlyList<T> still lets callers read and count. Copying hides edits silently; casting back defeats the point.

prompt: A depth-first walk over a folder tree that can be 100,000 levels deep is written recursively. Which design judgement is right?
optionA: Use a Stack<T> loop: deep recursion can overflow the call stack
optionB: Keep recursion: the CLR grows the call stack without limit
optionC: Use a Queue<T>: it gives depth-first order with less memory
optionD: Keep recursion but wrap each call in try/catch for safety
correctAnswerText: Use a Stack<T> loop: deep recursion can overflow the call stack
explanation: Each recursive call uses a call-stack frame, and a StackOverflowException cannot be caught in .NET — the process dies. An explicit Stack<T> lives on the heap. A Queue gives breadth-first order.

prompt: Products are sorted by price on one screen and by name on another. How should the ordering be designed?
optionA: Store the products twice, once in each order, and sync them
optionB: Pass an IComparer or lambda per screen; keep CompareTo for one order
optionC: Change Product.CompareTo before each screen sorts its list
optionD: Give Product two CompareTo methods with different names
correctAnswerText: Pass an IComparer or lambda per screen; keep CompareTo for one order
explanation: A type has one natural order (IComparable<T>). Other orders belong to the caller as an IComparer<T>, a Comparison<T> or OrderBy key — no shared state flips between screens.

prompt: A team writes Repository<T> where T : class, IEntity, so Find can read entity.Id. Another proposes taking object and casting inside. Which is the better design?
optionA: object: generic constraints slow every call at run time
optionB: The constraint, but only if T is also marked as a struct
optionC: object: it accepts any type, which is more flexible
optionD: The constraint: Id is checked at compile time, with no casts
correctAnswerText: The constraint: Id is checked at compile time, with no casts
explanation: The constraint tells the compiler every T has Id, so misuse fails to compile instead of throwing InvalidCastException at run time. Constraints cost nothing at run time.

prompt: Which delegate type fits a method that takes a string and an int and returns a bool?
optionA: Func<bool, string, int>
optionB: Func<string, int, bool>
optionC: Predicate<string, int>
optionD: Action<string, int, bool>
correctAnswerText: Func<string, int, bool>
explanation: In Func the last type argument is the return type and the others are parameters. Action never returns a value, and Predicate<T> takes exactly one argument.

prompt: What does an Action<T> delegate return?
optionA: A bool saying whether the call succeeded
optionB: Nothing; it is for methods declared void
optionC: A Task that completes once the call ends
optionD: The same T value that it was handed in
correctAnswerText: Nothing; it is for methods declared void
explanation: Action, Action<T>, Action<T1, T2> and so on wrap void methods. When a value comes back, use Func; when it is a yes/no test of one argument, Predicate<T> or Func<T, bool>.

prompt: What does marking a delegate field with the event keyword restrict outside the declaring class?
optionA: Others may only += or -=; they cannot invoke or reassign it
optionB: Others may invoke it, but only from the same assembly
optionC: Others may reassign it, but cannot add more handlers
optionD: Others may read it, but only through a public getter
correctAnswerText: Others may only += or -=; they cannot invoke or reassign it
explanation: An event exposes only add and remove to outside code. Only the declaring class can raise it or replace its handler list, so a subscriber cannot wipe out the others with =.

prompt: Which LINQ operator turns each element into a new shape, such as each Student into its Name?
optionA: Where
optionB: OrderBy
optionC: Select
optionD: Distinct
correctAnswerText: Select
explanation: Select projects each element through a function. Where filters, OrderBy sorts and Distinct removes duplicates; none of them change an element's shape.

prompt: Which operator flattens a sequence of lists into one sequence of their items?
optionA: SelectMany
optionB: Concat on its own
optionC: GroupBy
optionD: Zip
correctAnswerText: SelectMany
explanation: SelectMany maps each element to a sequence and concatenates all of them. GroupBy does the opposite (one sequence into groups), and Zip pairs two sequences element by element.

prompt: Which of these runs a LINQ query at once instead of deferring it?
optionA: Where(...)
optionB: OrderBy(...)
optionC: Select(...)
optionD: ToList()
correctAnswerText: ToList()
explanation: ToList, ToArray, ToDictionary and aggregates such as Count or First execute the query immediately. Where, Select and OrderBy only build a query that runs when enumerated.

prompt: Which operator returns default(T) instead of throwing when no element matches?
optionA: Single
optionB: First
optionC: FirstOrDefault
optionD: ElementAt(0)
correctAnswerText: FirstOrDefault
explanation: First and Single throw InvalidOperationException when nothing matches, and ElementAt(0) throws on an empty sequence. FirstOrDefault (and SingleOrDefault, LastOrDefault) return default(T): null for references, 0 for int.

prompt: What does declaring a type as a record (C# 9) generate for you?
optionA: Automatic validation that no property is ever left as null
optionB: Value-based equality, a hash code and a ToString over its data
optionC: A database table and a mapping for every one of its properties
optionD: A thread-safe copy of the object each time it is passed along
correctAnswerText: Value-based equality, a hash code and a ToString over its data
explanation: A record gets Equals, GetHashCode, ==, != and a readable ToString built from its properties, plus with-expression support. It does not persist anything or validate values.

prompt: With nullable reference types on (C# 8), what does the ! in name!.Length tell the compiler?
optionA: Return 0 for the length whenever name is null
optionB: Throw ArgumentNullException at once if name is null
optionC: "Trust me, this is not null" — it suppresses the warning
optionD: Negate name, so that the null case is handled first
correctAnswerText: "Trust me, this is not null" — it suppresses the warning
explanation: The null-forgiving operator only silences the compiler's nullable warning. It does nothing at run time: if name is null, .Length still throws NullReferenceException.

prompt: In the expression x => x * 2, what is x?
optionA: The value the lambda returns
optionB: A local declared before the lambda
optionC: The lambda's parameter
optionD: A field captured from the class
correctAnswerText: The lambda's parameter
explanation: Left of => are the parameters, right of it the body. x => x * 2 is a function of one parameter x returning twice its value, assignable to Func<int, int>.

prompt: Why can a Where query return items that were added to its source list after the query was written?
optionA: Each Add on a List<T> re-runs every query built over it
optionB: The query stores the source and filter and runs when enumerated
optionC: Where copies the list and watches it for later changes
optionD: The compiler rewrites the query to run after the last Add
correctAnswerText: The query stores the source and filter and runs when enumerated
explanation: Where returns an object holding the source and the lambda. Nothing is filtered until something enumerates it, and then it reads the list as it is at that moment.

prompt: What does it mean that a lambda captures a variable rather than a value?
optionA: It sees the variable's current value whenever it runs
optionB: It copies the value once, at the moment it is created
optionC: It makes a fresh copy of the variable on every single call
optionD: It can read the variable but is never allowed to change it
correctAnswerText: It sees the variable's current value whenever it runs
explanation: The compiler moves a captured local into a shared closure object. The lambda and the method both use that one variable, so later changes are visible to the lambda, and its writes to the method.

prompt: Why can a short-lived page object that subscribes to a long-lived service's event leak memory?

explanation: p.Saved += page.OnSaved stores a delegate that references page. While the service lives, the page is reachable and cannot be collected. Unsubscribe with -= when the page is done.

prompt: Why can EF Core turn db.Orders.Where(o => o.Total > 1000) into SQL, when the same Where over a List runs in memory?
optionA: Where on a DbSet is a different method that needs no lambda
optionB: On IQueryable the lambda is an expression tree EF Core can read
optionC: The List version is also turned into SQL, but runs locally
optionD: EF Core decompiles the lambda's IL at run time to rebuild it
correctAnswerText: On IQueryable the lambda is an expression tree EF Core can read
explanation: Queryable.Where takes Expression<Func<T, bool>>: the lambda as data that a provider translates. Enumerable.Where takes Func<T, bool>, compiled code that can only be run.

prompt: A Func<int> has three methods added with +=. Why does invoking it give only one number?
optionA: Only the method added most recently is ever invoked
optionB: All three run, but only the last method's result is returned
optionC: Only the first method runs; the others are kept as backups
optionD: The results are added together and that sum comes back
correctAnswerText: All three run, but only the last method's result is returned
explanation: A multicast delegate calls every method in its invocation list in order, but a call expression can return one value, so the earlier results are discarded. Use GetInvocationList to collect each.

prompt: Why must OrderBy read the whole source before it can return even the first element?
optionA: It must count the elements before it allocates a buffer
optionB: The smallest element might be the very last one in the source
optionC: OrderBy is an immediate operator, like ToList or Count
optionD: OrderBy copies the source to a database table to sort it
correctAnswerText: The smallest element might be the very last one in the source
explanation: Where and Select stream one element at a time, but no sort can know which element is first until it has seen them all. OrderBy is still deferred: the buffering happens on the first MoveNext.

prompt: Why would a developer use Single rather than First to fetch a user by email?

explanation: Single asserts there is exactly one match, so duplicate emails surface as an exception instead of silently picking one. To do that it must keep reading after the first match.

prompt: Why does List<T>.FindAll take a Predicate<T> instead of having one method per condition?
optionA: A Predicate<T> is checked by the compiler for side effects
optionB: It lets FindAll run its condition on several threads at once
optionC: Delegates run faster than if statements inside a loop do
optionD: The caller supplies the test, so one method serves any filter
correctAnswerText: The caller supplies the test, so one method serves any filter
explanation: Passing behaviour as a delegate separates the looping (written once, in the list) from the decision (written by each caller), so FindAll(n => n > 5) and FindAll(IsOverdue) share one method.

prompt: Why does a switch expression (C# 8) usually end with a discard arm, _ => ...?

optionD: The compiler checks arms bottom to top, so _ runs first
correctAnswerText: A value is always required, and _ covers every case left
explanation: A switch expression must produce a value for every input. When no arm matches it throws SwitchExpressionException, and the compiler warns that the arms are not exhaustive; _ catches the rest.

prompt: Why is enumerating the same LINQ query twice a performance and correctness risk?
optionA: The second foreach throws, because a query runs only once

explanation: A deferred query keeps no results. Each enumeration repeats every lambda and every call it makes, and if the source changed in between the two passes disagree. Materialise once with ToList.

prompt:

optionA: Take(20) must always read the whole table before it stops

optionD: AsEnumerable makes Where run in C#, after rows stream from SQL

prompt: A dashboard shows today's highest order with orders.Max(o => o.Total), where Total is an int. On a day with no orders it crashes. Why, when Sum works?
optionA: Max of an empty int sequence throws; Sum of one returns 0
optionB: Sum skips empty lists, but Max requires them to be sorted
optionC: Max reads the whole list twice and runs out of memory
optionD: Max is deferred, so its error appears on a later line
correctAnswerText: Max of an empty int sequence throws; Sum of one returns 0
