prompt: A method builds var flagged = orders.Where(o => IsFraud(o)); where IsFraud calls a web service, then uses flagged.Any(), flagged.Count() and a foreach. What is the best change?
optionA: Keep it lazy, since deferred queries are always cheaper
optionB: Add AsParallel() so the three runs overlap in time
optionC: Replace Any() with Count() > 0 so the work is shared
optionD: Call ToList() once and use the list for all three
correctAnswerText: Call ToList() once and use the list for all three
explanation: Each of the three enumerations re-runs IsFraud for every order, tripling the web calls and risking three different answers. One ToList() fixes the cost and the consistency.

prompt: A repository method returns IEnumerable<Order> from db.Orders.ToList(), and callers filter with Where. Which judgement is right?
optionA: Filter on the IQueryable before ToList, so SQL does the work
optionB: Load the table once at start-up and filter it in memory
optionC: It is fine: LINQ filters at the same speed on either side
optionD: Return IQueryable and let callers call ToList on each row
correctAnswerText: Filter on the IQueryable before ToList, so SQL does the work
explanation: ToList pulls every row across the network before any filter runs. Applying Where (and paging) on the IQueryable lets EF Core send a WHERE clause and return only the needed rows.

prompt: A long-lived PriceFeed service raises PriceChanged; screens open and close all day and subscribe in their constructors. Which design avoids the leak?
optionA: Call GC.Collect after every screen closes to free its memory
optionB: Make PriceChanged a static event shared by all screens
optionC: Subscribe with = instead of += so that only one handler stays
optionD: Unsubscribe with -= when each screen closes or is disposed
correctAnswerText: Unsubscribe with -= when each screen closes or is disposed
explanation: The feed holds a reference to every subscribed screen until it is removed. -= in Dispose or on close releases it. = is not allowed outside the class for an event, and GC.Collect cannot free reachable objects.

prompt: A hot loop runs 10 million times per second and sums an int[] of 64 items with a LINQ Where(...).Sum(). Profiling shows allocations. Which judgement is sound?
optionA: Rewriting the query in query syntax removes all allocations
optionB: A plain for loop here avoids per-call iterator and delegate costs
optionC: LINQ is always faster because it runs on multiple threads
optionD: LINQ allocates nothing, so the profiler must be mistaken
correctAnswerText: A plain for loop here avoids per-call iterator and delegate costs
explanation: Each call allocates an iterator and may allocate a closure, and every element goes through a delegate call. That is fine almost everywhere, but in a measured hot path a simple loop is cheaper.

prompt: An API returns order summaries that are created once, compared in tests and never changed. Which type is the best fit?
optionA: A record with init-only properties
optionB: A Dictionary<string, object> per order
optionC: A struct with a mutable Total field
optionD: A class with public fields and setters
correctAnswerText: A record with init-only properties
explanation: Records (C# 9) give immutable data, value equality for tests and a readable ToString with almost no code. A mutable class compares by reference; a dictionary loses typing.

prompt: A team turns on nullable reference types (C# 8) and gets 400 warnings. One developer proposes adding ! everywhere to silence them. Which judgement is right?
optionA: Turn the feature off; nullable analysis slows the program
optionB: Accept it: the ! operator adds null checks at run time
optionC: Fix each warning by checking or declaring null; ! hides real bugs
optionD: Accept it: the warnings are cosmetic and can never be bugs
correctAnswerText: Fix each warning by checking or declaring null; ! hides real bugs
explanation: Each warning marks a place a null could flow. ! tells the compiler to trust you and does nothing at run time, so blanket use keeps every NullReferenceException. The analysis has no run-time cost.

prompt: A discount rule is a single calculation that varies by festival. One proposal is an IDiscountRule interface with five classes; another is a Func<decimal, decimal> per festival. When is the Func the better choice?
optionA: Never, because a Func cannot be stored in a Dictionary
optionB: When each rule is one stateless function with no other members
optionC: When the rules need several methods and their own dependencies
optionD: Always, since interfaces are slower to call than delegates
correctAnswerText: When each rule is one stateless function with no other members
explanation: A one-method, stateless strategy is exactly what a delegate expresses, without a class per rule. Once a rule needs several members, configuration or injected services, an interface is clearer.

prompt: Looking up a user by email, where the email column is meant to be unique, which call best fits?
optionA: Where(...).ToList()[0]: it is the most explicit
optionB: First: duplicates should be resolved by taking one
optionC: Last: the newest registration should always win
optionD: SingleOrDefault: absent is normal, a duplicate is a bug
correctAnswerText: SingleOrDefault: absent is normal, a duplicate is a bug
explanation: SingleOrDefault returns null when no user has the email (an expected case) and throws when two do, surfacing broken data. First would hide the duplicate; ToList()[0] throws on the normal empty case.

prompt: For each of 50,000 orders, code finds the customer with customers.First(c => c.Id == o.CustomerId) over 20,000 customers. Which change is best?
optionA: Swap First for Single so that the scan stops sooner
optionB: Build a Dictionary by Id once (or use Join) and look up in O(1)
optionC: Run the loop with AsParallel so each scan is shorter
optionD: Sort the customers first so that First finds them faster
correctAnswerText: Build a Dictionary by Id once (or use Join) and look up in O(1)
explanation: First is a linear scan, so the loop does up to a billion comparisons. ToDictionary(c => c.Id), or a LINQ Join, which hashes the inner side, makes each lookup O(1). Single scans further, not less.

prompt: A fee calculator has a long if/else chain over a payment's type and amount. A reviewer suggests a switch expression with type and relational patterns (C# 9). What is its main benefit?
optionA: It removes the need to handle unmatched payment types
optionB: Each case is one arm, read top to bottom, with a checked fallback
optionC: It runs the cases in parallel and returns the fastest arm
optionD: It lets the cases be listed in any order with the same result
correctAnswerText: Each case is one arm, read top to bottom, with a checked fallback
explanation: A switch expression puts each rule on one line, returns a value, and with a _ arm guarantees every input is handled. Arms still run top to bottom, so order matters.

prompt: What should an async method that eventually produces an int declare as its return type?
optionA: int
optionB: Thread<int>
optionC: async int
optionD: Task<int>
correctAnswerText: Task<int>
explanation: An async method returns Task<T> when it has a result (Task when it has none); the body returns a plain int and the compiler wraps it. async is a modifier, not part of the type.

prompt: Which type is used to request cancellation of work that was handed a CancellationToken?
optionA: OperationCanceledException
optionB: CancellationToken itself
optionC: TaskCompletionSource
optionD: CancellationTokenSource
correctAnswerText: CancellationTokenSource
explanation: The source owns the cancel button: cts.Cancel() or cts.CancelAfter(...). Work receives cts.Token, which it can only observe — it cannot cancel anything itself.

prompt: Which call adds one to a shared int as a single atomic operation?
optionA: count = count + 1 in a for loop
optionB: Interlocked.Increment(ref count)
optionC: count++ inside a Task.Run
optionD: Volatile.Read(ref count) + 1
correctAnswerText: Interlocked.Increment(ref count)
explanation: Interlocked.Increment reads, adds and writes in one CPU-level atomic step. count++ is a read, an add and a write, and another thread can slip in between them.

prompt: What does a using statement guarantee for the object it declares?
optionA: The object is garbage collected as soon as the block ends
optionB: The object is copied onto the stack instead of the heap
optionC: The object can only be used by the thread that created it
optionD: Dispose is called when the block ends, even on an exception
correctAnswerText: Dispose is called when the block ends, even on an exception
explanation: using compiles to try/finally with Dispose in the finally, so a connection or file is released even when the block throws. It does not free memory; the GC still does that later.

prompt: By .NET convention, what should a method returning Task<Order> be named?
optionA: AwaitGetOrder
optionB: GetOrderThread
optionC: GetOrderAsync
optionD: GetOrderTask
correctAnswerText: GetOrderAsync
explanation: Task-returning methods end in Async (GetStringAsync, SaveChangesAsync), telling callers to await them. The convention is used across the whole base class library.

prompt: Which method returns a task that completes when every task in a set has completed?
optionA: Task.WhenAll
optionB: Task.Delay
optionC: Task.FromResult
optionD: Task.WhenAny
correctAnswerText: Task.WhenAll
explanation: await Task.WhenAll(a, b, c) waits for all of them without blocking a thread, and for Task<T> gives an array of their results. WhenAny completes when the first one does.

prompt: Which of these C# types is a value type, copied whole on every assignment?
optionA: string
optionB: object
optionC: int
optionD: int[]
correctAnswerText: int
explanation: int (System.Int32) is a struct, a value type copied on assignment. string, arrays and object are reference types; a variable of those holds a reference to a heap object.

prompt: Which collection is built for many threads to add and read keys at the same time?
optionA: ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, TValue>
optionB: Dictionary<TKey, TValue>
optionC: SortedDictionary<TKey, TValue>
optionD: ReadOnlyDictionary<TKey, TValue>
correctAnswerText: ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, TValue>
explanation: ConcurrentDictionary in System.Collections.Concurrent is safe for concurrent reads and writes and offers atomic helpers such as AddOrUpdate and GetOrAdd. Dictionary is not thread-safe for writes.

prompt: How many generations does the .NET garbage collector sort ordinary heap objects into?
optionA: Three: 0, 1 and 2
optionB: Two: young and old
optionC: Four: 0, 1, 2 and 3
optionD: One shared heap
correctAnswerText: Three: 0, 1 and 2
explanation: New objects start in generation 0, survivors are promoted to 1 and then 2. Most objects die young, so collecting gen 0 often and gen 2 rarely is cheap. (Large objects live on a separate large object heap.)

prompt: Which call tells an await not to resume on the captured synchronization context?
optionA: Task.Run(...).Wait()
optionB: ContinueOnContext(true)
optionC: GetAwaiter().GetResult()
optionD: ConfigureAwait(false)
correctAnswerText: ConfigureAwait(false)
explanation: await task.ConfigureAwait(false) lets the continuation run on any thread-pool thread. Library code uses it so it cannot deadlock a UI caller; ASP.NET Core has no context to capture.

prompt: When an async method reaches await on a database call that has not finished, what happens to the thread running it?
optionA: A new thread is created to wait for the reply on its behalf
optionB: The thread spins in a loop, checking whether the call has finished
optionC: The thread sleeps inside the method until the database replies
optionD: The method returns to its caller and the thread is free for other work
correctAnswerText: The method returns to its caller and the thread is free for other work
explanation: await on an incomplete task signs up the rest of the method as a continuation and returns an incomplete task to the caller. No thread waits; I/O completion later schedules the continuation.

prompt: Why can calling .Result on an async method from a WPF button handler freeze the window for good?
optionA: WPF cancels any task that runs for longer than one frame
optionB: The continuation needs the UI thread, which .Result is blocking
optionC: The UI thread has no thread pool, so the task never starts
optionD: .Result throws away the task, so it never gets to complete
correctAnswerText: The continuation needs the UI thread, which .Result is blocking
explanation: The await captured the UI context, so its continuation must run on the UI thread — which is stuck in .Result waiting for that very continuation. Neither can move: a deadlock.

prompt: Why should application code use async Task instead of async void outside event handlers?
optionA: async void methods cannot contain more than one await at all
optionB: A Task-returning method always finishes faster than a void one
optionC: Callers can await a Task and catch its exceptions; void allows neither
optionD: async void runs synchronously, so it blocks the calling thread
correctAnswerText: Callers can await a Task and catch its exceptions; void allows neither
explanation: An async void method hands back nothing to await, so the caller cannot know when it ends, and an exception inside it is raised on the context, typically crashing the process.

prompt: Why is wrapping an HTTP call in Task.Run pointless in an ASP.NET Core action?
optionA: It is I/O-bound; awaiting it already frees the thread
optionB: Task.Run cannot run code that makes network calls
optionC: HTTP calls are already run on a dedicated I/O thread
optionD: Task.Run makes the call synchronous inside a request
correctAnswerText: It is I/O-bound; awaiting it already frees the thread
explanation: Task.Run moves CPU work to a pool thread. An I/O call awaited directly holds no thread while it waits, so Task.Run only adds a thread hop and occupies another pool thread.

prompt: Why can two threads each running count++ a million times end with less than two million?
optionA: count++ is read, add, write; one thread's write can overwrite another's
optionB: int cannot hold two million, so the counter quietly wraps round
optionC: The thread pool skips work items once more than a million queue
optionD: The CPU drops increments when two threads touch one int at once
correctAnswerText: count++ is read, add, write; one thread's write can overwrite another's
explanation: Both threads can read the same old value, add one and write back the same new value, so one increment is lost. That interleaving is a race condition; Interlocked or lock removes it.

prompt: An async Task method throws, but the caller never awaits the task. Why does nothing visibly fail?
optionA: The exception is stored in the faulted task until someone awaits it
optionB: async methods catch and log every exception automatically
optionC: The compiler removes the throw because the task is unused
optionD: The exception is raised on a different process and is lost there
correctAnswerText: The exception is stored in the faulted task until someone awaits it
explanation: An exception inside an async Task method sets the task to Faulted and stores the exception there. It is rethrown only at await (or .Result/.Wait), so an un-awaited task fails silently.

prompt: What happens when an int is assigned to a variable of type object?
optionA: The variable stores a reference to the int on the stack
optionB: Nothing; the int and object variables share one slot
optionC: The int is turned into a string so object can hold it
optionD: A heap object is created holding a copy of the int
correctAnswerText: A heap object is created holding a copy of the int
explanation: Boxing copies the value into a new heap object and stores a reference to it. Later changes to the original int do not affect the boxed copy, and each box costs an allocation.

prompt: How does the .NET garbage collector decide an object can be freed?
optionA: It has not been used for longer than a set number of seconds
optionB: Its variable has been set to null by the code that made it
optionC: Its reference count drops to zero after the last assignment
optionD: No chain of references from any root reaches it any more
correctAnswerText: No chain of references from any root reaches it any more
explanation: The GC marks everything reachable from roots — locals on stacks, statics, CPU registers — and frees the rest. .NET does not count references, so cycles are collected too.

prompt: Why does calling cts.Cancel() not stop a loop that was given the token but never checks it?
optionA: Cancellation is cooperative: the work must observe the token
optionB: The loop must be started with Task.Run for Cancel to work
optionC: Cancel aborts the thread, but only after a timeout passes
optionD: Cancel only takes effect once the CPU becomes idle again
correctAnswerText: Cancellation is cooperative: the work must observe the token
explanation: A token just carries a flag. Code must check IsCancellationRequested, call ThrowIfCancellationRequested, or pass the token on to async APIs that honour it. Nothing forcibly stops a thread.

prompt: Why does a SqlConnection need Dispose when the garbage collector will reclaim its memory anyway?
optionA: Without Dispose the object is never garbage collected at all
optionB: The GC frees memory, not the pooled connection the object holds
optionC: Dispose turns the object into a value type for faster reuse
optionD: Dispose frees the memory sooner than the GC would on its own
correctAnswerText: The GC frees memory, not the pooled connection the object holds
explanation: The connection is a scarce unmanaged resource returned to the pool by Dispose/Close. The GC runs when memory is short, not when connections are, so waiting for it exhausts the pool.

optionB: abcde
optionC: acbde
optionD: abced
correctAnswerText: abcde
explanation: Outer runs a, then calls Inner, which runs b and hits an incomplete await. Inner returns an incomplete task, so Outer's await also returns to Main, which prints c. After the delay d prints, then e.

optionA: prq7
optionB: pr7q
optionC: rpq7
optionD: pqr7
correctAnswerText: pqr7
explanation: Task.FromResult is already complete, so await does not suspend: the method runs straight through, printing p and q, before returning a completed task. Main then prints r and 7.

optionA: About 2 seconds: WhenAll runs them one after another
optionB: About 2 seconds: each await blocks a thread in turn
optionC: About 1 second: both calls are in flight together
optionD: About 0 seconds: WhenAll returns before they finish
correctAnswerText: About 1 second: both calls are in flight together
explanation: Calling both methods starts both operations before anything is awaited, so they overlap and WhenAll completes when the slower finishes. Awaiting each call on its own line would take about 2 seconds.

optionA: q 2
optionB: none
optionC: p 3
optionD: p 2
correctAnswerText: p 2
explanation: await on a faulted WhenAll rethrows only the first exception, from the first failing task, "p". The task itself keeps both failures (not the success): t.Exception holds two inner exceptions.

optionA: Faulted
optionB: ranRanToCompletion
optionC: ranCanceled
optionD: Canceled
correctAnswerText: Canceled
explanation: The token passed to Task.Run is already cancelled, so the delegate never starts — "ran" is not printed — and the task ends in the Canceled state. Wait throws an AggregateException, which is caught.
Assigning to object boxes a copy of 5 on the heap. Changing x afterwards changes only the local int, so the box still holds 5.
Raise gets a copy of the struct, so its change is lost; RaiseRef works on the caller's variable, making X 2. A class argument copies the reference, so RaiseBox changes the one shared object.

prompt: Many threads record a sale by adding to both total and count, and a report divides total by count. Which fix keeps the two consistent?
optionA: Use Interlocked.Add on total and Interlocked.Increment on count
optionB: Wrap each update in Task.Run so each one runs separately
optionC: Mark both fields volatile so every thread sees fresh values
optionD: Update both fields inside one lock on a private object
correctAnswerText: Update both fields inside one lock on a private object
explanation: Interlocked makes each field atomic on its own, but a reader can still see the new total with the old count. A lock makes the pair change together and lets the reader take the same lock.

prompt: A call to a slow partner API must give up after 3 seconds. Which code applies the timeout correctly?
optionA: using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3)); await CallAsync(cts.Token);
optionB: var t = CallAsync(CancellationToken.None); Thread.Sleep(3000); if (!t.IsCompleted) return null; return t.Result;
optionC: await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3)); await CallAsync(CancellationToken.None);
optionD: await CallAsync(new CancellationToken(true)); await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3));
correctAnswerText: using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3)); await CallAsync(cts.Token);
explanation: A source created with a TimeSpan cancels itself after that time, and the token passed into the call (which must honour it) ends the work. using var is C# 8; older code uses a using block.

optionA: fast False
optionB: slow True
optionC: fast True
optionD: slow False
correctAnswerText: fast False
explanation: WhenAny completes with the first task to finish, the 50 ms one. The slow task is not cancelled; it is simply still running, so IsCompleted is False at that moment.

optionA: InvalidOperationException AggregateException
optionB: AggregateException InvalidOperationException
optionC: AggregateException AggregateException
optionD: InvalidOperationException InvalidOperationException
correctAnswerText: AggregateException InvalidOperationException
explanation: Wait and Result wrap a task's failure in an AggregateException. await unwraps it and rethrows the original exception, which is one more reason to await rather than block.

optionA: Cancel was called inside the task, which is never allowed
optionB: ThrowIfCancellationRequested always produces a Faulted task status
optionC: The token was not passed to Task.Run, so the throw counts as an error
optionD: Task.Run ignores cancellation unless the delegate is async
correctAnswerText: The token was not passed to Task.Run, so the throw counts as an error
explanation: A task becomes Canceled when it throws OperationCanceledException for the same token it was started with. Started without the token, the exception is treated as an ordinary failure. Pass cts.Token as Task.Run's second argument.

optionA: await blocks a thread, so the calls fight for the pool
optionB: The three methods must be marked async void to overlap
optionC: await adds a full second of overhead to every call
optionD: Each call starts only after the previous one finishes
correctAnswerText: Each call starts only after the previous one finishes
explanation: Awaiting each call before starting the next makes them sequential. Start all three first (var s = GetSalesAsync(); ...), then await Task.WhenAll, for about 1 second in total.

prompt: A worker calls async void SendReceiptAsync(), wrapped in try/catch. The email server fails and the whole process crashes despite the catch. Why?
optionA: The catch block needs its own await keyword before it can ever run
optionB: async void has no Task, so its exception escapes the caller's catch
optionC: try/catch does not work in a method that calls async code
optionD: Network exceptions can never be caught in managed C# code
correctAnswerText: async void has no Task, so its exception escapes the caller's catch
explanation: The call returns at the first await, leaving the try block. The later exception has no Task to live in, so it is raised on the synchronization context or thread pool, which crashes the process.

prompt: Transfer(a, b) locks a then b; Transfer(b, a) runs at the same time on another thread. Occasionally both threads hang at 0% CPU. What is the cause?
optionA: The thread pool ran out of threads and stopped both
optionB: lock cannot be used twice in one method, so it spins
optionC: The accounts were boxed, so the locks never matched
optionD: Each holds one lock and waits for the other's: a deadlock
correctAnswerText: Each holds one lock and waits for the other's: a deadlock
explanation: Thread 1 holds a and wants b while thread 2 holds b and wants a; neither can proceed. Always take locks in one global order (for example by account id).

prompt: A singleton cache uses a plain Dictionary<string, Product>, filled from many request threads at once. Under load it throws odd exceptions and sometimes loses entries. What is the cause?
optionA: Product objects are collected while they are still in the cache
optionB: Dictionary is not safe for concurrent writes; its state gets corrupted
optionC: string keys are compared by reference across different threads
optionD: The cache needs to be scoped per request, not a singleton
correctAnswerText: Dictionary is not safe for concurrent writes; its state gets corrupted
explanation: Concurrent Adds can corrupt Dictionary's internal arrays. Use ConcurrentDictionary (GetOrAdd) or guard every access with a lock. A singleton is fine once its state is thread-safe.

prompt: Memory climbs steadily in a long-running service. A heap snapshot shows thousands of old ReportView objects kept alive by a static event, AppEvents.Refresh. Why are they not collected?
optionA: ReportView objects were boxed and moved to generation 3
optionB: Static classes block the GC from running in that process
optionC: The GC only collects objects that implement IDisposable
optionD: The static event holds a reference to each subscribed view
correctAnswerText: The static event holds a reference to each subscribed view
explanation: A static is a GC root, and an event holds delegates that reference each subscriber. Every view that subscribed and never unsubscribed stays reachable. Unsubscribe when the view is done.

prompt: An ASP.NET Core API calls GetAsync(...).Result in every action. It is fine in testing but under load requests queue for seconds and CPU is low. What is happening?
optionA: Blocked request threads starve the thread pool
optionB: .Result runs the call twice, doubling the load
optionC: The JSON serializer locks when Result is used
optionD: A SynchronizationContext deadlock in every request
correctAnswerText: Blocked request threads starve the thread pool
explanation: ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so there is no classic deadlock, but each request holds a pool thread blocked in .Result. Under load the pool runs out and new work waits for threads to be injected.

prompt: An action starts two queries on the same EF Core DbContext and awaits them together with Task.WhenAll. It throws InvalidOperationException saying a second operation started before a previous one completed. Why?
optionA: Task.WhenAll cannot be used with database queries at all
optionB: A DbContext is not thread-safe and runs one operation at a time
optionC: DbContext needs ConfigureAwait(false) before it allows two
optionD: The two queries must be written with the same LINQ operator
correctAnswerText: A DbContext is not thread-safe and runs one operation at a time
explanation: A DbContext tracks one connection and one operation at a time. Await the queries one after another, or give each concurrent query its own context (for example from IDbContextFactory).

prompt: An action takes a CancellationToken ct, but when the browser disconnects the 20-second report query keeps running. The query is await db.Orders.ToListAsync(). What is missing?
optionA: ct is never passed on, so ToListAsync cannot see it
optionB: ToListAsync must be swapped for the synchronous ToList
optionC: ASP.NET Core does not support cancelling requests
optionD: The action must catch OperationCanceledException first
correctAnswerText: ct is never passed on, so ToListAsync cannot see it
explanation: A token only works where it is passed. ToListAsync(ct) lets EF Core cancel the command when the request is aborted; without it the token is never observed.

prompt: A team fixes a hanging WinForms button by replacing .Result with .GetAwaiter().GetResult(). Which judgement is right?
optionA: It is ideal, since it also unwraps the AggregateException
optionB: It fixes the hang because GetResult never captures the context
optionC: It is fine, provided the call is wrapped in a try/catch
optionD: It still blocks the UI thread; make the handler async and await
correctAnswerText: It still blocks the UI thread; make the handler async and await
explanation: GetAwaiter().GetResult() only changes how the exception surfaces; it blocks exactly like .Result, so the deadlock remains. An async void event handler that awaits is the right fix — the one place async void belongs.

prompt: A desktop app freezes while it resizes 500 photos on a button click. Which design is right?
optionA: await Task.Run for the CPU work so the UI thread stays free
optionB: Call Thread.Sleep between photos to let the UI repaint
optionC: Mark the method async and leave the resizing loop as it is
optionD: Use .Result on each resize so they finish one at a time
correctAnswerText: await Task.Run for the CPU work so the UI thread stays free
explanation: Resizing is CPU-bound, so marking the method async alone keeps the work on the UI thread. Task.Run moves it to the pool and await brings the result back. On a web server the same Task.Run would just swap one pool thread for another.

prompt: A web API counts hits per URL across all requests. Which design is the best fit?
optionA: A plain Dictionary, since requests never truly overlap
optionB: A lock around a Dictionary held for the whole request
optionC: A [ThreadStatic] Dictionary so each thread has its own
optionD: ConcurrentDictionary with AddOrUpdate for each URL's count
correctAnswerText: ConcurrentDictionary with AddOrUpdate for each URL's count
explanation: AddOrUpdate atomically creates or increments one key with fine-grained locking inside. A plain Dictionary corrupts, a request-long lock serialises the API, and per-thread copies never add up to a total.

prompt: A job must call a partner API for 10,000 invoices; the partner allows 10 calls at a time. Which design is right?
optionA: Limit concurrency, e.g. a SemaphoreSlim(10) around each call
optionB: Await each call in turn, one after another, for safety
optionC: Wrap each call in Task.Run so the pool spreads the load
optionD: Start all 10,000 tasks and Task.WhenAll them at once
correctAnswerText: Limit concurrency, e.g. a SemaphoreSlim(10) around each call
explanation: Unbounded WhenAll fires 10,000 calls and gets throttled or banned; strict one-by-one wastes the allowed parallelism. A SemaphoreSlim (or Parallel.ForEachAsync with MaxDegreeOfParallelism, .NET 6) keeps exactly ten in flight.

prompt: A search endpoint calls a service, which calls a repository, which runs an EF Core query. How should cancellation be designed?
optionA: Check a static IsCancelled flag inside the repository
optionB: Cancel by throwing an exception from the controller
optionC: Accept a CancellationToken in each layer and pass it down
optionD: Let the query finish; cancelling DB calls is unsafe
correctAnswerText: Accept a CancellationToken in each layer and pass it down
explanation: The framework supplies the request-aborted token to the action; passing it through every async method lets the query itself stop when the user leaves. Static flags affect every request at once.

prompt: A geometry library creates millions of short-lived 2D points of two doubles each. Is a struct a good choice for the point type?
optionA: No: a struct is always slower than a class in every case
optionB: Yes: structs are garbage collected sooner than classes
optionC: No: a struct cannot have methods, so it cannot compute
optionD: Yes: small, immutable value data avoids millions of heap objects
correctAnswerText: Yes: small, immutable value data avoids millions of heap objects
explanation: A small immutable struct lives inline (in arrays, locals and fields) with no per-object allocation or GC work. Large or mutable structs are the trap: copying is costly and edits land on copies.

prompt: A developer adds GC.Collect() at the end of every API request to "keep memory low". Which judgement is right?
optionA: Keep it: the GC never runs on its own in an ASP.NET Core app
optionB: Remove it: forced full collections cost CPU and pause the app
optionC: Move it to the start of each request so it runs earlier
optionD: Keep it: it also closes connections that were left open
correctAnswerText: Remove it: forced full collections cost CPU and pause the app
explanation: The GC tunes itself to allocation patterns; forcing full blocking collections every request burns CPU and adds pauses without freeing anything still reachable. Fix leaks and dispose resources instead.

prompt: A team writes a NuGet library that may be called from WPF apps and from ASP.NET Core. Where does ConfigureAwait(false) belong?
optionA: Only around the first await in each method, never the rest
optionB: On the library's awaits, so it never needs the caller's context
optionC: Nowhere: it is obsolete in .NET 8 and is ignored at run time
optionD: Only in the WPF app's button handlers, which own the UI context
correctAnswerText: On the library's awaits, so it never needs the caller's context
explanation: Library code does not touch the UI, so resuming on any thread is safe and avoids deadlocks if a caller blocks. UI code must resume on the UI thread, and ASP.NET Core app code gains nothing from it.

prompt: A ReportWriter class opens a FileStream in its constructor and keeps it as a field. What is the right design?
optionA: Rely on the garbage collector to close the stream later
optionB: Open a new FileStream on every write and never close it
optionC: Add a finaliser as the only place the stream is closed
optionD: ReportWriter implements IDisposable and disposes its stream
correctAnswerText: ReportWriter implements IDisposable and disposes its stream
explanation: A class that owns a disposable field becomes disposable itself, so callers can use using. The GC and finalisers run at unpredictable times, keeping the file locked meanwhile.

prompt: An order API calls _ = SendEmailAsync(order) without awaiting, so the response is faster. Which judgement is right?
optionA: It is fine, since an un-awaited task always retries on failure
optionB: Use async void instead, so that any errors are logged for you
optionC: It is fine: ASP.NET Core waits for every task before shutdown
optionD: Failures vanish unobserved; queue the email to a background worker
correctAnswerText: Failures vanish unobserved; queue the email to a background worker
explanation: An un-awaited task's exception is stored and never seen, and the work can die with the request or an app restart. A queue processed by a hosted BackgroundService (or a durable queue) gives retries and logging.

prompt: Which NuGet package is the current SQL Server provider for ADO.NET in a new .NET 8 project?
optionA: Microsoft.SqlServer.Smo
optionB: System.Data.OleDb
optionC: Microsoft.Data.SqlClient
optionD: System.Data.SqlClient
correctAnswerText: Microsoft.Data.SqlClient
explanation: Microsoft.Data.SqlClient is the actively developed provider. System.Data.SqlClient is the legacy one, frozen apart from security fixes; OleDb is a generic Windows bridge and SMO is a management library.

prompt: Which SqlCommand method runs an UPDATE and returns the number of rows it changed?
optionA: ExecuteXmlReader()
optionB: ExecuteReader()
optionC: ExecuteNonQuery()
optionD: ExecuteScalar()
correctAnswerText: ExecuteNonQuery()
explanation: ExecuteNonQuery is for INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and DDL and returns rows affected. ExecuteScalar returns one value, and ExecuteReader streams rows.

prompt: Which ADO.NET class is a forward-only, read-only stream over the rows a SELECT returns?
optionA: SqlBulkCopy
optionB: SqlParameter
optionC: SqlDataReader
optionD: SqlDataAdapter
correctAnswerText: SqlDataReader
explanation: ExecuteReader returns a SqlDataReader, which hands you each row once, in order. SqlDataAdapter fills DataSets, SqlBulkCopy loads many rows in, and SqlParameter is a bound value.

prompt: In ADO.NET, what value stands for a database NULL, both in a reader column and in a parameter?
optionA: DBNull.Value
optionB: null
optionC: default(object)
optionD: string.Empty
correctAnswerText: DBNull.Value
explanation: ADO.NET uses the singleton DBNull.Value for SQL NULL. A C# null parameter value means "not supplied", and default(object) is just null again.

prompt: What is the default Max Pool Size for a SqlClient connection pool?
explanation: SqlClient pools are capped at 100 physical connections per connection string unless Max Pool Size says otherwise. Min Pool Size defaults to 0.

prompt: How long may a SqlCommand run, by default, before it fails with an execution timeout?
optionA: No limit at all
optionB: 30 seconds
optionC: 60 seconds
optionD: 15 seconds
correctAnswerText: 30 seconds
explanation: CommandTimeout defaults to 30 seconds. The 15-second default belongs to Connect Timeout, which limits opening a connection, not running a command.

prompt: Which connection-string setting logs in with the Windows account running the program, with no password?
optionA: Integrated Security=True
optionB: TrustServerCertificate=True
optionC: Persist Security Info=True
optionD: Encrypt=Optional
correctAnswerText: Integrated Security=True
explanation: Integrated Security=True (or Trusted_Connection=True) uses Windows authentication. TrustServerCertificate skips certificate validation, and Persist Security Info controls whether the password stays readable.

prompt: What is Dapper?
optionA: A full ORM that generates SQL from LINQ and tracks changes to entities
optionB: A micro-ORM: extension methods on IDbConnection that map rows to objects
optionC: A connection pool that replaces the one built into Microsoft.Data.SqlClient
optionD: A SQL Server tool for designing tables and diagrams inside SSMS itself
correctAnswerText: A micro-ORM: extension methods on IDbConnection that map rows to objects
explanation: Dapper runs the SQL you write and maps the result columns to properties by name. It does not generate SQL or track changes — that is EF Core.

prompt: Which call starts a local transaction on an open SqlConnection conn?
optionA: conn.EnlistTransaction()
optionB: new SqlTransaction(conn)
optionC: conn.StartTransaction()
optionD: conn.BeginTransaction()
correctAnswerText: conn.BeginTransaction()
explanation: BeginTransaction (or BeginTransactionAsync) returns a SqlTransaction for that connection. SqlTransaction has no public constructor, and EnlistTransaction joins an existing System.Transactions transaction.

prompt: Which class assembles a connection string from parts and quotes each value correctly?
optionA: SqlCommandBuilder
optionB: StringBuilder
optionC: DbProviderFactory
optionD: SqlConnectionStringBuilder
correctAnswerText: SqlConnectionStringBuilder
explanation: SqlConnectionStringBuilder has typed properties (DataSource, InitialCatalog, Password) and escapes values, so a password with a semicolon cannot break the string. SqlCommandBuilder generates commands for a DataAdapter.

prompt: Why does a parameter such as @email stop SQL injection when string concatenation does not?
optionA: SqlClient deletes quote characters from every value before it is sent
optionB: SQL Server refuses any command whose text contains the word OR or DROP
optionC: Parameters are encrypted, so an attacker cannot read the query in transit
optionD: The SQL text is fixed and the value travels separately, never parsed as SQL
correctAnswerText: The SQL text is fixed and the value travels separately, never parsed as SQL
explanation: With a parameter, the statement is compiled with a placeholder and the value is bound to it (via sp_executesql), so input can only ever be data. Concatenation makes input part of the code.

prompt: Why is cmd.Parameters.AddWithValue("@code", code) risky when Code is an indexed VARCHAR column?
optionA: It sends the value as plain text inside the SQL, so injection becomes possible
optionB: It sends a C# string as NVARCHAR, so the column side is converted and may scan
optionC: It always sends NVARCHAR(MAX), which SQL Server refuses for VARCHAR columns
optionD: It cannot send strings at all and silently passes the value as an integer
correctAnswerText: It sends a C# string as NVARCHAR, so the column side is converted and may scan
explanation: AddWithValue infers the SQL type from the .NET type: string becomes NVARCHAR sized to the value. The implicit conversion can turn a seek into a scan, and varying sizes cache several plans. It is still a real parameter.

prompt: With pooling on, what actually happens when a SqlConnection is disposed?
optionA: Its physical connection is reset and returned to the pool for reuse
optionB: The TCP connection to SQL Server is closed and its login is dropped
optionC: Nothing happens until the garbage collector finalises the object later
optionD: The connection stays open and bound to this thread for its next use
correctAnswerText: Its physical connection is reset and returned to the pool for reuse
explanation: Dispose and Close hand the physical connection back to the pool, so the next Open with the same string is cheap. That is why a new SqlConnection per unit of work is the right pattern.

prompt: What does switching an API's ExecuteReader to await ExecuteReaderAsync improve?
optionA: The thread is freed during the wait, so the server handles more requests
optionB: The query runs on several threads, splitting its rows between them
optionC: The result is cached, so a second identical query skips the database
optionD: Each query runs faster on SQL Server, as async queries get a better plan
correctAnswerText: The thread is freed during the wait, so the server handles more requests
explanation: Async does not speed up one query; it returns the thread to the pool while waiting on the network, so the same threads serve more concurrent requests.

prompt: Why is TrustServerCertificate=True acceptable on a dev laptop but not in production?
optionA: It disables encryption entirely, so passwords cross the network in clear
optionB: It makes every login use the sa account instead of the configured user
optionC: It skips validating the server certificate, which allows impersonation
optionD: It turns off connection pooling, which only matters on a busy server
correctAnswerText: It skips validating the server certificate, which allows impersonation
explanation: The connection is still encrypted, but any certificate is accepted, so a man-in-the-middle could pose as the server. Locally the self-signed certificate is the only one; production should have a trusted one.

prompt: Two services in one process build connection strings that differ only in key order. How does pooling treat them?
optionA: Pooling is turned off for both, since the strings are ambiguous
optionB: As two separate pools, because a pool is keyed by the exact string
optionC: As one pool, because SqlClient normalises the keys before matching
optionD: As one pool per thread, whatever the connection strings contain
correctAnswerText: As two separate pools, because a pool is keyed by the exact string
explanation: SqlClient keeps one pool per distinct connection string per process, so trivially different strings split the connections. Keep one string in configuration.

prompt: Why look up columns with reader.GetOrdinal("Price") once rather than hard-coding GetDecimal(3)?
optionA: GetOrdinal makes the reader cache the column, so later rows read faster
optionB: Hard-coded positions start at 1, so GetDecimal(3) reads the fourth column
optionC: GetDecimal only accepts ordinals returned by GetOrdinal, not plain numbers
optionD: A hard-coded position breaks silently when the SELECT columns are reordered
correctAnswerText: A hard-coded position breaks silently when the SELECT columns are reordered
explanation: Ordinals are zero-based positions in the SELECT. If someone adds or reorders a column, index 3 now reads something else. GetOrdinal finds it by name and throws early if it is missing.

prompt: Why should a data-access method return a List<Product> rather than the SqlDataReader it read from?
optionA: A SqlDataReader cannot be passed between methods of different classes
optionB: Returning a reader exposes the connection string to the calling code
optionC: Lists are read from SQL Server faster than a reader can stream the rows
optionD: A reader needs its connection open, and the method disposes that connection
correctAnswerText: A reader needs its connection open, and the method disposes that connection
explanation: The reader is a live cursor on a busy connection. Once the method's using disposes the connection, the reader is dead; if it is not disposed, the connection leaks. Map to objects and return them.

prompt: Why is UPDATE Seats SET Left = Left - 1 WHERE ShowId = @s AND Left > 0 safer than reading Left into C#, checking it, then updating?
optionA: Read-then-write is fine; both are equally safe with two concurrent users
optionB: Reading into C# is slower, and the extra time is the only problem it causes
optionC: A single UPDATE is always sent through a serializable transaction by SqlClient
optionD: The check and the change happen atomically in one statement under a lock
correctAnswerText: The check and the change happen atomically in one statement under a lock
explanation: Between a separate read and write another request can take the last seat too. The guarded UPDATE checks and decrements the row while holding its lock; a row count of 0 means "sold out".

prompt: Code moved from conn.BeginTransaction() to new TransactionScope() and now blocks far more under load. Why?
optionA: TransactionScope opens a second connection for every command
optionB: TransactionScope commits only when the process exits normally
optionC: TransactionScope defaults to Serializable, not ReadCommitted
optionD: TransactionScope disables connection pooling for its connections
correctAnswerText: TransactionScope defaults to Serializable, not ReadCommitted
explanation: BeginTransaction uses SQL Server's ReadCommitted default; a new TransactionScope uses Serializable, which holds range locks. Pass TransactionOptions with ReadCommitted to match.

prompt: string? middleName may be null, and the column MiddleName allows NULL. Which line sets the parameter correctly?
optionA: cmd.Parameters.Add("@mid", SqlDbType.NVarChar, 50).Value = middleName ?? string.Empty;
optionB: cmd.Parameters.Add("@mid", SqlDbType.NVarChar, 50).Value = middleName;
optionC: cmd.Parameters.Add("@mid", SqlDbType.NVarChar, 50).Value = (object?)middleName ?? DBNull.Value;
optionD: cmd.Parameters.Add("@mid", SqlDbType.NVarChar, 50).Value = middleName ?? "NULL";
correctAnswerText: cmd.Parameters.Add("@mid", SqlDbType.NVarChar, 50).Value = (object?)middleName ?? DBNull.Value;
explanation: A null Value means "not supplied" and the command fails; DBNull.Value sends SQL NULL. "NULL" stores the four letters, and string.Empty stores an empty string, which is not NULL.

prompt: PaidOn is a nullable DATETIME2 column at ordinal ord. Which line reads it into DateTime? paidOn?
optionA: DateTime? paidOn = reader[ord] == null ? null : reader.GetDateTime(ord);
optionB: DateTime? paidOn = reader.IsDBNull(ord) ? null : reader.GetDateTime(ord);
optionC: DateTime? paidOn = (DateTime?)reader.GetValue(ord);
optionD: DateTime? paidOn = reader.GetDateTime(ord) ?? null;
correctAnswerText: DateTime? paidOn = reader.IsDBNull(ord) ? null : reader.GetDateTime(ord);
explanation: IsDBNull checks first, because GetDateTime throws on NULL. reader[ord] is DBNull.Value, never null, and casting DBNull to DateTime? throws InvalidCastException.

prompt: You insert a student and need the new INT IDENTITY id via (int)cmd.ExecuteScalar(). Which CommandText works?
optionA: INSERT INTO Students (Name) VALUES (@name); SELECT @@ROWCOUNT AS Id
optionB: INSERT INTO Students (Name) VALUES (@name) RETURNING Id INTO @id
optionC: INSERT INTO Students (Name) VALUES (@name); SELECT SCOPE_IDENTITY()
optionD: INSERT INTO Students (Name) OUTPUT INSERTED.Id VALUES (@name)
correctAnswerText: INSERT INTO Students (Name) OUTPUT INSERTED.Id VALUES (@name)
explanation: OUTPUT INSERTED.Id returns the identity as int. SCOPE_IDENTITY() is numeric(38,0), a boxed decimal that (int) cannot unbox; @@ROWCOUNT is the row count, and RETURNING is not T-SQL.

prompt: A search box should find courses whose Title contains the typed term. Which command is both correct and safe?
optionA: Text "WHERE Title LIKE %@t%", with @t set to term as typed
optionB: Text $"WHERE Title LIKE '%{term}%'", with no parameter added
optionC: Text "WHERE Title LIKE @t", with @t set to "%" + term + "%"
optionD: Text "WHERE Title LIKE '%@t%'", with @t set to term as typed
correctAnswerText: Text "WHERE Title LIKE @t", with @t set to "%" + term + "%"
explanation: The wildcards belong in the parameter value. Inside quotes, '%@t%' is a literal string containing the characters @t, the interpolated version is injectable, and %@t% is a syntax error.

prompt: You need a student's most recent login from Logins, where a student has many rows. Which Dapper call fits?
optionA: QuerySingleOrDefault<Login>("SELECT * FROM Logins WHERE StudentId = @Id ORDER BY At DESC", new { Id = id })
optionB: Execute("SELECT TOP (1) * FROM Logins WHERE StudentId = @Id ORDER BY At DESC", new { Id = id })
optionC: QuerySingle<Login>("SELECT * FROM Logins WHERE StudentId = @Id ORDER BY At DESC", new { Id = id })
optionD: QueryFirstOrDefault<Login>("SELECT TOP (1) * FROM Logins WHERE StudentId = @Id ORDER BY At DESC", new { Id = id })
correctAnswerText: QueryFirstOrDefault<Login>("SELECT TOP (1) * FROM Logins WHERE StudentId = @Id ORDER BY At DESC", new { Id = id })
explanation: Order newest first and take the first row, or null if none. QuerySingle* throws when more than one row comes back, and Execute returns a row count, not an object.

prompt: An API takes ?sort=fee or ?sort=title for a course list. How should the ORDER BY be built?
optionA: Concatenate the input as typed, since ORDER BY cannot run other statements
optionB: Add @sort as a parameter and write ORDER BY @sort in the command text
optionC: Concatenate the input after removing any single-quote characters from it
optionD: Switch on the input to a fixed column name, defaulting to one safe column
correctAnswerText: Switch on the input to a fixed column name, defaulting to one safe column
explanation: A parameter is a value, so ORDER BY @sort sorts by a constant. Concatenation is injectable whatever is stripped. Map the input to a known column in C# and reject or default the rest.

prompt: Inside using var tx = conn.BeginTransaction();, which line creates a command that runs within that transaction?
optionA: using var cmd = new SqlCommand(sql, conn); tx.Enlist(cmd);
optionB: using var cmd = new SqlCommand(sql, conn, tx);
optionC: using var cmd = tx.Connection.CreateCommand(sql, autoEnlist: true);
optionD: using var cmd = new SqlCommand(sql, new SqlConnection(cs), tx);
correctAnswerText: using var cmd = new SqlCommand(sql, conn, tx);
explanation: Pass the transaction (or set cmd.Transaction = tx) and use the transaction's own connection. A transaction belongs to one connection, and the last two methods do not exist.

prompt: An ASP.NET Core action receives a CancellationToken ct. Which body for reading rows asynchronously is right?
optionA: await using var c = new SqlConnection(cs); await c.OpenAsync(ct); ... while (await r.ReadAsync(ct)) { ... }
optionB: using var c = new SqlConnection(cs); c.OpenAsync(ct).Wait(); ... while (r.ReadAsync(ct).Result) { ... }
optionC: await using var c = new SqlConnection(cs); c.Open(); ... while (r.Read()) { await Task.Yield(); }
optionD: var c = new SqlConnection(cs); await c.OpenAsync(); ... while (await r.ReadAsync()) { ... } // no dispose
correctAnswerText: await using var c = new SqlConnection(cs); await c.OpenAsync(ct); ... while (await r.ReadAsync(ct)) { ... }
explanation: Use the Async methods, await them, dispose with await using and pass ct so a disconnected client cancels the query. .Wait() and .Result block a thread, and the third version leaks the connection.

prompt: With plain ADO.NET (no Dapper), how do you safely query WHERE Id IN (...) for a List<int> ids of varying length?
optionA: Build IN (1,2,3) with string.Join, since ints from a List are always safe
optionB: Add one parameter @ids whose value is the List<int> itself, as IN (@ids)
optionC: Generate @p0, @p1, ... in the SQL and add one Int parameter per id
optionD: Add one parameter @ids holding string.Join(",", ids), as IN (@ids)
correctAnswerText: Generate @p0, @p1, ... in the SQL and add one Int parameter per id
explanation: Each value needs its own placeholder (or a table-valued parameter). A single @ids holding "1,2,3" is one string, not three numbers, and SqlClient cannot bind a List as a scalar.

prompt: A transfer transaction occasionally fails with a SqlException chosen as deadlock victim. How should the code respond?
optionA: catch (SqlException ex) when (ex.Number == 1205): rerun only the failed command
optionB: Raise CommandTimeout to 300 seconds so the deadlock has time to clear
optionC: catch (SqlException ex) when (ex.Number == 1205): rerun the whole transaction
optionD: Catch every SqlException and commit whatever part already succeeded
correctAnswerText: catch (SqlException ex) when (ex.Number == 1205): rerun the whole transaction
explanation: Error 1205 means SQL Server rolled the victim's transaction back, so all its work is gone and the whole unit must be retried (a few times at most). A timeout does not resolve deadlocks.

prompt:
while (reader.Read()) { var tutor = new SqlCommand("SELECT Name FROM Tutors WHERE Id = @id", conn); ... tutor.ExecuteScalar(); }
This throws on the first row. What is the cause and the better fix?
optionA: The reader is closed by Read(); call reader.Open() again before ExecuteScalar
optionB: Commands cannot be created inside a loop; create the tutor command beforehand
optionC: The connection is busy with the open reader; JOIN Tutors into the first query
optionD: ExecuteScalar is not allowed in a loop; call ExecuteReader for each tutor row
correctAnswerText: The connection is busy with the open reader; JOIN Tutors into the first query
explanation: One connection serves one open reader, hence "There is already an open DataReader...". MARS would hide it, but a query per row is N+1; one JOIN fetches the names together.

optionA: The INSERT is rolled back first, so ExecuteScalar returns DBNull.Value instead
optionB: ExecuteScalar cannot run two statements, so it returns the SQL text as a string
optionC: SCOPE_IDENTITY() returns numeric, so the boxed value is a decimal, not an int
optionD: ExecuteScalar returns the row count of the INSERT, which is a long, not an int
correctAnswerText: SCOPE_IDENTITY() returns numeric, so the boxed value is a decimal, not an int
explanation: SCOPE_IDENTITY() is numeric(38,0), which SqlClient returns as a boxed decimal, and unboxing to int fails. Use OUTPUT INSERTED.Id, CAST(SCOPE_IDENTITY() AS int), or Convert.ToInt32.

optionA: Returning null from a data method makes SqlClient mark the pool as broken
optionB: The pool is too small by default and needs Max Pool Size set to a thousand
optionC: Close() does not return connections to the pool; only Dispose() does that
optionD: The early return skips Close, so each such call keeps a pooled connection
correctAnswerText: The early return skips Close, so each such call keeps a pooled connection
explanation: Every early return (or exception) leaks a connection until the pool's 100 are gone. Close and Dispose are equivalent; using var conn makes release happen on every path.

prompt: After conn.BeginTransaction(), the first command runs but the second throws "ExecuteNonQuery requires the command to have a transaction...". What is wrong?
optionA: ExecuteNonQuery is not allowed inside transactions; use Scalar
optionB: The second command was created without the transaction object
optionC: The first command already committed the transaction implicitly
optionD: Only one command may run inside a SqlTransaction at any time
correctAnswerText: The second command was created without the transaction object
explanation: Once a connection has a pending local transaction, every command on it must carry that transaction. Pass tx to the constructor or set cmd.Transaction = tx.

prompt:
cmd.Parameters.Add("@phone", SqlDbType.VarChar, 15).Value = student.Phone;
For students with no phone it fails: "...expects the parameter '@phone', which was not supplied." Why?
optionA: student.Phone is a C# null, which SqlClient treats as no value at all
optionB: VarChar parameters must be at least 50 long to accept missing values
optionC: The column is NOT NULL, and SQL Server reports that in these words
optionD: The parameter name must not start with @ when it is added from C#
correctAnswerText: student.Phone is a C# null, which SqlClient treats as no value at all
explanation: A null Value is not sent, so the query sees @phone as missing. Send (object?)student.Phone ?? DBNull.Value for SQL NULL. A NOT NULL violation would give a different error.

prompt:
string? note = reader["Note"] == null ? null : reader.GetString(reader.GetOrdinal("Note"));
Rows with a NULL Note throw "Data is Null". Why does the check not help?
optionA: reader["Note"] reads the column, which moves the reader to the next row
optionB: reader["Note"] is DBNull.Value for NULL, so the comparison with null is false
optionC: GetOrdinal throws for NULL columns, before the GetString call is reached
optionD: The indexer returns an empty string for NULL, so the check never matches
correctAnswerText: reader["Note"] is DBNull.Value for NULL, so the comparison with null is false
explanation: A NULL column comes back as DBNull.Value, which is an object, not null; the test is false and GetString then throws SqlNullValueException. Use reader.IsDBNull(ord).

prompt: A DBA changed Payments.Id from INT to BIGINT. The unchanged code reader.GetInt32(0) now fails. Why?
optionA: BIGINT values come back as strings, so only GetString can read them
optionB: Typed getters do not convert; a bigint column must be read with GetInt64
optionC: GetInt32 reads only the first four bytes and so returns a wrong number
optionD: Changing a column type invalidates every reader until the app restarts
correctAnswerText: Typed getters do not convert; a bigint column must be read with GetInt64
explanation: SqlDataReader getters require the matching type: bigint is long, so GetInt32 throws InvalidCastException. Update the getter and the C# property to long.

prompt:
string cs = "Server=localhost\SQLEXPRESS;Database=Shop;Integrated Security=True";
written exactly like that in a C# file (one backslash). What happens?
optionA: It does not compile: \S is an unrecognised escape sequence
optionB: It compiles, and SqlClient fails with "Login failed" at Open
optionC: It compiles and connects, since SqlClient fixes the backslash
optionD: It connects to the default instance, ignoring the \SQLEXPRESS part
correctAnswerText: It does not compile: \S is an unrecognised escape sequence
explanation: In a regular string literal \S is not a valid escape, so the compiler reports CS1009. Write "localhost\\SQLEXPRESS" or a verbatim string @"localhost\SQLEXPRESS".

prompt: An app moved from System.Data.SqlClient to Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 5 and now fails against a local SQL Server: "The certificate chain was issued by an authority that is not trusted." Why?
optionA: Microsoft.Data.SqlClient supports only Windows logins, not SQL Server logins
optionB: Encrypt now defaults to True, and the local server's certificate is self-signed
optionC: The new package needs the SQL Server service to be reinstalled on the machine
optionD: The connection string key Server was renamed and is now read as a certificate
correctAnswerText: Encrypt now defaults to True, and the local server's certificate is self-signed
explanation: Since Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 4.0, Encrypt defaults to True, so the server certificate is validated and a self-signed one fails. Add TrustServerCertificate=True on dev; use a trusted certificate in production.

optionA: False, True, True
optionB: True, True, True
optionC: False, True, False
optionD: True, False, True
correctAnswerText: False, True, True
explanation: DBNull.Value is a real object, so v == null is False. It is a DBNull, so both the type test and Convert.IsDBNull are True. This is why null checks on reader values fail.

prompt: Pool timeouts appear under load while SQL Server's CPU is idle. A teammate proposes Max Pool Size=2000. Your judgement?
optionA: Find the code holding connections first; a bigger pool only delays it
optionB: Lower Max Pool Size to 5 so that leaks are reported more quickly
optionC: Agree, and also set Pooling=False so connections are never shared
optionD: Agree: a larger pool always gives more throughput at no other cost
correctAnswerText: Find the code holding connections first; a bigger pool only delays it
explanation: An idle server with pool timeouts points to connections that are borrowed and not returned (a missing using) or held by long transactions. Raising the cap hides the leak until it bites harder.

prompt: An EF Core app needs a read-only placement dashboard built from a hand-tuned 60-line SQL query with window functions. Which choice is most sensible?
optionA: Raw ADO.NET with DataSets, as Dapper and EF Core cannot be combined
optionB: Run that query with Dapper, mapped to a DTO, beside EF Core for writes
optionC: Move the whole app from EF Core to raw ADO.NET to keep one approach
optionD: Rewrite it as LINQ, since an EF Core app must never send its own SQL
correctAnswerText: Run that query with Dapper, mapped to a DTO, beside EF Core for writes
explanation: Dapper runs existing SQL with almost no overhead and maps it to a DTO; many .NET codebases use EF Core for writes and Dapper for heavy reads side by side.

prompt: A fee payment opens a SqlTransaction, inserts a pending row, calls a payment gateway over HTTP (up to 15 s), then updates the row and commits. Your judgement?
optionA: Good: the transaction makes the gateway call roll back on any failure too
optionB: Use one SqlConnection for the whole app so the transaction never waits
optionC: Good, but switch to Serializable so the payment cannot be seen half-done
optionD: Do the HTTP call outside the transaction and keep the transaction short
correctAnswerText: Do the HTTP call outside the transaction and keep the transaction short
explanation: A rollback cannot undo a charge made over HTTP, and the open transaction holds locks and a pooled connection for the whole call. Record state in short transactions around the remote call.

prompt: A repository method catches SqlException, logs it, and returns an empty list. Is that a good choice?
optionA: Yes: callers should never need to know that a database exists at all
optionB: No: "database down" now looks like "no rows"; let the error surface
optionC: No: it should return null instead so the caller can check for it
optionD: Yes, because an empty list cannot cause an error anywhere further on
correctAnswerText: No: "database down" now looks like "no rows"; let the error surface
explanation: Swallowing the exception turns an outage into wrong data. Let it propagate (wrapped with context if useful), and catch only specific numbers you can handle, such as 2627 for a duplicate.

prompt: To "save opening costs", a singleton repository opens one SqlConnection at startup and uses it for every API request. Your judgement?
optionA: Open a new connection per operation and dispose it; the pool makes it cheap
optionB: Good, as long as the connection string sets MultipleActiveResultSets
optionC: Good, but reopen it every hour so it does not time out on the server
optionD: Good: one open connection is the fastest pattern for a busy web API
correctAnswerText: Open a new connection per operation and dispose it; the pool makes it cheap
explanation: A SqlConnection is not thread-safe and runs one command at a time, so concurrent requests collide or queue. Pooling already makes open-late, dispose-early cheap.

prompt: To fix "There is already an open DataReader" from a per-row lookup, someone adds MultipleActiveResultSets=True. Your judgement?
optionA: Wrong: MARS is not supported by SQL Server 2022, so it will fail later
optionB: Fine, but also raise CommandTimeout so the many lookups never time out
optionC: Ideal: MARS is the standard fix and makes per-row lookups efficient
optionD: It hides the error but keeps one query per row; use one JOIN instead
correctAnswerText: It hides the error but keeps one query per row; use one JOIN instead
explanation: MARS allows a second command while the reader is open, but 500 rows still mean 501 round trips — the N+1 problem. A JOIN, or loading the rows into a list first, fixes the design.

prompt: A login query runs thousands of times a minute: WHERE Email = @email on an indexed VARCHAR(200). Which parameter style is best?
optionA: Parameters.Add("@email", SqlDbType.VarChar, 200).Value = email
optionB: Parameters.AddWithValue("@email", email), since it is the shortest
optionC: Concatenation, as parameters add overhead on very frequent queries
optionD: Parameters.Add("@email", SqlDbType.NVarChar, -1).Value = email
correctAnswerText: Parameters.Add("@email", SqlDbType.VarChar, 200).Value = email
explanation: Matching type and size lets SQL Server seek the index and reuse one cached plan. AddWithValue sends NVARCHAR of varying length, NVARCHAR(MAX) converts the column, and concatenation is injectable.

prompt: Two clerks sometimes oversell the last hostel bed. One proposal: run read-check-update under IsolationLevel.Serializable. Another: one guarded UPDATE ... WHERE BedsLeft > 0. Which is better?
optionA: Serializable: stricter isolation is always the more correct design
optionB: Neither: the overselling can only be fixed with a C# lock statement
optionC: The guarded UPDATE: atomic, with less blocking and fewer deadlocks
optionD: Both equally: isolation level has no effect on locking behaviour
correctAnswerText: The guarded UPDATE: atomic, with less blocking and fewer deadlocks
explanation: The guarded UPDATE checks and changes the row in one locked statement; rows affected = 0 means full. Serializable also works but blocks more and deadlocks more. A C# lock fails across servers.

prompt: Which repository design for an IStudentRepository is the soundest?
optionA: Methods speak in domain objects; the service keeps the business rules
optionB: One method Run(string sql) so every service can write the SQL it needs
optionC: The repository also decides discounts, since it already sees the data
optionD: Methods return SqlDataReader so callers can choose what columns to read
correctAnswerText: Methods speak in domain objects; the service keeps the business rules
explanation: An interface returning domain objects hides SqlConnection and DBNull and lets services be tested with a fake. Readers leak connections, Run(sql) invites injection, and rules belong in the service.

prompt: All three commands of a refund run in one method on one connection. Which transaction approach fits best?
optionA: A SqlTransaction from that connection, passed to each of the commands
optionB: A TransactionScope with the default options, awaited without async flow
optionC: No transaction: three autocommitted commands rarely fail in practice
optionD: A TransactionScope that opens a separate connection for each command
correctAnswerText: A SqlTransaction from that connection, passed to each of the commands
explanation: With one method and one connection, SqlTransaction is explicit and simple. Several open connections in a scope escalate to a distributed transaction, and awaits inside a scope need TransactionScopeAsyncFlowOption.Enabled.

prompt: Which EF Core class is your session with the database, holding the model and the change tracker?
optionA: DbSet<T>
optionB: ModelBuilder
optionC: DbContext
optionD: SqlConnection
correctAnswerText: DbContext
explanation: A DbContext holds connection settings, the model and the change tracker. DbSet<T> is one entity collection on it, ModelBuilder configures the model, and SqlConnection is ADO.NET.

prompt: What type does a context expose for each entity, so you can query it with LINQ and add to it?
optionA: List<TEntity>
optionB: IDbCommand
optionC: DataTable
optionD: DbSet<TEntity>
correctAnswerText: DbSet<TEntity>
explanation: A DbSet<Student> Students property is queried with LINQ (it is an IQueryable) and accepts Add and Remove. It also gives the table its default name.

prompt: Which NuGet package lets EF Core talk to SQL Server through UseSqlServer?
optionA: Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer
optionB: Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Proxies
optionC: Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design
optionD: Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.InMemory
correctAnswerText: Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer
explanation: The SqlServer package is the provider that translates queries to T-SQL. Design supports the dotnet ef tools, Proxies enables lazy loading, and InMemory is a test provider.

prompt: Which CLI command creates a new migration named AddFeeColumn from the current model?
optionA: dotnet ef migrations create AddFeeColumn
optionB: dotnet ef database update AddFeeColumn
optionC: dotnet ef migrations add AddFeeColumn
optionD: dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold AddFeeColumn
correctAnswerText: dotnet ef migrations add AddFeeColumn
explanation: migrations add writes a migration from the difference between the model and the snapshot. database update applies migrations, and dbcontext scaffold reverse-engineers an existing database.

prompt: In which table does EF Core record the migrations that have been applied to a database?
optionA: __EFMigrationsHistory
optionB: __SchemaVersions
optionC: sys.migrations
optionD: dbo.ModelSnapshot
correctAnswerText: __EFMigrationsHistory
explanation: __EFMigrationsHistory holds a row per applied migration (MigrationId, ProductVersion), so database update runs only the missing ones. The snapshot is a C# file, not a table.

prompt: Which query method loads a related navigation, such as each order's Customer, in the same query?
optionA: Load
optionB: Join
optionC: Attach
optionD: Include
correctAnswerText: Include
explanation: Include eager-loads a navigation in the same query (ThenInclude goes a level deeper). Attach tracks an entity, and Load on an entry is explicit loading, a separate query.

prompt: With which service lifetime does AddDbContext register a context in ASP.NET Core by default?
optionA: Transient
optionB: Pooled singleton
optionC: Scoped
optionD: Singleton
correctAnswerText: Scoped
explanation: AddDbContext registers the context as scoped, so each HTTP request gets its own instance, disposed at the end of the request.

prompt: Which attribute on a byte[] property maps it to a SQL Server rowversion used for concurrency checks?
optionA: [Required]
optionB: [DatabaseGenerated]
optionC: [Timestamp]
optionD: [Key]
correctAnswerText: [Timestamp]
explanation: [Timestamp] (or IsRowVersion() in the Fluent API) makes the property a rowversion concurrency token. [Key] marks the primary key and [Required] makes a column NOT NULL.

prompt: Which method makes a query return entities that the context does not track?
optionA: AsEnumerable()
optionB: AsNoTracking()
optionC: IgnoreQueryFilters()
optionD: AsSplitQuery()
correctAnswerText: AsNoTracking()
explanation: AsNoTracking skips snapshots and identity resolution, saving memory for read-only data. AsSplitQuery changes how includes are fetched, and AsEnumerable switches to in-memory LINQ.

prompt: After db.Students.Add(s) and before SaveChanges, what is the entity state of s?
optionA: Added
optionB: Unchanged
optionC: Modified
optionD: Detached
correctAnswerText: Added
explanation: Add marks the entity Added, so SaveChanges will INSERT it; afterwards it becomes Unchanged. Detached means the context does not know it at all.

prompt: var q = db.Courses.Where(c => c.Fee < 5000).OrderBy(c => c.Title); When does SQL reach the database?
optionA: When the DbContext is disposed at the end of the HTTP request
optionB: Twice: once for Where and once more for the OrderBy on top of it
optionC: Immediately, when Where is called, with OrderBy applied in memory
optionD: Only when q is enumerated, for example by ToListAsync or a foreach
correctAnswerText: Only when q is enumerated, for example by ToListAsync or a foreach
explanation: An IQueryable only builds an expression tree. Enumerating it (ToListAsync, FirstAsync, CountAsync, foreach) translates the whole chain into one SELECT.

prompt: Why is .Select(s => new StudentRow(s.Id, s.Name, s.Batch.Name)) usually the best query for a list page?
optionA: It loads full Student entities, so later edits can be saved more easily
optionB: It runs the projection in C# after loading all the rows into memory
optionC: It fetches only those columns, joins Batch for you, and tracks nothing
optionD: It forces a split query, so each column is fetched in its own SELECT
correctAnswerText: It fetches only those columns, joins Batch for you, and tracks nothing
explanation: A projection becomes a SELECT of just the needed columns with the JOIN written for you, and non-entity results are never tracked — less data, less memory, one query.

prompt: Why does EF Core (since 3.0) throw "could not be translated" for Where(s => IsEligible(s)) with a C# method?
optionA: It cannot see inside compiled C# and refuses to load the table to filter it
optionB: C# methods are allowed only in Where clauses on string properties
optionC: The method must be marked async before EF Core is able to call it
optionD: EF Core translates C# methods only when the provider is SQLite, not SQL Server
correctAnswerText: It cannot see inside compiled C# and refuses to load the table to filter it
explanation: The method body is compiled IL, not an expression EF Core can turn into SQL. Older versions silently loaded every row and filtered in memory; now it fails loudly so you rewrite the condition inline.

prompt: A tracked student's Phone is changed and SaveChanges is called. How does EF Core know to update only Phone?
optionA: It re-reads the row from the database and compares the two copies
optionB: Entity properties raise events that write each change to SQL at once
optionC: It always updates every column, so it never needs to know what changed
optionD: It compares each tracked entity with the snapshot taken when it loaded
correctAnswerText: It compares each tracked entity with the snapshot taken when it loaded
explanation: A tracking query stores original values. SaveChanges calls DetectChanges, compares, and writes UPDATE ... SET only for modified properties — all inside one transaction.

prompt: A column was added to the database by hand in SSMS. Why does the next migrations add not mention it?
optionA: Migrations compare the model with the snapshot file, not with the database
optionB: Hand-made columns are recorded in __EFMigrationsHistory automatically
optionC: EF Core ignores columns whose names do not end in Id when scanning tables
optionD: The migration includes it only when the database is SQL Server Express
correctAnswerText: Migrations compare the model with the snapshot file, not with the database
explanation: migrations add diffs the current model against the ModelSnapshot class; it never reads the live schema. Changes made outside migrations are invisible to it and drift from the model.

prompt: A fresh context runs db.Enrolments.FirstAsync() with no Include. Why is enrolment.Course null?
optionA: Related data loads only when asked for; lazy loading is off by default
optionB: Navigations load on the second access, so the first read is null
optionC: Course is null because the foreign key column was never saved
optionD: FirstAsync never loads navigations, though ToListAsync always does
correctAnswerText: Related data loads only when asked for; lazy loading is off by default
explanation: EF Core loads related entities only by Include, explicit loading, or proxies you opt into. Without them the navigation stays null unless the entity is already tracked.

prompt: One context queries student 5 with tracking, another process updates the row, then the same context queries student 5 again. What does the second query give?
optionA: A new instance with the latest values, replacing the tracked one entirely
optionB: The same instance, refreshed with the new values from the database
optionC: The same tracked instance, still holding the values loaded the first time
optionD: An exception, because one context may not query the same key twice
correctAnswerText: The same tracked instance, still holding the values loaded the first time
explanation: Identity resolution maps each key to one instance, and a tracking query does not overwrite an already-tracked entity. Use a new context or Entry(e).ReloadAsync() for fresh values.

prompt: Why should a DbContext be short-lived rather than shared for the life of the application?
optionA: It holds a database lock for as long as the instance remains alive
optionB: A long-lived context stops translating LINQ after one hour
optionC: It is not thread-safe and its tracker grows with every entity it loads
optionD: It can run only one SaveChanges call in its whole lifetime
correctAnswerText: It is not thread-safe and its tracker grows with every entity it loads
explanation: A context supports one operation at a time and keeps every tracked entity and snapshot, so sharing it causes concurrency errors, stale data and growing memory. One per request or unit of work.

prompt: With a [Timestamp] RowVersion on Seat, how does EF Core detect that someone else changed the row since it was loaded?
optionA: EF Core re-reads every column before saving and compares them in memory
optionB: The UPDATE includes the original RowVersion in WHERE; 0 rows means a conflict
optionC: SQL Server sends EF Core a notification whenever a tracked row is changed
optionD: EF Core locks the row from the moment it is loaded until SaveChanges ends
correctAnswerText: The UPDATE includes the original RowVersion in WHERE; 0 rows means a conflict
explanation: SQL Server changes rowversion on every update. EF Core adds WHERE RowVersion = @original; if another save got there first, no row matches and DbUpdateConcurrencyException is thrown.

prompt: How does ExecuteUpdateAsync (EF Core 7+) differ from changing tracked entities and calling SaveChanges?
optionA: It loads every matching row first and then updates each one in turn
optionB: It updates tracked entities in memory only and never touches the database
optionC: It queues the change until the next SaveChanges, like any other edit
optionD: It sends one UPDATE at once, bypassing the tracker; tracked copies go stale
correctAnswerText: It sends one UPDATE at once, bypassing the tracker; tracked copies go stale
explanation: ExecuteUpdate translates to a single set-based UPDATE that runs immediately. It is not part of SaveChanges, does not refresh tracked entities and does not check concurrency tokens.

prompt: Course.Fee is a decimal that must map to DECIMAL(10,2). Which OnModelCreating line does it?
