prompt: A group has Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 30 minutes; its values above Q3 are 38, 44, 47 and 60. In a standard box plot, where does the upper whisker end?
optionA: At 47
optionB: At 44
optionC: At 45
optionD: At 60
correctAnswerText: At 44
explanation: The fence is 30 + 1.5 × 10 = 45, and the whisker stops at the last actual value inside it, 44. The values 47 and 60 are drawn as separate points.

prompt: Power BI's display units offer thousands, millions and billions but not crore. How do you show revenue as "₹72.4 cr"?
optionA: A measure DIVIDE([Revenue], 100000) with 1 decimal, labelled ₹ cr
optionB: Set display units to Millions and change the axis label to crore
optionC: A measure DIVIDE([Revenue], 10000000) with 1 decimal, labelled ₹ cr
optionD: Set display units to Billions and multiply the result by 100
correctAnswerText: A measure DIVIDE([Revenue], 10000000) with 1 decimal, labelled ₹ cr
explanation: One crore is 1,00,00,000 (10 million); 1,00,000 is a lakh. A dedicated measure with one decimal and "₹ crore" in the title or axis reads naturally for Indian managers.

prompt: You must compare delivery-time distributions across 12 city zones. Which Seaborn call reads best?
optionA: sns.histplot(df, x="delivery_min", hue="zone")
optionB: sns.barplot(df, x="zone", y="delivery_min")
optionC: sns.displot(df, x="delivery_min", col="zone", col_wrap=4)
optionD: sns.kdeplot(df, x="delivery_min", hue="zone", fill=True)
correctAnswerText: sns.displot(df, x="delivery_min", col="zone", col_wrap=4)
explanation: Twelve overlapping colours are unreadable, and a bar of means hides the distribution. Small multiples give each zone its own panel on shared axes.

prompt: A monthly sales line runs Apr, Aug, Dec, Feb, Jan, Jul… and zigzags wildly. What is wrong?
optionA: The line chart is plotting the months in a random order
optionB: The months with fewer days are being drawn out of place
optionC: Month names are sorted as text instead of in calendar order
optionD: Sales really did swing that much between alternate months
correctAnswerText: Month names are sorted as text instead of in calendar order
explanation: Text sorts alphabetically. Sort by a month number or a date (in Power BI, set "Sort by column" or use the Date table) and the zigzag disappears.

prompt: A daily orders line built with df.groupby(df["date"]).size() looks smooth, but the app was down for two whole days. Why do the outages not show?
optionA: Line charts always smooth out single days with zero orders
optionB: groupby fills empty days with the average of their neighbours
optionC: Days with no rows are absent, so the line joins straight across
optionD: size() counts the outage days twice to make up for the gap
correctAnswerText: Days with no rows are absent, so the line joins straight across
explanation: groupby only creates groups for dates that occur. resample("D") on a datetime index (or reindexing to every date) inserts the missing days as 0, and the dip appears.

prompt: A slide titled "Biryani revenue, March" shows a seaborn barplot bar of about ₹447, but finance says Biryani earned ₹72,423 that month. What went wrong?
optionA: Seaborn divides each total by the number of cuisines shown
optionB: barplot draws only a sample of 100 orders from each group
optionC: The bar is the mean order value; totals need estimator="sum"
optionD: The bar shows the median order and so is far below the total
correctAnswerText: The bar is the mean order value; totals need estimator="sum"
explanation: barplot averages by default, so the bar is a typical Biryani order. Pass estimator="sum" (or pre-aggregate) and say in the title whether bars are totals or means.

prompt: A correlation heatmap shows one pair in the deepest red, and a manager concludes it is a "very strong" link. The annotated value is 0.28. What caused the impression?
optionA: The heatmap rounded 0.28 up to 1.0 before choosing its colour
optionB: Deep red always marks the largest value in any correlation
optionC: Correlations of 0.28 are in fact considered very strong ones
optionD: The colour scale was stretched to the data's own narrow range
correctAnswerText: The colour scale was stretched to the data's own narrow range
explanation: Without vmin=-1, vmax=1 the strongest cell in the matrix gets the strongest colour, whatever its value. Fixing the limits makes 0.28 look as weak as it is.

prompt: A stacked area chart shows five product lines over time. Readers think the middle line, Snacks, is growing — but its own values are flat. Why?
optionA: Its band sits on growing layers, so its edges rise anyway
optionB: The legend lists Snacks in the wrong order of the stack
optionC: Stacked charts always add a trend to each middle series
optionD: Area charts double the values of all the middle layers
correctAnswerText: Its band sits on growing layers, so its edges rise anyway
explanation: Only the bottom layer has a flat baseline. A middle band's thickness is its value, but its position rises with the layers below, which the eye reads as growth. Use lines or small multiples.

prompt: A weekly orders chart for March shows the first week "crashing" to a third of the others. March began on a Friday. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The weekly totals were averaged instead of summed
optionB: The first week was plotted on a separate y-axis
optionC: The first week holds only a few March days, not seven
optionD: Orders always collapse in the first week of a month
correctAnswerText: The first week holds only a few March days, not seven
explanation: With weeks starting on Monday, March's first "week" contains only Friday to Sunday. Show per-day averages, drop partial weeks or mark them clearly.

prompt: An infographic shows this year's sales as a coin icon twice as tall and twice as wide as last year's, for sales that doubled. Why does growth look exaggerated?
optionA: Icons always look smaller than bars of the same value
optionB: The icon should have been three times as tall to match
optionC: Coins are round, so their size cannot be compared at all
optionD: Doubling both sides makes the icon four times the area
correctAnswerText: Doubling both sides makes the icon four times the area
explanation: Readers judge the area, and 2 × 2 = 4. Scale area, not height, to the value — or use a bar, which needs no such care.

prompt: A district map shaded by total complaints is darkest over the two biggest cities, and the slide calls them the "worst-served" areas. What is the flaw?
optionA: The colour scale should be diverging, centred on the mean district
optionB: Maps cannot be shaded by a count, only by a percentage of a total
optionC: Totals track population; complaints per 1,000 orders compare fairly
optionD: Big cities are always darkest because their districts are larger
correctAnswerText: Totals track population; complaints per 1,000 orders compare fairly
explanation: More orders produce more complaints. A rate removes size, and may show a small district is worse served. Shading a map by raw totals mostly redraws where people live.

prompt: A script calls plt.show() and then plt.savefig("chart.png"). The window shows the chart, but the saved PNG is blank. Why?
optionA: show() closes the figure, so savefig saves a new empty one
optionB: savefig only works for files with the .jpg extension
optionC: plt.show() deletes any file named chart.png on disk
optionD: The PNG was saved before the chart had been drawn
correctAnswerText: show() closes the figure, so savefig saves a new empty one
explanation: In a script, show() hands the figure to the window and it is closed afterwards, so the later plt call starts a fresh figure. Call fig.savefig(...) before show(), or save from the fig object.

prompt: A Power BI matrix colours YoY % cells red or green by a rule. One regional head keeps misreading which regions are down. What is the best fix?
optionA: Remove the YoY % column and show only the revenue in the matrix
optionB: Replace red and green with two different shades of the same green
optionC: Keep the colour but add an icon or the sign so it is not colour alone
optionD: Change the rule to a gradient so every cell gets its own colour
correctAnswerText: Keep the colour but add an icon or the sign so it is not colour alone
explanation: A red-green-only cue fails for colour-blind readers. Conditional formatting icons, or a visible minus sign, carry the meaning without depending on hue.

prompt: A regional head asks every Monday: are we ahead of last year, which region is dragging, and is margin holding? Which page design is best?
optionA: Twelve visuals covering every measure, so no question is missed
optionB: A gauge for revenue, a pie by region and a map of all the stores
optionC: One large matrix of all 64 stores by month with conditional colours
optionD: A card with YoY %, a sorted bar of YoY % by region, a margin % line
correctAnswerText: A card with YoY %, a sorted bar of YoY % by region, a margin % line
explanation: One visual per question answers all three in seconds. Twelve visuals bury them, a store matrix belongs on a detail page, and gauges, pies and maps answer other questions poorly.

prompt: A designer wants a large gauge for "revenue against target". Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: A KPI visual or card with target and variance says it in less space
optionB: A pie of revenue and the gap to target shows the same thing better
optionC: The gauge is best, since dials are what managers find most familiar
optionD: A gauge is fine only if it is drawn in 3-D to make it easy to read
correctAnswerText: A KPI visual or card with target and variance says it in less space
explanation: A gauge spends a big arc on one value and a target. A card or KPI visual shows the value, the target and the direction compactly, leaving room for the context.

prompt: You must show monthly orders (thousands) and average rating (1–5) for a year to a product team. Which design is best?
optionA: A pie chart for each month of the year shown
optionB: One chart with orders and rating on two y-axes
optionC: One chart with both series on a single y-axis
optionD: Two panels stacked with a shared month axis
correctAnswerText: Two panels stacked with a shared month axis
explanation: Different units need different scales, but dual axes let the scaling invent a relationship. Stacked panels show both honestly and still line the months up; one shared axis flattens the rating.

prompt: Operations wants to compare delivery times across areas, and the worry is the long tail of very late orders. Which chart serves best?
optionA: A bar chart of mean delivery time by area with 95% error bars
optionB: A pie chart of each area's share of all delivery minutes
optionC: A single card with the overall mean delivery time for the city
optionD: Box plots by area, which show the median, the spread and the tail
correctAnswerText: Box plots by area, which show the median, the spread and the tail
explanation: The question is about the tail, which a mean bar hides — its error bar describes uncertainty in the mean, not lateness. Box plots show where the late orders are.

prompt: Store revenues span ₹2 lakh to ₹40 crore, and the audience is store managers who rarely read log axes. Which choice is best?
optionA: Use one linear axis, accepting that small stores look like zero
optionB: Use a log axis with no label, as managers will read it correctly
optionC: Split into size bands, each on its own linear axis, labelled clearly
optionD: Drop the largest stores from the chart so the rest become visible
correctAnswerText: Split into size bands, each on its own linear axis, labelled clearly
explanation: A log axis is right for analysts but easily misread by others; one linear axis hides the small stores; dropping stores misleads. Size bands (or small multiples) keep every store readable on a familiar scale.

prompt: A bar chart of eight regions is meant to show that West fell behind. Which colour scheme serves that message best?
optionA: A rainbow from red to violet across the eight regions
optionB: West in one strong colour, the other seven in grey
optionC: A different bright colour for each of the eight regions
optionD: Every bar in the company's main brand colour
correctAnswerText: West in one strong colour, the other seven in grey
explanation: Colour should point at the finding. Grey context plus one highlight makes West the first thing seen; eight colours or a rainbow decorate and imply categories mean something.

prompt: A team wants to show only the three weeks after a campaign, when orders rose, leaving out the months before. How should this be judged?
optionA: Acceptable, if the y-axis is started at zero to stay honest
optionB: Show the longer period so the rise is seen against normal variation
optionC: Acceptable, since the campaign weeks are the only ones of interest
optionD: Show only the single best week, to make the message even clearer
correctAnswerText: Show the longer period so the rise is seen against normal variation
explanation: Without the baseline, readers cannot tell a real lift from an ordinary fluctuation or a seasonal rise. A cherry-picked window can mislead even with every value drawn correctly.

prompt: For a manager's report comparing order values by cuisine, an analyst must choose between violin plots and box plots. Which is the better judgement?
optionA: Violin plots, since box plots cannot show the median of each group
optionB: Violin plots: more shape is always better for any audience at all
optionC: Neither: only a pie chart shows a comparison between cuisines
optionD: Box plots: they carry the key comparison and managers read them easily
correctAnswerText: Box plots: they carry the key comparison and managers read them easily
explanation: Violins show more of each distribution's shape but are harder to read; for a report, box plots give median, spread and outliers in a familiar form. Use violins in exploration.

prompt: A stakeholder asks for 3-D columns with shadows "to make the dashboard look premium". What is the best response?
optionA: Decline, and use 3-D pie charts that are much easier to read
optionB: Agree, but only for the columns that show the largest values
optionC: Agree, since a premium look makes the numbers more trusted
optionD: Decline: depth distorts lengths; use flat bars and a clean theme
correctAnswerText: Decline: depth distorts lengths; use flat bars and a clean theme
explanation: Perspective makes front bars look bigger and hides where a bar actually ends. Polish should come from a consistent theme, spacing and clear titles, not effects.

prompt: A chart will rank branches by loan defaults to decide where to send auditors. Branches differ tenfold in loans issued. What should the bars show?
optionA: Total loans issued, since defaults follow directly from volume
optionB: Total defaults on a log scale, to shrink the differences in size
optionC: Total defaults, since bigger branches deserve the most attention
optionD: Default rate per loans issued, with the loan count beside each bar
correctAnswerText: Default rate per loans issued, with the loan count beside each bar
explanation: Raw totals rank branches mostly by size. A rate compares risk fairly, and showing the count beside it stops a tiny branch with 2 of 10 loans from topping the list unchallenged.

prompt: By default, what does pandas Series.std() divide the sum of squared deviations by?
optionA: n − 1, giving the sample standard deviation
optionB: n, giving the population standard deviation
optionC: n + 1, giving a shrunken standard deviation
optionD: n − 2, giving the residual standard deviation
correctAnswerText: n − 1, giving the sample standard deviation
explanation: pandas defaults to ddof=1, so std() divides by n − 1 (the sample SD). NumPy's np.std defaults to ddof=0 and divides by n, which is why the two can disagree on the same numbers.

prompt: How is the interquartile range (IQR) of a column calculated?
optionA: Mean plus or minus one standard deviation
optionB: Median minus the first quartile
optionC: Third quartile minus first quartile
optionD: Maximum value minus minimum value
correctAnswerText: Third quartile minus first quartile
explanation: IQR = Q3 − Q1, the width of the middle half of the values. Max − min is the range, which one extreme value can blow up; the IQR ignores the outer quarters entirely.

prompt: Under the common 1.5 × IQR rule, a value is flagged as a high outlier when it lies above which point?
optionA: Maximum − 1.5 × IQR
optionB: Median + 1.5 × IQR
optionC: Q3 + 1.5 × IQR
optionD: Mean + 1.5 × SD
correctAnswerText: Q3 + 1.5 × IQR
explanation: The upper fence is Q3 + 1.5 × IQR and the lower fence Q1 − 1.5 × IQR. The fence is built from quartiles so that the outliers it hunts for cannot move it much.

prompt: An operations report says "p90 delivery time is 47 minutes". What does that state?
optionA: About 90% of deliveries took longer than 47 minutes
optionB: About 90% of deliveries took 47 minutes or less
optionC: Deliveries took 47 minutes with 90% confidence
optionD: The average of the slowest 10% of deliveries was 47
correctAnswerText: About 90% of deliveries took 47 minutes or less
explanation: The 90th percentile is the value at or below which about 90% of observations fall. It is a description of the data, not a confidence statement and not an average of the tail.

prompt: Which rows of pandas describe() on a numeric column together form the five-number summary?
optionA: mean, std, 25%, 50% and 75%
optionB: count, mean, 50%, std and max
optionC: count, mean, std, min and max
optionD: min, 25%, 50%, 75% and max
correctAnswerText: min, 25%, 50%, 75% and max
explanation: The five-number summary is minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum — the 25%, 50% and 75% rows plus min and max. count, mean and std are describe()'s other rows.

prompt: For right-skewed data such as order values or salaries, how do the mean and median usually compare?
optionA: The mean sits below the median
optionB: The mean sits above the median
optionC: The median sits above the maximum
optionD: The mean and median are equal
correctAnswerText: The mean sits above the median
explanation: A long tail of large values pulls the mean upward while the median stays with the bulk of the data, so mean > median is the usual signature of right skew.

prompt: Between which limits can Pearson's correlation coefficient r fall?
optionA: 0 and +1
optionB: −∞ and +∞
optionC: 0 and 100
optionD: −1 and +1
correctAnswerText: −1 and +1
explanation: r runs from −1 (a perfect falling straight line) through 0 (no linear association) to +1 (a perfect rising straight line). It has no units, so it cannot exceed these bounds.

prompt: What does Pearson's r measure about two numeric columns?
optionA: Whether a change in one causes a change in the other
optionB: How steep the line through the two columns would be
optionC: How closely they follow a straight-line relationship
optionD: How much larger one column's mean is than the other's
correctAnswerText: How closely they follow a straight-line relationship
explanation: Pearson's r is the strength and direction of a linear association. It says nothing about cause and is not the slope: a shallow line and a steep one can both have r = 0.95.

prompt: Which Excel function gives the same percentile as pandas quantile() with its default settings?
optionA: PERCENTRANK.EXC
optionB: MEDIAN.IFS
optionC: PERCENTILE.EXC
optionD: PERCENTILE.INC
correctAnswerText: PERCENTILE.INC
explanation: pandas interpolates linearly by default, the same rule as PERCENTILE.INC. PERCENTILE.EXC uses a different position rule and can give different values; PERCENTRANK goes the other way, value to rank.

prompt: What does a z-score of a single value tell you?
optionA: How likely it is that the value is a data error
optionB: How many standard deviations it lies from the mean
optionC: How far it lies from the median in rupees or units
optionD: What percentage of values are smaller than it is
correctAnswerText: How many standard deviations it lies from the mean
explanation: z = (x − mean) / SD: the distance from the mean in standard-deviation units. It turns into a percentile only if you assume a distribution, and it never proves a value is an error.

prompt: A seller's twelve orders have a median of ₹509.50. The largest order changes from ₹8,999 to ₹89,999. Why does the median stay at ₹509.50?
optionA: It depends only on the middle sorted values, not on how big the top one is
optionB: The median is rounded to the nearest price point, which hides the change
optionC: It does change, but only after the data is re-sorted in descending order
optionD: pandas excludes the largest value from a median when it is far from the rest
correctAnswerText: It depends only on the middle sorted values, not on how big the top one is
explanation: With 12 values the median is the average of the 6th and 7th sorted values. Making the top order ten times bigger leaves those two untouched; the mean, by contrast, jumps from ₹1,285 to ₹8,035.

prompt: Orders are mostly ₹400–₹750, yet the standard deviation is ₹2,441 because of one ₹8,999 order. Why is the SD so misleading here?
optionA: A standard deviation can only be computed for normally distributed data
optionB: The SD is measured in squared rupees, so it cannot be compared with orders
optionC: Squaring deviations lets the one extreme value dominate the whole figure
optionD: pandas uses n − 1, which inflates the SD whenever n is under one hundred
correctAnswerText: Squaring deviations lets the one extreme value dominate the whole figure
explanation: Each deviation is squared, so one order ₹7,700 above the mean contributes far more than all the ordinary ones. For skewed data, the IQR and percentiles describe the typical spread far better.

prompt: Finance asks "how much revenue did we make per order last month?" on skewed order data. Why is the mean the right answer this time?
optionA: Finance teams require the mean by accounting rules for any report
optionB: Revenue equals mean × number of orders, so big orders really count
optionC: The mean is always the right centre once there are over 1,000 orders
optionD: The median cannot be computed for currency values held as decimals
correctAnswerText: Revenue equals mean × number of orders, so big orders really count
explanation: Total revenue / orders is the mean by definition, and the large orders are real money. The median answers a different question — what a typical customer spends.

prompt: How does Spearman's rank correlation differ from Pearson's r?
optionA: It correlates the raw values, but only after removing values beyond 3 SD
optionB: It measures cause and effect, whereas Pearson only measures association
optionC: It correlates the ranks, so it captures any steady rise and resists outliers
optionD: It is the square of Pearson's r, so it is never negative and never above 1
correctAnswerText: It correlates the ranks, so it captures any steady rise and resists outliers
explanation: Spearman is Pearson's r computed on ranks. Any monotonic relationship scores highly, and an extreme value is just the top rank, so it cannot dominate the way it does in Pearson.

prompt: Sales rise with discount up to 20% and then fall as deeper discounts cheapen the brand. Pearson's r comes out near 0. Why?
optionA: r only picks up straight-line patterns, and this one is an arch
optionB: The two columns are unrelated, so r near 0 is the correct reading
optionC: r is near 0 because the sample must be too small to show anything
optionD: Discount is a percentage, and r cannot be used with percentage data
correctAnswerText: r only picks up straight-line patterns, and this one is an arch
explanation: An arch has a rising half and a falling half that cancel in a linear measure. A strong relationship can have r ≈ 0; always plot before reading r.

prompt: Why does plotting heavily right-skewed order values on a log scale usually make the histogram readable?
optionA: It turns the mean into the median, so the skew no longer has an effect
optionB: It spreads out the crowded small values and pulls in the long tail
optionC: It converts the values into ranks, so every bar has the same height
optionD: It removes the large orders, which are treated as outliers by the log
correctAnswerText: It spreads out the crowded small values and pulls in the long tail
explanation: Money data often grows multiplicatively, so equal ratios become equal distances on a log axis. The bulk stops being one tall bar and the tail stops stretching the axis; no data is removed.

prompt: Monthly spend shows two humps, one near ₹600 and one near ₹3,200, and the mean is ₹1,700. Why is that mean a poor description?
optionA: It falls in the gap between the humps, where few customers actually sit
optionB: It is pulled upward by outliers, so the median would be the honest figure
optionC: The mean is fine; two humps only matter when plotting, not in summary
optionD: Means cannot be computed for spend that is spread across two months
correctAnswerText: It falls in the gap between the humps, where few customers actually sit
explanation: Two humps usually mean two kinds of customer. The overall mean describes almost nobody; split the segments and summarise each one.

prompt: Across cities, ice-cream sales and AC repair calls rise together. What is a confounder in this situation?
optionA: A city whose values lie far from the rest of the scatter plot
optionB: The column that causes the other once the correlation is high
optionC: A data error that creates a correlation where there is none
optionD: A third factor, such as temperature, that drives both columns
correctAnswerText: A third factor, such as temperature, that drives both columns
explanation: Hot weather raises both. A confounder produces a correlation between two things that do not affect each other, which is why association alone never establishes cause.

prompt: On the same five numbers, pandas .std() gives 3.16 and np.std() gives 2.83. Why do they differ?
optionA: NumPy rounds each value before squaring, and pandas does not
optionB: pandas silently drops the largest value when n is under ten
optionC: pandas divides by n − 1 by default and NumPy divides by n
optionD: NumPy uses the median as its centre while pandas uses the mean
correctAnswerText: pandas divides by n − 1 by default and NumPy divides by n
explanation: pandas defaults to ddof=1 (sample SD) and NumPy to ddof=0 (population SD). For 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 that is √10 = 3.16 against √8 = 2.83; pass ddof explicitly when tools must match.

prompt: Across products, discount depth and gross margin have r = −0.8. What is the accurate reading?
optionA: Discounts cause margins to fall in 80% of the products in the data set
optionB: Each extra 1% of discount lowers margin by exactly 0.8 percentage points
optionC: There is little relationship, since the correlation is below zero
optionD: Deeper-discount products tend to have lower margins, fairly consistently
correctAnswerText: Deeper-discount products tend to have lower margins, fairly consistently
explanation: A strong negative r means the two tend to move in opposite directions along a line. It is not a slope, not a percentage of products, and not proof that discounting caused the margin.

prompt:
What do these return?

s = pd.Series([310, 275, 460, 390, 520, 280, 345, 1980])
s.median(), s.mean()
explanation: Sorted: 275, 280, 310, 345, 390, 460, 520, 1980. With eight values the median averages the 4th and 5th, (345 + 390) / 2 = 367.5. The total is 4,560, so the mean is 570.0 — dragged up by 1,980.

prompt: Ticket resolution hours: [12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, 19, 21, 22, 48]. pandas quantile gives Q1 = 15.0 and Q3 = 20.5. Which values does the 1.5 × IQR rule flag as high?
optionA: Only 48, as the upper fence is 28.75
optionB: None, as the upper fence is 48.75
optionC: Only 48, as the upper fence is 41.0
optionD: 22 and 48, as the upper fence is 21.5
correctAnswerText: Only 48, as the upper fence is 28.75
explanation: IQR = 20.5 − 15.0 = 5.5; the fence is 20.5 + 1.5 × 5.5 = 28.75. Only 48 lies above it.

prompt: Three stores: 1,200 orders averaging ₹450, 300 orders averaging ₹900 and 500 orders averaging ₹600. What is the average order value across all 2,000 orders?
explanation: Revenue = 1,200×450 + 300×900 + 500×600 = ₹11,10,000; divided by 2,000 orders that is ₹555. The plain average of the three averages, ₹650, ignores that the ₹450 store has most of the orders.

prompt: Daily sign-ups average 40 with a standard deviation of 8. Yesterday had 58 sign-ups. What is yesterday's z-score?
explanation: z = (58 − 40) / 8 = 2.25: yesterday was 2.25 standard deviations above the average. 18 is the raw difference, not yet divided by the SD.

prompt:
What do these return, to two decimals?

s = pd.Series([4, 6, 8, 10, 12])
s.std(), s.std(ddof=0)
explanation: Squared deviations from the mean 8 sum to 40. Divided by n − 1 = 4 gives variance 10 and SD 3.16; divided by n = 5 gives 8 and SD 2.83. 10 and 8 are the variances, not the SDs.

prompt:
Ad spend (₹ lakh) and orders (hundreds) for five weeks:

x = pd.Series([2, 4, 5, 7, 9])
y = pd.Series([30, 34, 41, 44, 52])
x.corr(y)

About what is returned?
explanation: Series.corr defaults to Pearson; the points lie close to a rising straight line, giving r ≈ 0.984. r can never exceed 1, and it is positive because both rise together.

prompt: Order values: [150, 180, 200, 220, 240, 260, 3100]. How many of the seven orders are above the mean?
optionA: Four — the mean is about ₹200
optionB: Three — the mean is about ₹220
optionC: None — the mean is about ₹3,100
optionD: One — the mean is about ₹621
correctAnswerText: One — the mean is about ₹621
explanation: The total is 4,350, so the mean is ₹621.4. Only the ₹3,100 order exceeds it; the other six sit far below. That is right skew in miniature.

prompt:
pm = pd.Series(["UPI", "Card", "UPI", "COD", "UPI", "Card", "COD", "UPI"])

Which call answers "what is the most common payment method?" and what does it return?
optionA: pm.median() — it returns "Card"
optionB: pm.mean() — it returns the string "UPI"
optionC: pm.max() — the most common, "UPI"
optionD: pm.mode() — a Series holding "UPI"
correctAnswerText: pm.mode() — a Series holding "UPI"
explanation: mode() returns the most frequent value(s) as a Series — here UPI, with 4 of 8. Median and mean are undefined for text; max() returns the alphabetically last value, which only happens to be UPI.

prompt: Daily units sold over five days. Product A: [95, 100, 105, 98, 102] (mean 100, SD 3.8). Product B: [20, 35, 15, 40, 30] (mean 28, SD 10.4). Which is the more erratic seller, relative to its own level?
optionA: B — its SD is about 37% of its mean, against 4% for A
optionB: A — its values are larger, so its swings matter more
optionC: Neither — SDs on different means cannot be compared
optionD: A — its SD of 3.8 counts in hundreds of units each day
correctAnswerText: B — its SD is about 37% of its mean, against 4% for A
explanation: The coefficient of variation, SD / mean, puts spread on a relative scale: 3.8 / 100 ≈ 0.04 for A and 10.4 / 28 ≈ 0.37 for B. B is far less predictable to stock.

prompt:
x = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7])
y = pd.Series([5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 80])

What do x.corr(y) and x.corr(y, method="spearman") return, roughly?
explanation: y rises with x at every step, so the ranks match perfectly and Spearman is 1.0. The jump to 80 bends the straight-line fit, so Pearson falls to about 0.66.

prompt: City X had 9,000 orders at an average of ₹400; City Y had 1,000 at ₹1,200. A dashboard reports a company average order value of ₹800, but total revenue ÷ total orders is ₹480. What went wrong?
optionA: It counted City Y's orders twice when it joined the two tables
optionB: It used the median for one city and the mean for the other one
optionC: It averaged the two city averages without weighting by order count
optionD: It divided total revenue by the number of cities, not by orders
correctAnswerText: It averaged the two city averages without weighting by order count
explanation: (400 + 1,200) / 2 = 800 treats each city as equally important. Weighted by orders, (9,000×400 + 1,000×1,200) / 10,000 = ₹480 — the real revenue per order.

prompt: On five call durations [12, 15, 9, 14, 10], a colleague's Excel sheet reports SD 2.28 and your pandas notebook reports 2.55. Both are "right". What explains it?
optionA: pandas dropped one of the five values because it treated it as NaN
optionB: The two tools sort the values differently before computing the SD
optionC: Excel rounds each value to whole minutes before computing the SD
optionD: The sheet uses STDEV.P (divide by n) and pandas divides by n − 1
correctAnswerText: The sheet uses STDEV.P (divide by n) and pandas divides by n − 1
explanation: STDEV.P divides by n and gives 2.28; pandas std() (like STDEV.S) divides by n − 1 and gives 2.55. With five values the gap is about 12%; agree on ddof before comparing.

prompt: Seven branches: staff = [3, 5, 4, 6, 5, 4, 40], sales = [20, 18, 22, 19, 21, 20, 95]. r = 0.995, and a manager concludes "more staff, more sales". Dropping the 40-staff head office, r becomes −0.40. What is the diagnosis?
optionA: The second r is wrong because six rows are too few for Pearson
optionB: Dropping a row is invalid, so the 0.995 is the true correlation
optionC: One far-off row created the correlation; the branches show none of it
optionD: The correlation is real but negative, so more staff lowers sales
correctAnswerText: One far-off row created the correlation; the branches show none of it
explanation: A single point far from the rest can manufacture a near-perfect r. Among the six ordinary branches the relationship is weak and slightly negative. Plot first, and report r with and without high-leverage rows.

prompt:
Late deliveries:

| Fleet | Short routes | Long routes | Overall |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 30/600 (5.0%) | 120/400 (30%) | 15.0% |
| B | 60/900 (6.7%) | 35/100 (35%) | 9.5% |

A is better on both route types, yet worse overall. Why?
optionA: A runs far more long routes, which are late more often for everyone
optionB: Route type has no effect, so only the overall rates should be compared
optionC: B's long-route sample is too small, so its 35% should be ignored
optionD: The overall rates are miscalculated and A should be 9.5% overall
correctAnswerText: A runs far more long routes, which are late more often for everyone
explanation: This is Simpson's paradox. 40% of A's deliveries are long routes against 10% of B's, and long routes are late about a third of the time. Compare like with like: within each route type, A is better.

prompt: Product ratings are 1–5, and the export writes 0 where a customer did not rate. ratings = [4, 5, 0, 3, 0, 5, 4, 0, 4, 5]; ratings.mean() = 3.0. What is wrong and what is the fair figure?
optionA: The zeros should become 1, the lowest real score, giving 3.3
optionB: Nothing is wrong; a 0 is a valid score, so 3.0 is the fair figure
optionC: The median should be used instead, which gives 4.0 here
optionD: The zeros are "not rated", not scores; excluding them gives 4.29
correctAnswerText: The zeros are "not rated", not scores; excluding them gives 4.29
explanation: A 0 cannot be a 1–5 rating, so it encodes missing. Replace it with NaN (pandas skips NaN in mean) and the average of the seven real ratings is 4.29. Report the rating rate separately: 7 of 10.

prompt: Average order value rose 15% this month while the median order and the order count barely moved. What is the most likely explanation to check first?
optionA: The median is broken, as it should have risen by 15% too
optionB: A small number of very large orders pulled the mean up
optionC: Most customers began spending about 15% more per order
optionD: Fewer orders were placed, so each one averaged out higher
correctAnswerText: A small number of very large orders pulled the mean up
explanation: If most customers spent more, the median would rise as well. A mean that moves alone points to the tail — a few bulk or corporate orders. Look at the top orders before calling it growth.

prompt: For [10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 25, 30], pandas quantile(0.75) gives 22.5 but a colleague's Excel cell gives 25. Neither has a bug. What explains the difference?
optionA: Excel rounds percentiles to the nearest value present in the data before display
optionB: pandas drops the maximum value from quantile calculations by default
optionC: The Excel cell uses PERCENTILE.EXC, which places the 75th percentile by another rule
optionD: pandas interpolates only when the column has an even number of values
correctAnswerText: The Excel cell uses PERCENTILE.EXC, which places the 75th percentile by another rule
explanation: pandas (like PERCENTILE.INC) uses position 0.75 × (n − 1) = 4.5 from the start, halfway between 20 and 25, giving 22.5. PERCENTILE.EXC uses position 0.75 × (n + 1) = 6, the 6th value, 25. On small samples state which rule you used.

prompt: Over 36 months, the company's app downloads and the number of UPI merchants in India have r = 0.97. A slide claims merchants drive downloads. What is the likeliest flaw?
optionA: Both simply grew over time, and any two rising series correlate
optionB: The causation runs the other way: downloads create the UPI merchants
optionC: The correlation is too high to be real and must be a calculation slip
optionD: Monthly data cannot be correlated unless it is first converted to weeks
correctAnswerText: Both simply grew over time, and any two rising series correlate
explanation: Two trending series correlate strongly whether or not they are connected; time is the shared driver. Correlating the month-on-month changes, or checking against a control, is the minimum before any causal claim.

prompt: On 5,000 genuine, heavily right-skewed order values, the 1.5 × IQR rule flags about 6% as outliers. On the log of the values, it flags about 0.4%. What does that show?
optionA: The IQR was computed wrongly; the rule always flags close to 0.7% of values
optionB: The fence assumes rough symmetry, so on skewed data it flags normal big orders
optionC: The log transform hides real outliers and should never be used for detection
optionD: About 6% of the orders are data errors and should be deleted before analysis
correctAnswerText: The fence assumes rough symmetry, so on skewed data it flags normal big orders
explanation: On a long right tail the upper fence sits too low, so ordinary large orders get flagged. Applying the rule on a log scale, or using a business threshold, separates genuine extremes from the normal tail. A flag means "look", not "delete".

prompt: A company finds almost no correlation between its hiring-test score and first-year rating, using only the people it hired — all of whom scored above 80. Why can this understate the link?
optionA: People who scored above 80 are too few to compute a correlation on
optionB: Only a narrow band of scores is present, which weakens any correlation
optionC: Ratings are subjective, so they can never correlate with a test score
optionD: The test must be useless, since the correlation among hires is weak
correctAnswerText: Only a narrow band of scores is present, which weakens any correlation
explanation: Restricting one variable to a narrow range shrinks r even when the full-range relationship is strong. The people who scored under 80 were never hired, so their ratings are missing from the data.

prompt: A college's placement data: mean package ₹9.2 LPA, median ₹4.5 LPA, with a few offers above ₹40 LPA. Which headline is the most honest for prospective students?
optionA: Highest ₹40+ LPA, since it shows what the best students can reach
optionB: Average ₹9.2 LPA, with the median left out to keep the page simple
optionC: Average ₹9.2 LPA, as it uses every offer that was actually made
optionD: Median ₹4.5 LPA, with the share of offers above ₹10 LPA beside it
correctAnswerText: Median ₹4.5 LPA, with the share of offers above ₹10 LPA beside it
explanation: Students ask "what will someone like me get" — a typical-value question, which the median answers. A share above a threshold adds the upside honestly; the mean is inflated by a handful of offers.

prompt: A verified ₹8,999 order (a real customer furnishing a flat) sits among orders of ₹350–₹750. For next month's revenue forecast, what should the analyst do with it?
optionA: Replace it with the median so that the forecast is not pulled upward
optionB: Cap it at Q3 so it still counts but no longer shifts the average
optionC: Keep it, since it is real revenue, and report the typical order separately
optionD: Delete it, since anything beyond the IQR fence will distort the forecast
correctAnswerText: Keep it, since it is real revenue, and report the typical order separately
explanation: An outlier that is genuine is data, not noise. Revenue questions need it; "typical customer" questions are better served by the median. Deleting or capping real orders makes the revenue forecast wrong.

prompt: Marketing wants one "average customer" spend figure for a campaign, but spend has two clear humps (students near ₹600, families near ₹3,200). What is the best advice?
optionA: Use the mean, since it includes every customer in a single number
optionB: Use the trimmed mean, which removes both humps' extreme values first
optionC: Describe the two segments separately and target each with its own offer
optionD: Use the median, as it is robust and gives one number for the whole base
correctAnswerText: Describe the two segments separately and target each with its own offer
explanation: With two populations, no single centre describes anyone well — the median just lands in or near one hump and hides the other. The useful summary is per segment, and the campaign should be per segment too.

prompt: Customers who set up auto-pay churn 35% less. The product head wants to force auto-pay on everyone to cut churn. What is the soundest response?
optionA: Agree; a 35% difference is too big to be explained by anything else
optionB: Committed customers may choose auto-pay; test the push before claiming the effect
optionC: Agree, provided the correlation is above 0.5 across the customer base
optionD: Disagree; auto-pay cannot affect churn, so the pattern must be noise
correctAnswerText: Committed customers may choose auto-pay; test the push before claiming the effect
explanation: Auto-pay users self-selected, and loyal customers are the ones who set it up. Forcing it may change nothing or annoy people. A randomised nudge (or at least comparing like-for-like customers) is what tests the cause.

prompt: Two stores both average 3.6 on a 1–5 satisfaction scale. Store P has nearly everyone at 3 or 4; Store Q has many 1s and many 5s. Which report serves the regional manager best?
optionA: The two medians alone, since ratings should never be averaged
optionB: The two averages, since 3.6 versus 3.6 shows that they perform alike
optionC: The share of ratings in each level, or 4–5 and 1–2 shares per store
optionD: The standard deviation alone, as it shows which store is more varied
correctAnswerText: The share of ratings in each level, or 4–5 and 1–2 shares per store
explanation: Equal averages hide that Q has a large unhappy group needing action. For ordinal ratings, the distribution (or top-two and bottom-two box shares) shows what the manager must act on.

prompt: You want to know whether apps with more reviews tend to have more downloads. Downloads range from 500 to 5 crore and the relationship clearly curves. Which measure suits best?
optionA: Spearman's rank correlation, as it handles skew and any steady rise
optionB: Pearson's r after deleting every app above the 1.5 × IQR fence first
optionC: Pearson's r on raw values, as it is the standard correlation measure
optionD: The covariance, as it keeps the original units of downloads and reviews
correctAnswerText: Spearman's rank correlation, as it handles skew and any steady rise
explanation: With values spanning five orders of magnitude, a few giant apps would dominate Pearson. Spearman asks "does more of one go with more of the other?" — exactly the question — without assuming a straight line. Pearson on log values is a reasonable alternative.

prompt: A candidate scored 78 on aptitude test A (mean 65, SD 5) and 85 on test B (mean 75, SD 10). A recruiter says test B was the stronger result because 85 > 78. Is that the right comparison?
optionA: Yes; B's mean is higher, so beating it is the harder of the two feats
optionB: No; scores from different tests can never be compared in any way
optionC: No; A is 2.6 SD above its mean against 1.0 SD on B, so A is stronger
optionD: Yes; the higher raw score is the stronger result on any pair of tests
correctAnswerText: No; A is 2.6 SD above its mean against 1.0 SD on B, so A is stronger
explanation: Raw scores on tests with different centres and spreads are not comparable. z = (78 − 65)/5 = 2.6 against (85 − 75)/10 = 1.0, so A stands out far more relative to other candidates.

prompt: Return rates by department reverse when split by store size: Department A is lower overall but higher in both small and large stores. Leadership must decide which department's process to copy. What should the report lead with?
optionA: Neither, since a reversal means the data cannot support any decision
optionB: The overall rates, as they cover every return in a single comparison
optionC: Whichever table shows the bigger gap, to make the decision clear
optionD: The per-store-size rates, because the departments' store mix differs
correctAnswerText: The per-store-size rates, because the departments' store mix differs
explanation: The overall figure mixes department performance with store mix. Process decisions are made like-for-like, so the stratified rates are the fair comparison — with the overall shown and the mix difference explained.

prompt: An analyst has all 2 lakh of March's transactions and spends an hour debating ddof=0 versus ddof=1 for the SD. How should a reviewer judge that time?
optionA: Mostly wasted: at this n the two differ by a negligible fraction
optionB: Well spent: ddof=1 is wrong whenever the whole population is used
optionC: Well spent: the choice changes the SD by roughly half at any n
optionD: Mostly wasted: the SD should never be computed on a full population
correctAnswerText: Mostly wasted: at this n the two differ by a negligible fraction
explanation: The ratio of the two SDs is √(n / (n − 1)); at n = 2,00,000 that is about 1.0000025. ddof matters for small samples, not here. Time is better spent on whether the SD is even the right spread measure.

prompt: A support team's weekly "typical handling time" KPI keeps jumping because of one or two stuck tickets a week. Ten tickets: [22, 25, 27, 28, 30, 31, 33, 35, 36, 95] minutes give mean 36.2, median 30.5, 10% trimmed mean 30.6. Which KPI is the best choice?
optionA: Median or trimmed mean, tracked with a separate count of stuck tickets
optionB: The mean after deleting tickets above the 1.5 × IQR fence each week
optionC: The mean, because hiding the stuck tickets would flatter the team
optionD: The maximum, because the stuck tickets are what customers complain about
correctAnswerText: Median or trimmed mean, tracked with a separate count of stuck tickets
explanation: A "typical" KPI should not swing on one ticket, so a robust centre fits. The stuck tickets are a separate problem and deserve their own visible metric rather than being buried in, or silently deleted from, the average.

prompt: In a churn analysis, what does P(churn | no login in 30 days) stand for?
optionA: The chance of churning among users with no login in 30 days
optionB: The chance that a user both churns and has no login in 30 days
optionC: The chance of no login in 30 days among users who churned
optionD: The chance of churning, multiplied by the chance of no login
correctAnswerText: The chance of churning among users with no login in 30 days
explanation: P(A | B) is the probability of A within the group where B is true — here, churn among inactive users. Swapping the two sides gives a different number, which is the commonest error in reading these.

prompt: Events A and B are independent exactly when which statement holds?
optionA: P(A and B) equals zero
optionB: P(A) plus P(B) equals 1
optionC: P(A | B) equals P(B | A)
optionD: P(A | B) equals P(A)
correctAnswerText: P(A | B) equals P(A)
explanation: Independence means knowing B happened does not change the chance of A, so P(A | B) = P(A), equivalently P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). P(A and B) = 0 describes events that cannot happen together, which is a different idea.

prompt: What is the usual formula for the standard error of a sample mean?
optionA: s / √n
optionB: s / n
optionC: s × √n
optionD: √s / n
correctAnswerText: s / √n
explanation: SE = s / √n, the sample SD divided by the square root of the sample size. It measures how much the sample mean would vary from sample to sample, not how much individual values vary.

prompt: What does the central limit theorem say about the mean of a reasonably large random sample?
optionA: It equals the population mean exactly once n is large enough
optionB: Its sampling distribution is close to normal, whatever the data's shape
optionC: The values in the sample become close to normal once n passes 30
optionD: Its standard error grows in step with the size of the sample
correctAnswerText: Its sampling distribution is close to normal, whatever the data's shape
explanation: The CLT is about how sample means are distributed across repeated samples. The data stays as skewed as it was; it is the mean that behaves like a normal variable.

prompt: For a normal distribution, roughly what share of values lies within one standard deviation of the mean?
optionA: About 50%
optionB: About 68%
optionC: About 95%
optionD: About 99.7%
correctAnswerText: About 68%
explanation: About 68% lies within ±1 SD, about 95% within ±1.96 SD and about 99.7% within ±3 SD. 50% is the share on either side of the mean.

prompt: Which situation fits the binomial distribution?
optionA: Counting how many orders arrive at a store in each hour of the day
optionB: Measuring how many minutes each of 20 deliveries took on Saturday
optionC: Counting how many of 20 independent leads convert, each with chance 0.1
optionD: Recording which of five payment methods each of 20 customers used
correctAnswerText: Counting how many of 20 independent leads convert, each with chance 0.1
explanation: Binomial needs a fixed number of independent yes/no trials with the same success chance, counting the yeses. Minutes are continuous, hourly arrivals are a Poisson-style count, and five payment methods are categories.

prompt: Which distribution is the usual first model for the number of support tickets arriving per hour?
optionA: Uniform
optionB: Normal
optionC: Binomial with n = 2
optionD: Poisson
correctAnswerText: Poisson
explanation: Poisson models counts of independent events in a fixed interval at a steady average rate — arrivals, calls, tickets per hour. Its one parameter is that average rate.

prompt: An auditor pulls 400 of March's 2 lakh orders and computes their mean value. What is that mean called?
optionA: A standard error, since it comes from a sample
optionB: A population mean, as the sample was random
optionC: A parameter, since it describes March's orders
optionD: A statistic, estimating the population parameter
correctAnswerText: A statistic, estimating the population parameter
explanation: A statistic is computed from a sample; a parameter is the true value for the whole population (the mean of all 2 lakh orders), usually unknown. Inference is the gap between them.

prompt: An edtech platform measures "average customer tenure" using only its current subscribers. What kind of bias does this build in?
optionA: Confirmation bias — the analyst wants long tenure
optionB: Survivorship bias — early churners are missing
optionC: Non-response bias — some users skipped a survey
optionD: Measurement bias — tenure is recorded in months
correctAnswerText: Survivorship bias — early churners are missing
explanation: Everyone who left early has dropped out of the data, so the measured tenure is longer than the true tenure of all customers who ever joined.

prompt: A 95% interval for a mean uses the SD estimated from a sample of 12. Which distribution supplies the critical value?
optionA: The chi-square distribution with 11 degrees
optionB: The t distribution with 11 degrees of freedom
optionC: The standard normal, which always gives 1.96
optionD: The t distribution with 12 degrees of freedom
correctAnswerText: The t distribution with 11 degrees of freedom
explanation: When the SD is estimated from the sample, the t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom is used; its critical value (2.20 here) is larger than 1.96 and approaches it as n grows.

prompt: A survey team quadruples its random sample from 500 to 2,000. What happens to the standard error of the mean, and why?
optionA: It falls to a quarter, because SE shrinks in proportion to n
optionB: It is unchanged, because the population SD stays the same
optionC: It halves, because SE shrinks with the square root of n
optionD: It doubles, because more values add more variability
correctAnswerText: It halves, because SE shrinks with the square root of n
explanation: SE = s / √n, and √4 = 2, so four times the data buys half the uncertainty. Precision is expensive: halving the SE again would need 8,000.

prompt: Average delivery time is estimated at 34 minutes, 95% CI 31.6 to 36.3. What does the "95%" describe?
optionA: The estimate: 34 minutes is correct to within 95% of its value
optionB: This interval: there is a 95% chance the true mean lies inside it
optionC: The deliveries: 95% of them took between 31.6 and 36.3 minutes
optionD: The method: such intervals capture the true mean in 95% of samples
correctAnswerText: The method: such intervals capture the true mean in 95% of samples
explanation: The true mean is fixed; this interval either contains it or not. The 95% is the long-run success rate of the procedure. The interval is about the mean, not about individual deliveries.

prompt: Order values have SD ₹800 and the mean of 400 orders has SE ₹40. What is the difference between the two figures?
optionA: SD is the spread of single orders; SE is the spread of the sample mean
optionB: SD applies to the population and SE applies to any random sample
optionC: SE is the spread of single orders; SD is the spread of the mean
optionD: They measure the same spread, but SE is rounded to fewer digits
correctAnswerText: SD is the spread of single orders; SE is the spread of the sample mean
explanation: Individual orders vary by around ₹800; the average of 400 of them varies far less, by about 800 / √400 = ₹40. Confusing the two makes data look far more or far less variable than it is.

prompt: "80% of fraudulent card transactions happen between midnight and 5 a.m." Why does this NOT mean most night transactions are fraud?
optionA: It is about a sample, so it says nothing about fraud in the population
optionB: It is P(night | fraud); P(fraud | night) also depends on how rare fraud is
optionC: Night transactions are excluded, as the 80% only counts fraudulent ones
optionD: It does mean that, since 80% is a clear majority of all the transactions
correctAnswerText: It is P(night | fraud); P(fraud | night) also depends on how rare fraud is
explanation: The statement conditions on fraud. Because fraud is rare and genuine night transactions are many, P(fraud | night) can still be tiny. Turning one conditional into the other needs the base rates.

prompt: Why does collecting a bigger sample reduce sampling error but not bias?
optionA: Bias only appears in small samples, so it vanishes once n passes 1,000
optionB: Sampling error depends on how units are chosen, and bias depends on n
optionC: Chance errors average out as n grows; a skewed selection rule stays skewed
optionD: A bigger sample reduces both, but the bias shrinks more slowly than error
correctAnswerText: Chance errors average out as n grows; a skewed selection rule stays skewed
explanation: Random error shrinks like 1 / √n. Bias comes from how units were picked or who answered, and repeating the same faulty process at scale gives a confidently wrong answer.

prompt: An order is paid by UPI or by card, never both, and each happens in a sizeable share of orders. Why are "paid by UPI" and "paid by card" NOT independent?
optionA: Only events with exactly equal probabilities can be independent of each other
optionB: They are independent, because the two probabilities add up to less than 1
optionC: Knowing it was UPI makes card impossible, so one changes the other's chance
optionD: They are independent, because neither payment method influences the other one
correctAnswerText: Knowing it was UPI makes card impossible, so one changes the other's chance
explanation: Mutually exclusive events with non-zero chances are strongly dependent: P(card | UPI) = 0 while P(card) > 0. "Cannot happen together" and "do not affect each other" are different ideas.

prompt: A cashback offer has an expected profit of ₹45 per customer. What does that figure mean?
optionA: Averaged over many customers, profit per customer is about ₹45
optionB: At least half of the customers will produce ₹45 or more
optionC: Every single customer will generate exactly ₹45 of profit
optionD: The most common profit from one customer will be ₹45
correctAnswerText: Averaged over many customers, profit per customer is about ₹45
explanation: Expected value is a long-run average weighted by probabilities. Individual customers may give ₹0 or ₹150, and no customer need produce exactly ₹45; it is not the mode or the median.

prompt: Why is the t critical value for a 95% interval larger than 1.96 when the sample is small?
optionA: A small sample has a smaller mean, so a bigger multiplier compensates
optionB: The SD is itself estimated, which adds uncertainty and fattens the tails
optionC: Small samples are always biased, so the interval is widened to correct it
optionD: The t value is chosen by the analyst to be more cautious than is required
correctAnswerText: The SD is itself estimated, which adds uncertainty and fattens the tails
explanation: With few values the sample SD can be well off the true SD; the t distribution accounts for that with heavier tails. At n = 6 the value is 2.57; by n = 100 it is 1.98.

prompt: The 20 sales reps with the worst January numbers are sent for coaching, and in February their numbers improve. Why is that not, on its own, evidence the coaching worked?
optionA: Extreme months are partly bad luck, so the worst tend to drift back anyway
optionB: Coaching cannot be measured with sales numbers, only with surveys
optionC: The reps were not chosen at random from the region's population
optionD: February always has more working days, so sales must rise every year
correctAnswerText: Extreme months are partly bad luck, so the worst tend to drift back anyway
explanation: Selecting on an extreme score picks up people whose luck was bad that month; next month their luck is average and the numbers rise with no help. A comparison group of similar reps who were not coached is needed.

prompt: A screening model is "95% accurate", yet most transactions it flags turn out to be genuine. How can both be true?
optionA: The model must be overfitted, as accurate models cannot behave this way
optionB: Accuracy counts only fraud cases, so it ignores flags on genuine ones
optionC: Most flagged transactions are fraud; the report must be miscounting
optionD: Fraud is so rare that false alarms on genuine ones outnumber true catches
correctAnswerText: Fraud is so rare that false alarms on genuine ones outnumber true catches
explanation: A small false-positive rate applied to a huge number of genuine transactions produces more flags than the few fraud cases do. The base rate, not just accuracy, decides what a flag means.

prompt: 0.5% of transactions are fraud. A rule flags 95% of fraud and 2% of genuine transactions. What is the chance that a flagged transaction is fraud?
optionA: About 2.5%
optionB: About 95%
optionC: About 19%
optionD: About 98%
correctAnswerText: About 19%
explanation: Per 1,00,000 transactions: 500 fraud × 0.95 = 475 true flags; 99,500 genuine × 0.02 = 1,990 false flags. 475 / 2,465 ≈ 19.3%. 2.5% is the share of all transactions flagged.

prompt:
Visits and purchases by device:

| Device | Visits | Purchases |
|---|---|---|
| Android | 2,400 | 96 |
| iOS | 1,600 | 112 |

What is P(purchase | iOS)?
explanation: Condition on iOS: 112 / 1,600 = 7.0%. 4.0% is Android's rate, 5.2% the overall rate (208 / 4,000), and 53.8% is P(iOS | purchase) = 112 / 208.

prompt: Each of 5 independent customers redeems a coupon with probability 0.2. What is the probability that at least one of them redeems?
optionA: Exactly 1.00
optionB: About 0.67
optionC: About 0.0003
optionD: About 0.20
correctAnswerText: About 0.67
explanation: P(none) = 0.8⁵ = 0.328, so P(at least one) = 1 − 0.328 = 0.672. Adding 0.2 five times gives 1.0, which overcounts; 0.2⁵ is the chance that all five redeem.

prompt: Complaints arrive at an average of 2 per hour, roughly Poisson. What does stats.poisson.cdf(1, 2) give, and what does it mean?
optionA: 0.406 — the chance of at most one complaint in an hour
optionB: 0.500 — the chance of fewer complaints than average
optionC: 0.594 — the chance of at most one complaint in an hour
optionD: 0.135 — the chance of exactly one complaint in an hour
correctAnswerText: 0.406 — the chance of at most one complaint in an hour
explanation: cdf(1, 2) = P(0) + P(1) = e⁻² (1 + 2) = 0.135 + 0.271 = 0.406. 0.135 is P(0) alone, and 0.594 is the chance of two or more.

prompt: Assembly times are roughly normal with mean 30 and SD 5 minutes. About what share take longer than 40 minutes?
optionA: About 2.3%
optionB: About 25%
optionC: About 5%
optionD: About 16%
correctAnswerText: About 2.3%
explanation: 40 is (40 − 30) / 5 = 2 SDs above the mean; stats.norm.sf(2) = 0.0228. 5% is the share beyond ±1.96 SD on both sides combined, and 16% lies beyond 1 SD.

prompt: Loan amounts have an SD of ₹900 (in hundreds). A random sample of 225 loans is drawn. What is the standard error of its mean?
explanation: SE = 900 / √225 = 900 / 15 = 60. Dividing by n gives 4, and 15 is just √225.

prompt: 132 of 600 randomly chosen users say they would pay for a premium tier. Using p ± 1.96 × √(p(1 − p)/n), what is the 95% interval?
optionA: About 21.8% to 22.2%
optionB: About 20.3% to 23.7%
optionC: About 12.0% to 32.0%
optionD: About 18.7% to 25.3%
correctAnswerText: About 18.7% to 25.3%

prompt: 16 randomly timed onboarding calls have mean 52 minutes and sample SD 8. With stats.t.ppf(0.975, 15) = 2.131, what is the 95% interval for the mean?
optionA: About 35.0 to 69.0 minutes
optionB: About 47.7 to 56.3 minutes
optionC: About 48.1 to 55.9 minutes
optionD: About 50.0 to 54.0 minutes
correctAnswerText: About 47.7 to 56.3 minutes
explanation: SE = 8 / √16 = 2; margin = 2.131 × 2 = 4.26; so 52 ± 4.26. Using 1.96 gives 48.1 to 55.9, slightly too narrow; ±2.131 × 8 describes individual calls, not the mean.

prompt: A team wants a margin of ±4 percentage points at 95% confidence and has no idea of the proportion. Using n = 1.96² × 0.25 / margin², how many responses are needed?
explanation: 1.96² × 0.25 / 0.04² = 600.25, rounded up to 601. p = 0.5 is the worst case, so 601 is enough for any proportion. 1,068 is the figure for ±3 pp.

prompt: A ₹100 cashback is sent to inactive customers. 30% come back and each returner brings ₹250 of margin before the cashback is paid; non-returners cost nothing. What is the expected profit per customer targeted?
explanation: Only returners claim the cashback: 0.3 × (250 − 100) + 0.7 × 0 = ₹45. ₹75 ignores the cashback cost; ₹150 is the profit from one returner, not the average over everyone targeted.

prompt: From 400 orders, the 95% CI for mean order value is ₹640 to ₹720. A slide says "95% of our customers spend between ₹640 and ₹720". What is wrong?
optionA: The interval is for the mean; single orders spread far more widely
optionB: The interval should be widened by 1.96 before talking about customers
optionC: Nothing; a 95% interval covers 95% of the orders it was built from
optionD: It should say 95% of customers spend at least ₹640, not between
correctAnswerText: The interval is for the mean; single orders spread far more widely
explanation: An interval for a mean narrows as n grows; individual orders do not. With order SD around ₹400, most orders lie far outside ₹640–₹720. A statement about customers needs percentiles of the data.

prompt: Of 1,000 shoppers, 200 bought a phone, 150 a charger and 120 both. An analyst estimates P(phone and charger) as 0.20 × 0.15 = 3%. The actual share is 12%. What went wrong?
optionA: The 120 should have been subtracted from both groups before multiplying
optionB: Nothing; the 12% must be a counting error in the order table
optionC: The figures should have been added, giving 35% for buying both items
optionD: Multiplying assumes independence, but phone buyers often add a charger
correctAnswerText: Multiplying assumes independence, but phone buyers often add a charger
explanation: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) only for independent events. Here P(charger | phone) = 120 / 200 = 60%, far above 15%, so the purchases are strongly linked and P(both) = 0.20 × 0.60 = 12%.

prompt: A survey of 2,000 users has a ±2.2 pp margin. The report applies ±2.2 pp to the 125 respondents from Pune too. Roughly what should the Pune margin be?
optionA: About ±0.1 pp — a subgroup is more precise
optionB: About ±8.8 pp — the subgroup is 16× smaller
optionC: About ±2.2 pp — the margin belongs to the survey
optionD: About ±35 pp — the margin grows in step with n
correctAnswerText: About ±8.8 pp — the subgroup is 16× smaller
explanation: Margin ∝ 1/√n: at p = 0.5, 1.96 × √(0.25 / 125) = 0.088. A sixteen-times-smaller group has a four-times-larger margin, so small city differences may be noise.

prompt: From 6 pilot stores (mean 20, SD 3), an analyst reports a 95% interval of 20 ± 2.40 using 1.96. What is the problem?
optionA: With n = 6 the t value 2.571 applies, giving ±3.15 — wider
optionB: Nothing; 1.96 is correct for any 95% interval for a mean
optionC: The SD must be divided by n − 1, giving a margin of ±1.18
optionD: With n = 6 the margin should use n, not √n, giving ±0.98
correctAnswerText: With n = 6 the t value 2.571 applies, giving ±3.15 — wider
explanation: SE = 3 / √6 = 1.22. With the SD estimated from 6 values, t(5) = 2.571, so the margin is 3.15. The 1.96 interval is about 24% too narrow and over-states the precision.

prompt: An early-warning rule fires for 90% of borrowers who later default. 10% of borrowers default, and the rule also fires for 20% of those who do not. A manager says "a flagged borrower has a 90% chance of default". What is the actual chance?
optionA: About 90%
optionB: About 33%
optionC: About 50%
optionD: About 10%
correctAnswerText: About 33%
explanation: Per 1,000 borrowers: 100 defaulters × 0.9 = 90 flagged; 900 others × 0.2 = 180 flagged. P(default | flag) = 90 / 270 = 1/3. The 90% is P(flag | default).

prompt: 2 of 40 beta users reported a crash. The p ± 1.96 × √(p(1 − p)/n) interval comes out as −1.8% to 11.8%. What does the negative lower end show?
optionA: The simple formula fails with so few events; a Wilson interval fits
optionB: Nothing; a negative lower end is normal and can be reported as is
optionC: The analyst should have used 2.576 instead of 1.96 for this case
optionD: The crash rate could really be negative, so the result is suspect
correctAnswerText: The simple formula fails with so few events; a Wilson interval fits
explanation: The Wald interval assumes a roughly normal sampling distribution, which breaks down with 2 yeses. The Wilson interval (binomtest(2, 40).proportion_ci(method="wilson")) gives about 1.4% to 16.5% and stays inside 0–100%.

prompt: A report on 1,600 deliveries states "delivery times vary by only ±0.3 minutes", quoting the standard error. The sample SD is 12 minutes. What is the error?
optionA: The SE should be 12 / 1,600, so the variation is even smaller than stated
optionB: Nothing; the SE is the correct measure of how much deliveries vary
optionC: The SD should have been divided by n − 1 before being reported
optionD: The SE (12 / 40) describes the mean, not how much single deliveries vary
correctAnswerText: The SE (12 / 40) describes the mean, not how much single deliveries vary
explanation: SE = 12 / √1,600 = 0.3 is the uncertainty in the average. Individual deliveries vary by around 12 minutes; quoting the SE as variation makes the service look forty times more consistent than it is.

prompt: A poll of 50,000 users who opted into notifications reports 71% ± 0.4 pp. Leadership treats ±0.4 pp as the total uncertainty about all users. What is missing?
optionA: The margin covers chance only; opted-in users may differ from all users
optionB: The margin should be ±4 pp, since it was computed with the wrong n
optionC: Nothing; with 50,000 responses any bias becomes negligible
optionD: The margin is too wide; with 50,000 users it should be ±0.04 pp
correctAnswerText: The margin covers chance only; opted-in users may differ from all users
explanation: 1.96 × √(0.71 × 0.29 / 50,000) ≈ 0.4 pp is correct for random error. Opted-in users are a self-selected group, and that bias is not in the formula and does not shrink with n.

prompt: Three replica servers each fail on 1% of days. An engineer says all three fail together on 0.01³ = one day in a million. They share one power supply and one data centre. What is wrong?
optionA: The figure should be 3 × 0.01 = 3%, since the three risks add together
optionB: The figure should be 1 − 0.99³ ≈ 3%, the chance that all three fail together
optionC: A shared cause makes failures dependent, so joint failure is far likelier
optionD: Nothing; replicas are independent by design, so multiplying is correct
correctAnswerText: A shared cause makes failures dependent, so joint failure is far likelier
explanation: Multiplying needs independence. A power cut takes all three down at once, so P(all fail) is at least the chance of that shared failure. 1 − 0.99³ ≈ 3% is the chance that at least one fails, a different event.

prompt: An analyst plans to flag "unusual" refund amounts as those beyond mean ± 2 SD, arguing: "we have 5,000 refunds, so by the CLT the amounts are normal". What is the flaw?
optionA: The CLT needs at least 10,000 values before it applies to any data
optionB: Nothing; with 5,000 values the CLT makes the amounts close to normal
optionC: The CLT is about sample means; the refund amounts themselves stay skewed
optionD: The CLT applies only to proportions, not to amounts in rupees
correctAnswerText: The CLT is about sample means; the refund amounts themselves stay skewed
explanation: A large sample makes the mean's sampling distribution normal; it does not reshape the data. On skewed refunds, mean ± 2 SD flags the wrong things. Use percentiles or a log scale for the amounts.

prompt: A payments team must report the chargeback rate: 3 of 250 orders (1.2%). Which interval should they report, and why?
optionA: Wald widened to 99% — rare events need extra confidence
optionB: No interval — with 3 events the rate cannot be estimated
optionC: Wilson, about 0.4% to 3.5% — it stays valid with few events
optionD: Wald, about −0.1% to 2.5% — it is the standard formula
correctAnswerText: Wilson, about 0.4% to 3.5% — it stays valid with few events
explanation: With 3 events the Wald interval dips below zero and under-covers. Wilson (computed with SciPy) gives roughly 0.41% to 3.47%, an honest range that stays within 0–100%. Three events still carry information.

prompt: A survey of 1,000 customers must give usable estimates for Tier-3 towns, which are 5% of the base. What is the best sampling plan?
optionA: Survey only Tier-3 towns, since that is the segment of real interest
optionB: A simple random sample of 1,000, which keeps everything unbiased
optionC: Use volunteers from Tier-3 towns to raise their count quickly and cheaply
optionD: Stratify and oversample Tier-3 towns, then weight back to the true mix
correctAnswerText: Stratify and oversample Tier-3 towns, then weight back to the true mix
explanation: A simple random sample gives about 50 Tier-3 responses (margin near ±14 pp). Oversampling the stratum gives it a usable size, and weighting restores the correct mix for overall figures. Volunteers would add bias.

prompt: For 400 responses at p = 30%, the margin is ±3.8 pp at 90%, ±4.5 pp at 95% and ±5.9 pp at 99%. A manager asks for the 99% interval "to be safer". What is the trade-off to explain?
optionA: All three intervals carry the same information, so any one will do
optionB: Higher confidence buys a wider, less precise range from the same data
optionC: Higher confidence makes the estimate more accurate as well as wider
optionD: Higher confidence removes the chance that the sample was biased
correctAnswerText: Higher confidence buys a wider, less precise range from the same data
explanation: Same data, so more confidence must cost precision. Choosing the level is a judgement about the cost of being wrong; no level protects against bias, and none makes the estimate itself better.

prompt: Nationally 48% of 1,500 respondents like a new pack design (±2.5 pp). Among the 120 from Kochi it is 42% (±8.8 pp). A regional head wants to drop the design in Kochi. What is the best advice?
optionA: Keep it everywhere, since subgroup results can never be trusted at all
optionB: Drop it, since 42% is six points below the national figure of 48%
optionC: Drop it nationally, since one weak city shows the design has failed
optionD: The Kochi figure is consistent with the national one; collect more first
correctAnswerText: The Kochi figure is consistent with the national one; collect more first
explanation: Kochi's interval runs from about 33% to 51% and comfortably includes 48%. Six points is well within noise for 120 people; a targeted follow-up sample would settle it.

prompt: A launch goes ahead if interest exceeds 20%. A pilot survey shows 35% ± 2 pp (about 2,200 responses). Someone proposes surveying about 8,700 people to reach ±1 pp. Is it worth it?
optionA: Yes; quadrupling the sample also removes any bias in the original survey
optionB: Yes; ±1 pp is the industry standard, so the launch must wait for it
optionC: No; the whole interval is far above 20%, so precision will not change the call
optionD: No; a survey can never inform a launch, so neither one is worth running
correctAnswerText: No; the whole interval is far above 20%, so precision will not change the call
explanation: Precision is worth buying only if it could change the decision. 33%–37% is nowhere near 20%, and halving the margin would cost four times the responses for no change. Bias is a separate question that a bigger sample does not answer.

prompt: A fraud desk sees 1.2 escalations a day on average and wants to know how often a day brings 4 or more. Which model suits best?
optionA: Normal with mean 1.2, which gives about 0% of days
optionB: Binomial with n = 4, which gives about 30% of days
optionC: Poisson with mean 1.2, giving about 3.4% of days
optionD: Uniform from 0 to 4, giving 25% of all the days
correctAnswerText: Poisson with mean 1.2, giving about 3.4% of days
explanation: Rare independent events at a steady rate are what the Poisson describes; 1 − poisson.cdf(3, 1.2) ≈ 0.034. A normal curve is a poor fit for small counts that cannot go below zero.

prompt: A report must give an interval for the MEDIAN delivery time from 300 skewed timings. A colleague suggests median ± 1.96 × s / √n. What is the better approach?
optionA: Take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the 300 raw delivery times
optionB: Use the colleague's formula, since s / √n works for any statistic
optionC: Bootstrap: resample with replacement and take percentiles of the medians
optionD: Report the interval for the mean instead, as medians have no interval
correctAnswerText: Bootstrap: resample with replacement and take percentiles of the medians
explanation: s / √n is the standard error of the mean, not of the median. Resampling the data many times and reading the middle 95% of the bootstrap medians gives a sound interval. Percentiles of raw times describe deliveries, not the median.

prompt: Fraud is 1% of transactions; a rule catches 90% of fraud and flags 4% of genuine ones, so about 19% of flags are fraud. Ops wants every flagged transaction auto-declined. What is the best judgement?
optionA: Auto-decline, since 19% of flags is well above the 1% base rate of fraud
optionB: Route flags to step-up checks; auto-declining would block ~4 genuine per fraud
optionC: Ignore the rule; with only 19% of flags being fraud it has no value at all
optionD: Auto-decline; a rule that catches 90% of fraud is accurate enough to act on
correctAnswerText: Route flags to step-up checks; auto-declining would block ~4 genuine per fraud
explanation: P(fraud | flag) = 0.009 / (0.009 + 0.0396) ≈ 18.5%: roughly four genuine customers per fraud would be declined. The flag is valuable (about 18 times the base rate) but suits a cheap second check, not a hard block.

prompt: A survey sample is 70% iOS users, while the customer base is 25% iOS, and iOS users spend more. Before reporting average spend, what should the analyst do?
optionA: Weight responses to the true device mix, or report each device separately
optionB: Report the raw figure, since device mix cannot affect average spend
optionC: Drop iOS responses until the sample matches the 25% share exactly
optionD: Report the raw average, as it still reflects the customers who responded
correctAnswerText: Weight responses to the true device mix, or report each device separately
explanation: Comparing the sample with known population figures exposes the skew. Weighting (or stratified reporting) corrects for the known imbalance; dropping data wastes responses. Unknown differences remain, so the caveat stays.

prompt: Which sentence best reports "26% of 1,200 surveyed customers want the feature; 95% CI 23.5% to 28.5%" to a leadership team?
optionA: "There is a 95% chance exactly 26% of customers want the feature."
optionB: "26% of customers want the feature, so it should go on the roadmap."
optionC: "We estimate 26% want it; the true share is plausibly 23.5%–28.5%."
optionD: "Between 23.5% and 28.5% of the 1,200 surveyed want the feature."
correctAnswerText: "We estimate 26% want it; the true share is plausibly 23.5%–28.5%."
explanation: The good sentence gives the estimate and the plausible range for the population share. The others misread the 95%, drop the uncertainty and jump to a decision, or describe the sample — whose share is exactly 26%.

prompt: In an A/B test of a new checkout button, what is the null hypothesis H₀?
optionA: The new button converts better than the old one does
optionB: The new button's true conversion rate equals the old one's
optionC: The new button converts worse than the old one does
optionD: The observed difference between the groups is exactly zero
correctAnswerText: The new button's true conversion rate equals the old one's
explanation: H₀ is a statement about the true rates: no difference. The observed difference is almost never exactly zero even when H₀ holds; the test asks whether it is surprising under H₀.

prompt: What is the significance level α in a hypothesis test?
optionA: The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true
optionB: The chance of detecting a real effect of the chosen size
optionC: The false-positive rate you accept, fixed before seeing data
