optionB: Short tickets always look alike; pad them all to a fixed length first
optionC: The threshold is too strict; raise it to 0.95 and keep the same pooling
optionD: The model is overfitted to tickets; fine-tune it on news text instead
correctAnswerText: The [CLS] vector was never trained for similarity; use masked mean pooling
explanation: With the pooling the model was trained for, the same pairs score much lower (0.13–0.32 in the lesson). Fix the pooling (or use the sentence-transformers wrapper), then re-set the threshold.

prompt: Semantic search returns different results for a query depending on what else was in its batch. The pooling line is v = h.mean(dim=1). What is wrong?
optionA: The model is in training mode, so dropout changes each of the vectors
optionB: h.mean averages over the hidden size; it should be dim=2 instead
optionC: The mean includes padding positions; weight it by the attention mask
optionD: Batches must be sorted alphabetically before they are embedded
correctAnswerText: The mean includes padding positions; weight it by the attention mask
explanation: The amount of padding depends on the longest text in the batch, so averaging it in moves the vector. (h * mask).sum(1) / mask.sum(1) gives the same vector in any batch.

prompt: An index ranks by inner product. A handful of the same documents appear near the top for almost every query, and their vectors have the largest lengths in the collection. Diagnosis?
optionA: Those documents are the most relevant, which is why they appear
optionB: Inner product cannot be used with vectors of more than 128 numbers
optionC: The index needs more memory, so it returns cached results each time
optionD: Vectors were not normalised, so length is inflating the scores
correctAnswerText: Vectors were not normalised, so length is inflating the scores
explanation: An inner product grows with vector length as well as with alignment. Normalise documents and queries to unit length (or use cosine) unless the model's card says inner product on raw vectors is intended.

prompt: A duplicate detector merges "payment failed but money deducted" with "payment successful, thank you" at cosine 0.81. Agents complain complaints are vanishing. What explains it, and what helps?
optionA: The threshold is fine; the agents' labels are what is inconsistent
optionB: Same topic, opposite outcome; check such pairs and add a guard rule
optionC: Cosine ignores the verbs, so the vectors must be built from nouns
optionD: The model is broken, since opposite meanings must score below zero
correctAnswerText: Same topic, opposite outcome; check such pairs and add a guard rule
explanation: Embeddings weigh topic heavily and outcome lightly. Measure on labelled pairs that include such opposites, add a rule (or a pair classifier) for resolved-versus-complaint, and suggest merges rather than auto-merge.

prompt: Swapping an English embedding model for a larger "multilingual" one made Hinglish ticket matching worse, not better. What is the most likely reason?
optionA: Multilingual models output shorter vectors, which lose meaning
optionB: It learned Hindi in Devanagari, not Hindi typed in Latin letters
optionC: The Hinglish tickets were truncated by the multilingual tokenizer
optionD: Larger models always do worse on short texts such as tickets
correctAnswerText: It learned Hindi in Devanagari, not Hindi typed in Latin letters
explanation: "Multilingual" describes the training data, which for Hindi is mostly Devanagari script. Romanised Hinglish is a different surface form, so test on your own mix; transliteration or a model trained on romanised text may help.

prompt: After switching to a new embedding model (and re-embedding everything), the "related articles" widget shows either nothing or everything. The 0.75 cutoff was kept from the old model. Diagnosis?
optionA: The new model spreads scores differently; re-set the cutoff on labelled pairs
optionB: Cosine cutoffs only work with models below 512 dimensions in size
optionC: Re-embedding failed, so old and new vectors are still mixed in the index
optionD: The new model is worse, so the team must roll back to the earlier model
correctAnswerText: The new model spreads scores differently; re-set the cutoff on labelled pairs
explanation: Everything was re-embedded, so nothing is mixed; the cutoff, though, belonged to the old model's score scale. Re-derive it from labelled related/unrelated pairs for the new model.

prompt: k-means on support-ticket embeddings gives one cluster containing nearly all Hinglish tickets, mixing refunds, KYC and OTP problems. What does this show?
optionA: k-means failed to converge, so the clusters are random groups
optionB: Hinglish customers all have the same problem in these tickets
optionC: The number of clusters is too high, which splits by language
optionD: The vectors encode language and wording as strongly as intent
correctAnswerText: The vectors encode language and wording as strongly as intent
explanation: A cluster forms around whatever dominates the vectors; here the surface language does. Read samples per cluster, and consider clustering within each language or using a model that aligns them.

prompt: Long product descriptions open with the same 300 tokens of brand boilerplate, and the model reads 256 tokens. Near-duplicate detection flags every pair of products from the brand. Cause?
optionA: Cosine similarity saturates near 1 for any text longer than 200 words
optionB: The specs past token 256 are cut, so every vector is the boilerplate
optionC: Long texts always score as duplicates, whatever their real content
optionD: The brand name is repeated, and the model weighs repeated words most
correctAnswerText: The specs past token 256 are cut, so every vector is the boilerplate
explanation: Truncation keeps only the shared opening, so all the vectors embed the same text. Strip boilerplate before embedding, or embed the distinguishing sections, and check token lengths first.

prompt: A fraud model uses nn.Embedding(5000, 16) for merchant ids 0–4,999. In production it crashes with "IndexError: index out of range in self" when a new merchant arrives as id 5000. What is the right fix?
optionA: Reserve an "unknown" row and map unseen merchants to it
optionB: Use the merchant id as a plain number instead of an embedding
optionC: Re-train the model from scratch each time a merchant joins
optionD: Wrap the call in try/except and skip transactions that fail
correctAnswerText: Reserve an "unknown" row and map unseen merchants to it
explanation: An embedding table has rows only for ids seen at training. Map unseen or rare values to a shared unknown id (trained on rare merchants) and retrain on a schedule. Skipping fraud checks is not acceptable.

prompt: A team reports its new FAQ matcher is better because "average top-1 cosine rose from 0.71 to 0.83" after switching models. Why is that evidence weak?
optionA: Higher cosine always means worse matches, so the change is a loss
optionB: Averages hide outliers, so the median cosine should be reported
optionC: Cosine scales differ by model and say nothing about correct matches
optionD: Top-1 cosine is fine, but it should have been top-5 cosine instead
correctAnswerText: Cosine scales differ by model and say nothing about correct matches
explanation: A model that scores everything higher raises average cosine without matching better. Quality is measured against labelled query–answer pairs: the share of queries whose correct FAQ is ranked first or in the top few.

prompt: A team with 2,000 labelled tickets must choose features for a router. Which plan is soundest?
optionA: Compare TF-IDF and frozen embeddings on a later-period test set
optionB: Pick whichever scores higher on a random split of the tickets
optionC: Use TF-IDF only, since embeddings cannot be used as features
optionD: Use embeddings without a baseline, since they always beat TF-IDF
correctAnswerText: Compare TF-IDF and frozen embeddings on a later-period test set
explanation: TF-IDF is the cheap number to beat; frozen embeddings often win on new wording. A time-based split shows the wording drift production will see, which a random split hides.

prompt: Two embedding models are on offer: a small English one and a large multilingual one with better public benchmark scores. Tickets mix English and Hinglish. How should the team choose?
optionA: Take the higher public benchmark score, since it reflects all uses
optionB: Take the larger model, since more parameters always embed better
optionC: Take the smaller model, since small models always generalise better
optionD: Score both on labelled ticket pairs and queries from its own data
correctAnswerText: Score both on labelled ticket pairs and queries from its own data
explanation: Public benchmarks rarely contain romanised Hinglish support tickets, and bigger was worse in the lesson's own test. A few hundred labelled pairs from the real stream decide it, along with speed and cost.

prompt: A support team wants duplicate tickets merged automatically when cosine ≥ 0.85. Which design is most defensible?
optionA: Show "possible duplicate" to the agent, log accepts, tune on labels
optionB: Merge automatically at 0.99, since nothing above it can be wrong
optionC: Merge automatically at 0.85, since high cosine means the same issue
optionD: Skip embeddings and merge any tickets from the same customer
correctAnswerText: Show "possible duplicate" to the agent, log accepts, tune on labels
explanation: Merging two different problems loses a complaint, and opposite outcomes can score high. A suggestion keeps a person in the loop, and the accept/reject log becomes labelled data for the threshold.

prompt: A team stores 50,000 FAQ vectors today and is choosing between exact (brute-force) search and an ANN index. Which judgement is sound?
optionA: Exact search is fast enough at this size; move to ANN when scale demands
optionB: ANN is required at any size, since exact search cannot run in production
optionC: Exact search is always wrong, since it returns slightly different results
optionD: ANN should be avoided at every size, since it can miss the true neighbour
correctAnswerText: Exact search is fast enough at this size; move to ANN when scale demands
explanation: 50,000 × 384 dot products is one small matrix multiplication, milliseconds on a CPU, and exact. ANN pays off at millions of vectors, where a small recall loss buys a large speed-up; measure that recall.

prompt: For 5 crore product embeddings, a team weighs a 384-dimensional model against a 1,024-dimensional one. What is the sound basis for the choice?
optionA: The larger dimension always, since more dimensions always mean more accuracy
optionB: The smaller dimension always, since dimension never affects result quality
optionC: Whichever dimension the vector database lists first in its documentation
optionD: Measured quality on its own task against the 2.7× storage and search cost
correctAnswerText: Measured quality on its own task against the 2.7× storage and search cost
explanation: 1,024 / 384 = 2.7 times the memory and per-query compute, which at 5 crore vectors is real money (about 77 GB against 205 GB in float32). Whether the larger model earns that is an empirical question on your own data.

prompt: A delivery-time network has a pincode column with about 19,000 values, many with few rows. Which encoding is best justified?
optionA: The pincode as a single number, since nearby codes are nearby places
optionB: One-hot encoding, adding 19,000 sparse input columns to the network
optionC: Drop the column, since networks cannot use high-cardinality columns
optionD: A small learned embedding, with rare pincodes sharing an unknown row
correctAnswerText: A small learned embedding, with rare pincodes sharing an unknown row
explanation: A 16-dimensional embedding learns which pincodes behave alike with far fewer weights than one-hot, and pooling rare values limits overfitting. Pincode digits are not a reliable distance, so the raw number misleads.

prompt: A product manager wants k-means clusters of 50,000 reviews to become the official complaint categories for a dashboard. What is the best advice?
optionA: Adopt the clusters, but re-run k-means every week to keep them current
optionB: Adopt the clusters directly, since unsupervised groups remove human bias
optionC: Use clusters to propose themes; people then define and label categories
optionD: Reject clustering entirely, since embeddings carry no meaning of reviews
correctAnswerText: Use clusters to propose themes; people then define and label categories
explanation: Clusters mix intent with wording and language and change with k and the data. Reading samples per cluster gives candidate themes; written definitions and labelled examples make categories that stay stable.

prompt: To save storage, an engineer proposes keeping only the embeddings of customer messages and deleting the original text. How do you judge it?
optionA: Unwise: a model upgrade needs the text to re-embed everything
optionB: Sound, provided the vectors are stored at float64 precision
optionC: Unwise only for short messages, which embeddings handle poorly
optionD: Sound: the vector holds everything the text did, in less space
correctAnswerText: Unwise: a model upgrade needs the text to re-embed everything
explanation: Vectors from a new model cannot be derived from an old model's vectors; they need the source text. Keep text (subject to retention rules), the vector and the model version together.

prompt: A team says embeddings of customer complaints are "anonymous numbers", so they can be shared freely with a vendor. How should that claim be judged?
optionA: Right, provided the vectors are normalised to unit length first
optionB: Wrong only if the vendor also has the same embedding model weights
optionC: Right: a vector of numbers cannot reveal anything about its source
optionD: Wrong: embeddings can leak the text, so treat them as personal data
correctAnswerText: Wrong: embeddings can leak the text, so treat them as personal data
explanation: Embeddings preserve meaning by design, and inversion attacks can recover much of the original text, names included. Apply the same masking, contracts and access rules as for the text.

prompt: HR proposes shortlisting candidates automatically whenever the cosine between a resume and the job description exceeds 0.8. What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Unsound only because 0.8 is too low; at 0.95 the shortlist would be fair
optionB: Sound, provided the resumes are embedded with the largest model available
optionC: Sound, since a cosine above 0.8 means the candidate matches the job well
optionD: Similarity is topical overlap, not suitability; use it to rank, with review
correctAnswerText: Similarity is topical overlap, not suitability; use it to rank, with review
explanation: A resume that repeats the job's words scores high whatever the person can do, and wording varies with background. Treat similarity as a ranking aid, validate against hiring outcomes, check for bias, and keep a person deciding.

prompt: A churn model was trained as a scikit-learn Pipeline (scaler, encoder, classifier). What should be written to the model file for serving?
optionA: Only the training data, so the server can refit the model at startup
optionB: The notebook that trained it, so the server can re-run all its cells
optionC: The whole fitted pipeline, preprocessing and classifier together
optionD: Only the fitted classifier, since it holds the learned coefficients
correctAnswerText: The whole fitted pipeline, preprocessing and classifier together
explanation: The scaler's means and the encoder's category list are learned too. Saving the whole pipeline means a raw row goes in and a probability comes out, with no hand-rebuilt preprocessing to drift.

prompt: Why must you never load a pickle or joblib file whose source you cannot trace?
optionA: The file may silently send every prediction back to whoever wrote it
optionB: Pickle files lose their model weights when they are moved between drives
optionC: Loading it can call arbitrary functions, so the file can run code
optionD: Untraced files are always saved with an older pickle protocol version
correctAnswerText: Loading it can call arbitrary functions, so the file can run code
explanation: Unpickling rebuilds objects by calling functions named in the file. A malicious file can name os.system, so loading it runs a shell command on your machine.

prompt: What does skops.io do when it loads a file containing a type it does not trust by default?
optionA: It converts the unknown type to the nearest built-in scikit-learn class
optionB: It refuses to load until you name that reviewed type as trusted
optionC: It loads the file and silently skips the unknown step in the pipeline
optionD: It loads the file normally but writes a warning to the log for review
correctAnswerText: It refuses to load until you name that reviewed type as trusted
explanation: skops checks every type in the file against a trusted list and raises UntrustedTypesFoundException otherwise. You pass trusted=[...] naming only types you have reviewed.

prompt: In a FastAPI model service, where should the model file be loaded?
optionA: In a background thread that reloads the file every few seconds
optionB: Once at startup, in the lifespan handler, kept in app state
optionC: Inside the predict handler, so each request gets a fresh copy
optionD: In the client application, which then sends the model with requests
correctAnswerText: Once at startup, in the lifespan handler, kept in app state
explanation: Loading is slow (reading and unpickling a file). Doing it once at startup means each request pays only for the prediction, and a missing file fails the start rather than a request.

prompt: A request body fails the Pydantic model of a FastAPI endpoint. What status code does the caller receive?
optionA: 200, with the invalid fields set to null
optionB: 500, because the model raised on bad input
optionC: 422, with details naming each invalid field
optionD: 404, because no route matched the bad body
correctAnswerText: 422, with details naming each invalid field
explanation: FastAPI validates the body before the handler runs and answers 422 Unprocessable Entity, listing the location and type of each error. The model is never called.

prompt: With OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), how is a category never seen in training encoded at prediction time?
optionA: As all zeros across that feature's one-hot columns
optionB: As NaN in every column, which the model then imputes
optionC: As a new extra column that the encoder adds on the fly
optionD: As the most frequent category from the training data
correctAnswerText: As all zeros across that feature's one-hot columns
explanation: "ignore" turns an unknown value into a row of zeros for that feature, so the request still scores. The default "error" raises a ValueError instead.

prompt: What is a known-answer test for a deployed model?
optionA: Checking that the API answers 200 to a request with an empty JSON body
optionB: Asking the model owner to confirm that the model gives sensible answers
optionC: Scoring recorded inputs and checking the recorded outputs come back
optionD: Comparing the model's accuracy with a baseline that always says yes
correctAnswerText: Scoring recorded inputs and checking the recorded outputs come back
explanation: Rows whose probabilities were recorded at training time are scored after every load or build; any difference means the environment, the file or the code changed the model.

prompt: What is batch scoring?
optionA: Scoring a whole table on a schedule and storing the results
optionB: Splitting the training data into batches for gradient descent
optionC: Scoring one customer per HTTP request while the user waits
optionD: Retraining the model every night on the newest labelled rows
correctAnswerText: Scoring a whole table on a schedule and storing the results
explanation: Batch scoring runs the saved model over many rows at once (nightly, monthly) and writes scores to a table. Real-time serving scores one request as it arrives.

prompt: In a shadow deployment, what happens to the new model's predictions?
optionA: They are computed only on last year's data in an offline backtest
optionB: They replace the old model's answers for a random 5% of the users
optionC: They are averaged with the live model's answers before being used
optionD: They are computed on live requests and logged, but not acted on
correctAnswerText: They are computed on live requests and logged, but not acted on
explanation: Shadow mode runs the candidate on real traffic with no user impact, exposing real inputs, latency, failures and disagreement with the live model.

prompt: Why is uvicorn started with --host 0.0.0.0 inside a container?
optionA: So it picks a free port automatically when port 8000 is already used
optionB: So it listens on all interfaces and the published port can reach it
optionC: So it uses every CPU core in the container for the prediction work
optionD: So it refuses requests that come from outside the container network
correctAnswerText: So it listens on all interfaces and the published port can reach it
explanation: The default 127.0.0.1 accepts connections only from inside the container, so nothing outside can reach the API even with -p 8000:8000.

prompt: Why are the scikit-learn and NumPy versions recorded beside a saved model and pinned on the server?
optionA: The server cannot install any library unless a model file lists its version first
optionB: A pickled estimator stores version-specific internals that may not load the same
optionC: Recording versions encrypts the model file so that only matching servers open it
optionD: Newer versions of scikit-learn refuse to make predictions with older algorithms
correctAnswerText: A pickled estimator stores version-specific internals that may not load the same
explanation: Pickle saves private attributes, which change between releases; a mismatch gives InconsistentVersionWarning, an error, or slightly different predictions. Pin the versions, and retrain to upgrade.

prompt: Why is a FastAPI handler that calls predict_proba usually written as plain def rather than async def?
optionA: async def handlers cannot accept a Pydantic model as their request body
optionB: predict_proba is blocking CPU work, and def handlers run in a thread pool
optionC: def handlers are cached by FastAPI, so a repeated request is never rescored
optionD: scikit-learn models refuse to run inside any Python event loop at all
correctAnswerText: predict_proba is blocking CPU work, and def handlers run in a thread pool
explanation: Inside async def, blocking CPU work stalls the event loop for every other request. FastAPI runs plain def handlers in a thread pool, which keeps the loop free.

prompt: A churn API returns model_version alongside each probability. What does that make possible later?
optionA: Letting each caller choose which model version should score its own request
optionB: Letting the browser cache responses separately for each model version used
optionC: Tracing each logged score to the model that produced it, for audit or rollback
optionD: Making FastAPI validate the response, which it does only when a version is set
correctAnswerText: Tracing each logged score to the model that produced it, for audit or rollback
explanation: Once a model is replaced, old and new scores come from different models. The version in every response and log lets you compare them, audit a decision and roll back.

prompt: Why should a custom transformer used in a saved pipeline live in a module such as features.py, not in the training notebook?
optionA: A module compiles the function into the model file so the API needs no code
optionB: Pickle stores a function by module and name, so the API must import the same one
optionC: joblib refuses to save any pipeline containing a function from a notebook cell
optionD: Notebooks run custom functions more slowly than modules do in a deployed API
correctAnswerText: Pickle stores a function by module and name, so the API must import the same one
explanation: The file holds a reference such as __main__.cap_gb, not the code. The API process has no such name; a shared module lets both training and serving import features.cap_gb.

prompt: Why should a model container refuse to start when a required setting such as MODEL_VERSION is missing?
optionA: Docker restarts a missing setting from the image's previous configuration
optionB: Starting without it would silently retrain the model with default settings
optionC: A container that starts without settings gets a default model from Docker
optionD: The health check then fails, so the platform never routes traffic to it
correctAnswerText: The health check then fails, so the platform never routes traffic to it
explanation: Failing fast stops a misconfigured container before it serves anything. Starting anyway means untraceable scores or a 500 on every request until someone notices.

prompt: How does training–serving skew differ from data drift?
optionA: Skew affects only categorical features, while drift affects only the numeric features
optionB: Skew is one feature computed differently in the two pipelines; drift is the world changing
optionC: Skew and drift are two names for the same thing, both measured by PSI on the inputs
optionD: Skew is a change in customers over time; drift is a bug in the feature code at serving
correctAnswerText: Skew is one feature computed differently in the two pipelines; drift is the world changing
explanation: With skew nothing in the world moved: the serving code produces a different value (different window, unit or source) from the one training saw. Drift is real change in the population.

prompt: What does a canary release add after a shadow deployment has looked healthy?
optionA: A guarantee that the new model is fair across every customer segment
optionB: Real user impact on a small share of traffic, with instant rollback ready
optionC: A second offline evaluation on the same backtest data used before shadow
optionD: A full switch of all traffic, since shadow mode already proved the model
correctAnswerText: Real user impact on a small share of traffic, with instant rollback ready
explanation: Shadow shows behaviour without acting on it. A canary lets the new model's answers be used for, say, 5% of traffic, so real effects show while exposure and rollback cost stay small.

prompt: Why does a model Dockerfile copy requirements.txt and run pip install before copying the app code?
optionA: Installing first compiles the app against the libraries, making it run faster
optionB: Docker runs the instructions bottom to top, so the code must be copied last
optionC: A code edit then reuses the cached dependency layer instead of reinstalling
optionD: pip can only resolve versions when no Python source files are in the image
correctAnswerText: A code edit then reuses the cached dependency layer instead of reinstalling
explanation: Docker rebuilds from the first changed layer. With dependencies installed before the code is copied, editing main.py rebuilds only the cheap layers after the install.

prompt: Why should a Streamlit demo that managers use for weeks call the model API rather than load its own copy of the model?
optionA: So the demo always shows the model and version the product actually serves
optionB: So that managers can retrain the model from the demo's form when needed
optionC: Because HTTP calls are always faster than predicting inside the demo app
optionD: Because Streamlit has no way to read a joblib or skops file from its disk
correctAnswerText: So the demo always shows the model and version the product actually serves
explanation: A separate copy falls behind when the served model is replaced. Calling the API means what people try in the demo is exactly what customers are scored with.

prompt: What does fetching the model from a registry at container start give, compared with baking the file into the image?
optionA: A guarantee that the image tag identifies exactly which model is being served
optionB: Faster startup, because a registry download is quicker than reading local disk
optionC: A smaller attack surface, because the registry checks the model file for pickles
optionD: A model change without rebuilding the image, at the cost of a startup dependency
correctAnswerText: A model change without rebuilding the image, at the cost of a startup dependency
explanation: Fetching lets an alias move without a new image, but the container now needs the registry reachable and the alias right. Baking in makes the image tag pin code and model together.

prompt: Loading a model takes 150 ms and one prediction takes 30 ms. A single worker handles one request at a time. Roughly how many requests per second can it serve if it loads the model inside the handler, and if it loads it once?
optionA: About 6.7 per second, and about 5.6 per second
optionB: About 33 per second in both cases, as loads cache
optionC: About 2.8 per second, and about 16.7 per second
optionD: About 5.6 per second, and about 33 per second
correctAnswerText: About 5.6 per second, and about 33 per second
explanation: Per request: 150 + 30 = 180 ms, so 1000 / 180 ≈ 5.6/s. Loaded once, only the 30 ms prediction remains: 1000 / 30 ≈ 33/s — six times more from moving one line.

prompt: An API runs three uvicorn worker processes, and each loads a 120 MB model in its lifespan handler. About how much memory do the loaded models alone need?
optionA: About 480 MB, three copies plus a master copy
optionB: About 40 MB, as the model is split three ways
optionC: About 360 MB, one copy per worker process
optionD: About 120 MB, as the workers share one copy
correctAnswerText: About 360 MB, one copy per worker process
explanation: Workers are separate processes and each runs lifespan, so each holds its own model: 3 × 120 = 360 MB, before Python and the libraries themselves.

prompt: A bank scores 20 lakh customers each night. Scoring one row at a time takes 5 ms per row; scoring a 1,000-row DataFrame takes 10 ms per batch. Roughly how long does each approach take?
optionA: About 28 hours row by row, about 3.3 minutes in batches
optionB: About 2.8 hours row by row, about 2.8 hours in batches
optionC: About 17 minutes row by row, about 20 seconds in batches
optionD: About 2.8 hours row by row, about 20 seconds in batches
correctAnswerText: About 2.8 hours row by row, about 20 seconds in batches
explanation: 2,000,000 × 5 ms = 10,000 s ≈ 2.8 h. In batches: 2,000 batches × 10 ms = 20 s. Per-call overhead dominates single rows; nightly jobs should score in batches.

prompt: A Pydantic v2 model has tenure: int = Field(ge=0). Using default (lax) validation, which result do the bodies {"tenure": "6"} and {"tenure": 6.5} give?
optionA: "6" is a 422 for being a string; 6.5 is accepted and cut to 6
optionB: "6" is accepted as 6; 6.5 is a 422 because it has a fraction
optionC: Both are rejected with a 422, as neither one is a JSON integer
optionD: Both are accepted, as 6 and 7, after rounding to the nearest int
correctAnswerText: "6" is accepted as 6; 6.5 is a 422 because it has a fraction
explanation: Lax mode parses a numeric string into an int, but a float with a fractional part fails with int_from_float. Use Field(strict=True) where strings must be rejected too.

prompt: A loan API must reject any request where down_payment is not smaller than loan_amount. Both fields are already typed and range-checked. Which Pydantic construct enforces the rule?
optionA: A @field_validator on loan_amount that only sees itself
optionB: A @model_validator(mode="after") comparing the two fields
optionC: A Literal type listing every allowed down_payment value
optionD: Field(lt=loan_amount) placed on the down_payment field
correctAnswerText: A @model_validator(mode="after") comparing the two fields
explanation: Field constraints compare a value with constants. A rule involving two fields runs after both are validated, in a model validator that raises ValueError, which becomes a 422.

prompt: Which of these needs a real-time scoring API rather than a nightly batch job?
optionA: A fraud check on a UPI payment while the customer waits to pay
optionB: A quarterly forecast of branch footfall for staff planning
optionC: A weekly ranking of overdue loans for the collections team
optionD: A monthly list of customers who should get a retention offer
correctAnswerText: A fraud check on a UPI payment while the customer waits to pay
explanation: Real time is needed when the input arrives at decision time and the answer is needed then. The other decisions are made from lists on a schedule, where batch is simpler and cheaper.

prompt: The schema declares state: Literal["Telangana", "Karnataka", "Tamil Nadu"]. A request arrives with state = "Kerala". What does the caller receive?
optionA: A 500, because the encoder raises on the unseen state
optionB: A 200, with Kerala replaced by the most common state
optionC: A 422 whose message lists the three allowed states
optionD: A 200, with Kerala encoded as all zeros by the encoder
correctAnswerText: A 422 whose message lists the three allowed states
explanation: A Literal field is validated before the handler runs, so an unlisted value is rejected with a clear 422 and never reaches the encoder or the model.

prompt: A cloud host routes traffic only to containers whose /health check passes. Which /health implementation protects callers best?
optionA: Report ok only if the model is loaded, and return its version too
optionB: Load the model from disk on each health call, to prove it exists
optionC: Retrain on a small sample on each call, to prove training still works
optionD: Return {"status": "ok"} as soon as the web process is listening
correctAnswerText: Report ok only if the model is loaded, and return its version too
explanation: A bare "ok" proves only that the process is alive. Checking the model is in memory and naming its version means a container without a usable model never gets traffic, cheaply.

prompt:
Which line of this Dockerfile is a security problem?

FROM python:3.13-slim
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
ENV FEATURE_DB_PASSWORD=Kr1shna@2026
COPY app/ ./app/
optionA: The FROM line, since slim images skip all the security updates
optionB: The ENV line, since anyone with the image can read the password
optionC: The COPY app/ line, since copying code last leaks the source code
optionD: The pip line, since --no-cache-dir disables package verification
correctAnswerText: The ENV line, since anyone with the image can read the password
explanation: Image configuration and layers are readable by anyone who can pull the image. Secrets arrive at run time from the host's secret store as environment variables, never baked in.

prompt: At validation, applicant A was scored 0.412 by the default model. Which pytest assertion turns that into a known-answer test for the API response r?
optionA: assert 0.0 <= r.json()["p_default"] <= 1.0 for the response
optionB: assert r.json()["p_default"] == pytest.approx(0.412, abs=1e-3)
optionC: assert "p_default" in r.json() and r.status_code == 200
optionD: assert isinstance(r.json()["p_default"], float) is True
correctAnswerText: assert r.json()["p_default"] == pytest.approx(0.412, abs=1e-3)
explanation: Only a recorded input with its recorded output detects a changed score. The other assertions pass whether the model is right or silently different.

prompt:
The model loads in a lifespan handler. A test does:

client = TestClient(app)
print(client.get("/health").json())

and prints {"model_loaded": false}. The same app works under uvicorn. Why?
optionA: TestClient loads models lazily, so the first /predict call loads it
optionB: Health checks always report false until a real HTTP server is started
optionC: The model file is too large for TestClient, which skips files over 1 MB
optionD: TestClient runs the lifespan only when it is used as a context manager
correctAnswerText: TestClient runs the lifespan only when it is used as a context manager
explanation: Without "with TestClient(app) as client:", startup and shutdown are not run, so the model is never loaded. Using it as a context manager runs the lifespan as uvicorn does.

prompt: The day after a mobile-app release, the share of customers a churn API flags drops from 24% to 9%. No errors are logged and input PSI is huge for data_used only. The most likely cause?
optionA: The model's coefficients decayed in memory after running for a long time
optionB: Customers became more loyal overnight, so the model correctly flags fewer
optionC: The API is overloaded and returns cached scores from the previous week
optionD: The app now sends data_used in different units, so the model sees new values
correctAnswerText: The app now sends data_used in different units, so the model sees new values
explanation: A sudden shift right after an upstream release, in one feature, is training–serving skew such as MB instead of GB. State units and bounds in the schema and agree the contract.

prompt: An encoder was fitted as OneHotEncoder(drop="first", handle_unknown="ignore") on city ∈ {Agra, Bhopal, Chennai}. A request with city = "Delhi" scores exactly like an Agra customer. Why?
optionA: Both encode as all zeros: Agra was dropped and Delhi is unknown
optionB: The encoder maps unknown cities to the first city in sorted order
optionC: A coincidence: the model gives Delhi and Agra the same coefficient
optionD: Delhi is imputed with the training mode, which happened to be Agra
correctAnswerText: Both encode as all zeros: Agra was dropped and Delhi is unknown
explanation: With drop="first" the baseline Agra has no column, so it is all zeros; "ignore" also gives an unknown city all zeros. An unseen city is silently scored as the baseline.

prompt: A container with a 2 GB memory limit runs 4 uvicorn workers. Each loads a 600 MB gradient-boosting model at startup. The container keeps being killed during startup. What is happening?
optionA: Gradient boosting needs a GPU, so the CPU host dies
optionB: Four copies need about 2.4 GB, over the 2 GB limit
optionC: The health check times out because workers share RAM
optionD: The model is too deep for uvicorn, which caps trees
correctAnswerText: Four copies need about 2.4 GB, over the 2 GB limit
explanation: Each worker process loads its own copy: 4 × 600 MB = 2.4 GB before Python itself. Use fewer workers, a bigger limit, or a smaller model.

prompt:
The API fails at startup with:

AttributeError: Can't get attribute 'clip_income' on <module '__main__'>

The pipeline loads fine in the training notebook. What went wrong?
optionA: clip_income was defined in the notebook, so the API cannot import it
optionB: The pipeline was saved with skops, which deletes custom functions
optionC: The API runs a newer Python, which renamed the clip_income function
optionD: The model file is corrupted, so joblib cannot read its function table
correctAnswerText: clip_income was defined in the notebook, so the API cannot import it
explanation: Pickle stored a reference to __main__.clip_income. In the notebook that name exists; in the API it does not. Move it to a module both import, then retrain and re-save.

prompt: Server scores differ from the notebook's in the third decimal for the same rows, and the logs show InconsistentVersionWarning for StandardScaler. What explains it?
optionA: The notebook used float64 while the server always computes in float16
optionB: The server rounds probabilities to three decimals before returning them
optionC: StandardScaler refits on each request, so its means move slightly
optionD: The server installed a different scikit-learn than the one the file was saved with
correctAnswerText: The server installed a different scikit-learn than the one the file was saved with
explanation: The warning means the file was pickled under another version. Internals can differ, so predictions can shift. Pin the training versions, or retrain and re-save, then re-run the known-answer test.

prompt: A credit model with better offline AUC went straight to 100% of traffic. The approval rate jumped 15 points on day one. Which step would have caught this before customers were affected?
optionA: A shadow run comparing its live decisions with the current model's
optionB: Retraining the new model with more trees before switching it over
optionC: Raising the API timeout so the new model had more time to score
optionD: A longer offline backtest, measuring AUC again on older loan data
correctAnswerText: A shadow run comparing its live decisions with the current model's
explanation: AUC measures ranking; the business sees decisions at a threshold. Shadow mode shows on live traffic how many decisions flip, before any of them are acted on.

prompt: A new release loads the model on the first /predict call. Its /health returns {"status": "ok"}. After deploy every /predict is a 500 with FileNotFoundError, yet the platform kept routing traffic. Why?
optionA: The platform ignores health checks for containers that return JSON
optionB: Nothing at startup checked the model file, so health passed regardless
optionC: FileNotFoundError is a client error, so the platform does not count it
optionD: The model was in the image but uvicorn cannot read files from disk
correctAnswerText: Nothing at startup checked the model file, so health passed regardless
explanation: Load the model at startup and report it in /health. Then a missing file stops the container from starting, and the platform never sends it traffic.

prompt: monthly_income is Field(gt=0, le=300000). A dealer types an annual income of ₹2,64,000 into it. The API returns 200 with a much lower default risk. What does this show?
optionA: A range check accepts a plausible wrong value; a cross-field sanity check is needed
optionB: The model is broken, because a higher income must never lower default risk
optionC: The dealer's app must be sending strings, which Pydantic multiplies by twelve
optionD: Pydantic failed, since le=300000 should reject any income above one lakh
correctAnswerText: A range check accepts a plausible wrong value; a cross-field sanity check is needed
explanation: ₹2.64 lakh is inside the range, so validation passes. Checking income against EMI or loan amount, and deciding to reject or flag, catches values that are valid but wrong.

prompt: Every one-line code change makes docker build reinstall all libraries for six minutes. The Dockerfile has COPY . /app followed by RUN pip install -r requirements.txt. What is the cause?
optionA: Copying all code before installing breaks the cache of the install layer
optionB: pip always reinstalls everything because it does not keep any cache
optionC: requirements.txt is read only after all the code has been compiled
optionD: The base image is rebuilt from scratch whenever any file has changed
correctAnswerText: Copying all code before installing breaks the cache of the install layer
explanation: Any code change invalidates the COPY layer and every layer after it, including the install. Copy requirements.txt and install first, then copy the code.

prompt: Your team must send a fitted pipeline to a partner bank, which will load it on its own servers. Which approach is soundest?
optionA: Send a skops file and tell them to pass every reported type as trusted
optionB: Send a pickle with a checksum, since a checksum proves the file runs no code
optionC: Send a joblib file, since joblib compresses the pipeline and is the standard
optionD: Save it with skops; they review and trust only the types the file reports
correctAnswerText: Save it with skops; they review and trust only the types the file reports
explanation: The file crosses a trust boundary, so loading must not run arbitrary code. skops refuses unknown types until reviewed. Trusting everything it reports removes the protection; a checksum proves only integrity.

prompt: A loan-approval API may receive a state it was never trained on. Which policy is best for this regulated credit decision?
optionA: Return a default probability of 0.5 so the officer can decide
optionB: Use handle_unknown="ignore" and approve using the baseline state
optionC: Map unknown states to the most common state and score as normal
optionD: Declare allowed states, return a clear 422 for others, and log them
correctAnswerText: Declare allowed states, return a clear 422 for others, and log them
explanation: A credit decision for a region the model never saw should not be made silently as if it were a known one. Rejecting clearly and logging it routes the case to people and signals retraining.

prompt: A retention team sends offers once a month from a list. A colleague wants a real-time API and Kubernetes "to be future-proof". What is the best judgement?
optionA: Avoid both and email the notebook outputs to the retention team
optionB: Batch score monthly; add an API only when a live decision needs it
optionC: Use real time, as batch scores are too stale for a monthly campaign
optionD: Build the real-time API now, since it costs the same as a batch job
correctAnswerText: Batch score monthly; add an API only when a live decision needs it
explanation: The serving pattern follows when the decision is made. Batch is simpler, cheaper and easier to audit for a monthly list; real time earns its cost only when input arrives at decision time.

prompt: For a call-centre API, a 4 KB logistic pipeline has CV AUC 0.749 ± 0.02 and predicts in 3 ms; a 90 MB random forest has 0.752 ± 0.02 and takes 40 ms. Which is the better product?
optionA: Neither, since an AUC under 0.8 is never acceptable in production
optionB: The forest, because larger models drift less once they are deployed
optionC: The forest, because a higher AUC always outweighs latency and memory
optionD: The logistic pipeline: the AUCs tie and it is far cheaper to serve
correctAnswerText: The logistic pipeline: the AUCs tie and it is far cheaper to serve
explanation: A 0.003 gap against a fold standard deviation of 0.02 is a tie. On a tie, the smaller, faster, easier-to-explain model wins on memory per worker, latency and maintenance.

prompt: Which release plan for a new credit-scoring model best balances risk and evidence?
optionA: Deploy to all users and keep the old model's file in case of complaints
optionB: A/B test at 50% straight away, since shadow and canary add only delay
optionC: Shadow, then a small canary with rollback, then an A/B test if needed
optionD: Full switch-over on a Friday evening, when application traffic is lowest
correctAnswerText: Shadow, then a small canary with rollback, then an A/B test if needed
explanation: Shadow shows real inputs and decision changes at no risk; a canary limits exposure while effects become real; an A/B test measures business impact. The registry keeps rollback one step away.

prompt: A two-person team retrains quarterly and must answer auditors "what exactly was serving on 3 March?". Bake the model into the image, or fetch it from the registry at start?
optionA: Bake it in: the image tag then pins code and model for audit and rollback
optionB: Fetch it: baking a model into an image breaks scikit-learn version pins
optionC: Bake it in, and also download a newer model at startup if one exists
optionD: Fetch it: auditors prefer models that can change without a deployment
correctAnswerText: Bake it in: the image tag then pins code and model for audit and rollback
explanation: With quarterly retrains, a rebuild costs little, and a self-contained image makes one tag answer "which code and which model". Fetching adds a runtime dependency the audit must also reconstruct.

prompt: The platform team wants every service on the newest scikit-learn. Your model was saved with an older release. Which plan is soundest?
optionA: Convert the old file to skops, which makes it portable to newer releases
optionB: Keep the old version forever, since models can never move to new releases
optionC: Retrain and re-save under the new version, check metrics and known answers
optionD: Load the old file under the new version and silence the version warning
correctAnswerText: Retrain and re-save under the new version, check metrics and known answers
explanation: Pickled estimators are not guaranteed across releases, and skops is about safety, not compatibility. Retraining under the new version, then confirming metrics and recorded scores, upgrades safely.

prompt: You can add only three tests to a model API before launch. Which set protects users best?
optionA: Known-answer scores, invalid input gives 422, batch matches single
optionB: Health returns 200, response has a probability key, docs page loads
optionC: Probability lies in [0, 1], status is 200, response time is logged
optionD: Model file exists, requirements file exists, Dockerfile builds fine
correctAnswerText: Known-answer scores, invalid input gives 422, batch matches single
explanation: These three catch a silently changed model, bad input being scored, and a batch path that disagrees with the real-time one. The others pass whether the scores are right or wrong.

prompt: A student plans to put a churn demo on a public Streamlit page, loaded with 500 real customer rows "so it looks realistic". What is the right judgement?
optionA: Fine, since a demo is not production and so data rules do not apply to it
optionB: Fine, provided the page has no login so that reviewers can open it easily
optionC: Fine, provided the requirements file pins the same versions used in training
optionD: Use simulated or anonymised rows; real customer records in public are a breach
correctAnswerText: Use simulated or anonymised rows; real customer records in public are a breach
explanation: A public page with real customer data leaks personal data regardless of purpose. Demos use simulated or anonymised data, say so in a caption, and keep any secrets in the platform's settings.

prompt: Training features come from SQL; the serving team re-implements them in Java, and skew bugs keep appearing. Which long-term fix is soundest?
optionA: Retrain the model every week so it adapts to the Java version of each feature
optionB: Ask the Java team to review the SQL once more before each model release
optionC: Widen the API's input ranges so the Java values are always accepted as valid
optionD: Compute features in one shared place, log served features and compare them
correctAnswerText: Compute features in one shared place, log served features and compare them
explanation: Two implementations of one feature will diverge. One shared definition (shared code or a feature store), plus comparing logged serving features with training ones, removes and detects skew.

prompt: What does an experiment-tracking tool such as MLflow record for each training run?
optionA: Its parameters, metrics, artefacts, code version and data version
optionB: Only the notebook's printed output, captured as plain text for review
optionC: Only the final model file, so that it can be loaded by the serving API
optionD: Only the hardware used, so training costs can be charged to each team
correctAnswerText: Its parameters, metrics, artefacts, code version and data version
explanation: Tracking keeps every run's settings, results, files and the code and data behind them in one searchable place, so a number can be traced and reproduced.

prompt: In MLflow, what is the difference between a parameter and a metric?
optionA: A parameter must be numeric; a metric may be any string, such as a file path or name
optionB: A parameter is a number the model learned; a metric is the setting that was chosen
optionC: A parameter is logged once per experiment; a metric is logged once per whole project
optionD: A parameter is a setting chosen before training; a metric is a measured result
correctAnswerText: A parameter is a setting chosen before training; a metric is a measured result
explanation: Parameters are inputs such as C=1.0 or max_iter=200; metrics are outcomes such as cv_auc_mean. Learned weights belong in the model artefact, not in either.

prompt: In MLflow, what is a run?
optionA: A numbered version of a model kept in the model registry
optionB: A named group of related training attempts on one problem
optionC: A label such as "champion" pointing at one model version
optionD: One execution of training code, with everything it logged
correctAnswerText: One execution of training code, with everything it logged
explanation: A run is one training execution and its logged params, metrics and artefacts. An experiment groups runs; a registered version and an alias belong to the registry.

prompt: What does an MLflow model registry give a chosen model?
optionA: A name and numbered versions, each traceable to the run behind it
optionB: A faster file format that makes every prediction run several times quicker
optionC: A public download link so that any team can fetch it without logging in
optionD: An automatic retraining schedule that triggers whenever new data lands
correctAnswerText: A name and numbered versions, each traceable to the run behind it
explanation: Registering creates a named model with versions 1, 2, 3… each linked to its source run, so "which model is live?" has one answer.

prompt: In MLflow 3, what replaces the deprecated registry stages such as "Staging" and "Production"?
optionA: Separate experiments, one for each deployment stage
optionB: Aliases such as @champion that point at one version
optionC: Tags on each run naming the stage in free text
optionD: Run names that end in _prod or _staging by convention
correctAnswerText: Aliases such as @champion that point at one version
explanation: An alias names one version (models:/telecom-churn@champion). Moving it promotes or rolls back without code changes; stages are deprecated.

prompt: What does mlflow.search_runs(experiment_names=[...]) return by default?
optionA: A JSON string of the experiment settings
optionB: A plot comparing the runs on every metric
optionC: A pandas DataFrame with one row per run
optionD: A list of model files ready to be loaded
correctAnswerText: A pandas DataFrame with one row per run
explanation: Each run becomes a row with columns such as params.C, metrics.cv_auc_mean and tags.mlflow.runName, so comparison is ordinary pandas.

prompt: When training runs as a script inside a git repository, how does MLflow record the code version?
optionA: As a full copy of the repository saved into the run artefacts
optionB: As a metric holding the number of lines changed since last run
optionC: It does not; code versions can only be noted by hand in a wiki
optionD: As the commit hash in the run tag mlflow.source.git.commit
correctAnswerText: As the commit hash in the run tag mlflow.source.git.commit
explanation: MLflow tags the run with the commit it ran from. From a notebook it often cannot, so log the commit yourself.

prompt: What does mlflow.sklearn.autolog() do?
optionA: Deploys each fitted model to the registry under the "champion" alias
optionB: Logs only the data hash of each training set and nothing beyond that
optionC: Chooses the best hyperparameters and retrains the model automatically
optionD: Logs parameters, training metrics and the fitted model on each fit
correctAnswerText: Logs parameters, training metrics and the fitted model on each fit
explanation: Autolog hooks fit() and records the estimator's params, training metrics and the model. It does not know your CV scheme, test set or business metric.

prompt: Which of these is logged to a run as an artefact rather than as a param or metric?
optionA: The mean cross-validated AUC across all five folds
optionB: A calibration plot image saved from the evaluation
optionC: The random seed used to shuffle the CV splitter
optionD: The regularisation strength C chosen for the run
correctAnswerText: A calibration plot image saved from the evaluation
explanation: Artefacts are files: plots, the model, a feature list as JSON. Single settings are params and single measured numbers are metrics.

prompt: What does mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///mlflow.db") decide?
optionA: Where run records are stored: here a local SQLite file
optionB: Which model version is served by the production API
optionC: Which dataset is used for training in every later run
optionD: Which port the MLflow UI will listen on when started
correctAnswerText: Where run records are stored: here a local SQLite file
explanation: The tracking URI points at the store for runs. A team points it at a shared MLflow server instead; the logging code does not change.

prompt: Why log a hash of the training file (or a dataset ID) with every run?
optionA: Because the hash encrypts the run so other teams cannot read the metrics
optionB: So MLflow can rebuild the full training file from the hash when needed
optionC: Because MLflow refuses to store any metric until a data hash is present
optionD: To know whether two runs were trained on the same data before comparing
correctAnswerText: To know whether two runs were trained on the same data before comparing
explanation: A metric is comparable only with one from the same data. The hash identifies the data; it cannot reconstruct it, so the data itself must live in versioned storage.

prompt: Why should every candidate model be cross-validated with the same splitter and the same random seed?
optionA: So the models train faster by reusing each other's cached folds
optionB: Because MLflow will not log a run if its random seed has changed
optionC: So score differences come from the models, not from different folds
optionD: Because a fixed seed guarantees the best model is found every time
correctAnswerText: So score differences come from the models, not from different folds
explanation: Different folds give different scores even for one model. Holding the splits fixed removes that source of variation, so a comparison measures the models.

prompt: Why is the held-out test score logged only for the finally chosen model, not for every run?
optionA: The test set is too small to score more than one model with any accuracy
optionB: MLflow allows only one metric named test_auc in each experiment at a time
optionC: Logging test scores on many runs slows the tracking server down sharply
optionD: Choosing among runs by test score makes that score optimistically biased
correctAnswerText: Choosing among runs by test score makes that score optimistically biased
explanation: Picking the best of many by test score turns the test set into a validation set, so the reported number overstates future performance. Choose on CV; test once.

prompt: Autolog is switched on. Why must the team still log some metrics explicitly?
optionA: Autolog logs to a separate store that the registry cannot ever read
optionB: Autolog does not know the CV scheme or the business metric to report
optionC: Autolog records only parameters and never records any metric at all
optionD: Autolog stops working once more than one model is fitted in a script
correctAnswerText: Autolog does not know the CV scheme or the business metric to report
explanation: Autolog sees fit() calls and records training metrics. The cross-validated score, the threshold and the business cost come from your evaluation, which only you can log.

prompt: The serving app loads models:/telecom-churn@champion. Why does that make rollback easy?
optionA: MLflow rolls back automatically whenever a newer version scores less well
optionB: Moving the alias back to the old version changes the model with no code change
optionC: The alias deletes newer versions, so the app has only the old one to load
optionD: Aliases keep a copy of each model inside the app, so it can switch on its own
correctAnswerText: Moving the alias back to the old version changes the model with no code change
explanation: The app names a role, not a version number. Promotion moves the alias forward; rollback moves it back, and the app picks it up on its next load.

prompt: log_model writes a requirements.txt it infers from the environment. Why should you read it?
optionA: MLflow writes it only for deep learning models, not for scikit-learn ones
optionB: Inference can pick up packages the model does not need, or miss exact pins
optionC: The file is always empty unless the run was started from inside a notebook
optionD: Its contents are encrypted and must be decoded before anyone can install
correctAnswerText: Inference can pick up packages the model does not need, or miss exact pins
explanation: The lesson's churn run captured torch, which the model does not use. Passing pip_requirements with exact versions keeps the served environment small and matching.

prompt: Why does a team keep all churn-model runs in one MLflow experiment rather than one per person?
optionA: Runs in one experiment can be searched and compared side by side
optionB: Each experiment can hold only one person's runs before it locks
optionC: Separate experiments would each need their own copy of the data
optionD: MLflow deletes runs from experiments that have a single author
correctAnswerText: Runs in one experiment can be searched and compared side by side
explanation: An experiment is the unit search_runs and the UI compare within. Scattering one problem's runs across experiments hides them from the comparison.

prompt: Why should a team agree fixed metric names, such as cv_auc_mean, for every run?
optionA: MLflow rejects metric names that it has not seen before in an experiment
optionB: A shared name signals the same measurement and puts runs in one column
optionC: Short names make the tracking database much smaller and faster to query
optionD: Fixed names let MLflow recompute every metric whenever new data arrives
correctAnswerText: A shared name signals the same measurement and puts runs in one column
explanation: Runs logging "auc", "val_auc" and "roc_auc" usually measured different things and land in different columns. One name for one procedure keeps the comparison honest.

prompt: To reproduce a logged AUC exactly, which set of things must be recoverable from the run?
optionA: The model file only, since the model alone determines every evaluation
optionB: Code version, data version, parameters, random seeds and library versions
optionC: The run name, the author's name and the date on which the run was started
optionD: The final metric values only, since they define what the model achieved
correctAnswerText: Code version, data version, parameters, random seeds and library versions
explanation: A number is reproducible only if the code, the data, the settings, the randomness and the environment can all be recovered. Missing any one leaves the result unexplained.

prompt: Why would you call mlflow.log_metric("val_loss", v, step=epoch) inside a training loop?
optionA: To keep a curve of the metric over epochs, not just one final value
optionB: To log the loss as an artefact file instead of a number in the database
optionC: To overwrite the parameter epoch so the final run shows only the last one
optionD: To make MLflow stop training once the metric stops improving by itself
correctAnswerText: To keep a curve of the metric over epochs, not just one final value
explanation: A metric logged with steps keeps its full history, which the UI draws as a curve; the run summary shows the latest value. MLflow does not stop training for you.

prompt: Five runs logged C = 0.01, 1.0, 10.0, 0.1 and 2.0 with log_param. What order does search_runs(..., order_by=["params.C DESC"]) give?
optionA: 10.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.1, 0.01, because the values are sorted as numbers
optionB: 0.01, 1.0, 10.0, 0.1, 2.0, the order in which the runs were logged
optionC: 2.0, 10.0, 1.0, 0.1, 0.01, because params are stored as text
optionD: 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 2.0, 10.0, because DESC is ignored for any parameter
correctAnswerText: 2.0, 10.0, 1.0, 0.1, 0.01, because params are stored as text
explanation: MLflow stores params as strings, so ordering is lexical: "2.0" > "10.0" > "1.0" > "0.1" > "0.01". Sort numerically in pandas, or log the value as a metric if you must order by it.

prompt: Inside one run, code calls mlflow.log_param("lr", 0.1) and later mlflow.log_param("lr", 0.2). What happens?
optionA: MLflow silently ignores the second call and the run keeps lr = 0.1
optionB: The second call raises MlflowException: changing param values is not allowed
optionC: Both are kept as a history, the way repeated metric values are stored
optionD: The second value overwrites the first, so the run shows lr = 0.2 at the end
correctAnswerText: The second call raises MlflowException: changing param values is not allowed
explanation: A param records what a run was configured with, so it cannot change. Logging the same value again is allowed; a different one raises. Use a new run for a new setting.

prompt: A run logs loss with step 0, 1, 2 as 0.50, 0.40, 0.45. Which value does the run's metrics summary (and the search_runs column) show?
optionA: 0.45, and the earlier values 0.50 and 0.40 are discarded
optionB: 0.45 as the mean, since MLflow averages each logged step
optionC: 0.45, the latest step, with all three kept in its history
optionD: 0.40, the lowest value, since MLflow keeps the best one
correctAnswerText: 0.45, the latest step, with all three kept in its history
explanation: The summary holds the latest value (highest step); get_metric_history returns all three. If the best epoch matters, log it as its own metric.

prompt: Which filter_string makes search_runs return only logistic-regression runs whose cv_auc is above 0.75?
optionA: "params.model = 'logreg' and metrics.cv_auc > 0.75"
optionB: "params.model == \"logreg\" && metrics.cv_auc > 0.75"
optionC: "model = 'logreg' and cv_auc > 0.75 in this experiment"
optionD: "metrics.model = 'logreg' and params.cv_auc > 0.75"
correctAnswerText: "params.model = 'logreg' and metrics.cv_auc > 0.75"
explanation: Filters name the entity type (params., metrics., tags.), compare with = or >, quote strings in single quotes and join with "and". The other forms raise MlflowException or name the wrong entity.

prompt:
Comparable runs, 5-fold CV:

run   cv_auc_mean  cv_auc_std
A     0.812        0.018
B     0.809        0.021
C     0.771        0.015

What is the right reading?
optionA: A and B tie within noise; C is clearly worse than both
optionB: C is best, since it has the smallest standard deviation
optionC: A is clearly the best, since it has the highest mean
optionD: All three tie, since every std is above one hundredth
correctAnswerText: A and B tie within noise; C is clearly worse than both
explanation: A and B differ by 0.003 against fold spreads near 0.02 — a tie, to be broken on simplicity, cost or other evidence. C sits about 0.04 below, roughly twice the spread.

prompt: A registered model "fraud-detector" has an alias "champion". Which URI should the serving code pass to mlflow.sklearn.load_model?
optionA: mlruns/fraud-detector/champion
optionB: models:/fraud-detector/latest
optionC: runs:/fraud-detector/champion
optionD: models:/fraud-detector@champion
correctAnswerText: models:/fraud-detector@champion
explanation: models:/<name>@<alias> resolves to whichever version the alias points at. A latest-version URI follows any registration, good or bad; runs:/ URIs take a run ID.

prompt:
This code runs a search with one MLflow run per trial:

with mlflow.start_run(run_name="search"):
    for C in grid:
        with mlflow.start_run():
            ...

What happens on the first inner start_run?
optionA: It works, and each trial becomes a child of the search run automatically
optionB: It ends the outer run silently and starts the trial as a new top-level run
optionC: It raises: a run is already active, so the inner one needs nested=True
optionD: It reuses the outer run, so every trial logs into the same single run
correctAnswerText: It raises: a run is already active, so the inner one needs nested=True
explanation: MLflow refuses to start a second active run unless nested=True, which makes it a child of the active one. Parent and child runs keep a search grouped and searchable.

prompt: You want each run to store its feature list and decision threshold as a JSON file. Which call fits?
optionA: mlflow.set_tag("features.json", None) so the UI builds the file for you
optionB: mlflow.log_metric("features", NUM + CAT) followed by the threshold metric
optionC: mlflow.log_param("config", 0.278) with the features left out of the run
optionD: mlflow.log_dict({"features": NUM + CAT, "threshold": 0.278}, "config.json")
correctAnswerText: mlflow.log_dict({"features": NUM + CAT, "threshold": 0.278}, "config.json")
explanation: log_dict writes a dictionary as a JSON or YAML artefact of the run. Metrics must be numbers, and a list does not fit in one param or tag usefully.

prompt: Version 3 of "telecom-churn" is the champion. Version 4 wins on the latest labelled month. How do you promote it, and how would you roll back?
optionA: Set alias champion to version 4; to roll back, set it to 3 again
optionB: Copy version 4's file over version 3's, keeping the old as backup
optionC: Delete version 3 so 4 becomes the newest; restore 3 to roll back
optionD: Register version 4 under a new name, then edit the app to load it
correctAnswerText: Set alias champion to version 4; to roll back, set it to 3 again
explanation: set_registered_model_alias("telecom-churn", "champion", 4) promotes; pointing it at 3 again rolls back. No code changes, and every version stays in the registry.

prompt:
Logged runs:

run  data_hash  cv_scheme   cv_auc_mean
R1   9f2a…      5fold-s0    0.781
R2   9f2a…      5fold-s0    0.776
R3   c41d…      5fold-s0    0.802
R4   9f2a…      holdout     0.795

Which runs can be compared directly?
optionA: R1, R2 and R4, since all of them share one hash
optionB: All four, since every run reports a cv_auc_mean
optionC: R1, R2 and R3, since all of them used 5-fold CV
optionD: R1 and R2 only: same data and the same CV scheme
correctAnswerText: R1 and R2 only: same data and the same CV scheme
explanation: R3 trained on different data and R4 used a single holdout, so their numbers measure something else. Only runs matching on data and procedure are comparable.

prompt: One teammate's run tops the table with "auc" = 0.97; everyone else logged "cv_auc_mean" near 0.78. His code calls roc_auc_score(y_tr, model.predict_proba(X_tr)[:, 1]). What explains the gap?
optionA: roc_auc_score always reads higher than cross_val_score on AUC
optionB: His model is far better and the others should adopt his features
optionC: It is AUC on the training rows, an overfit figure, not a CV score
optionD: The run used a newer MLflow version, which reports AUC differently
correctAnswerText: It is AUC on the training rows, an overfit figure, not a CV score
explanation: Scoring the rows the model was fitted on measures memorisation, not generalisation. A different metric name was the clue that the measurement was different.

prompt: A team logged test AUC on 60 runs, shipped the one with the best test AUC (0.83) and reported 0.83. In production the model sits at 0.79. What went wrong?
optionA: MLflow rounds test metrics up, so the real test AUC was nearer 0.79
optionB: The test set was too large, which makes AUC estimates biased upwards
optionC: Production data is always worse, so a 0.04 drop proves concept drift
optionD: Selecting the max of 60 test scores made 0.83 an optimistic estimate
correctAnswerText: Selecting the max of 60 test scores made 0.83 an optimistic estimate
explanation: The best of many noisy scores is biased high by selection. Choosing on CV and scoring the test set once on the chosen model gives an honest estimate.

prompt: Re-running the code of the "best" run on the same data gives cv_auc_mean 0.774 instead of the logged 0.781. The run logged its params and data hash but the splitter was KFold(5, shuffle=True). What is missing?
optionA: A fixed random_state for the shuffle, logged with the run
optionB: A newer MLflow release, which would store the folds too
optionC: A larger number of folds, since five folds is not stable
optionD: A different metric, since AUC changes on every re-run
correctAnswerText: A fixed random_state for the shuffle, logged with the run
explanation: With shuffle=True and no random_state, each run uses different folds, so the score moves. Fix and log the seed so a run can be repeated exactly.

prompt: Runs launched from a team script carry mlflow.source.git.commit, but runs from Priya's notebook do not. Two of her runs are now unexplainable. What is the cause and fix?
optionA: Notebook runs hide their tags in the UI; switch the UI to show hidden tags
optionB: Git commits are recorded only for runs over an hour; train for longer
optionC: Her MLflow server lost those tags; re-sync the database from the team server
optionD: Notebooks often lack a git source; log the commit yourself or train from a script
correctAnswerText: Notebooks often lack a git source; log the commit yourself or train from a script
explanation: MLflow records the commit when it can see a script in a repository. From a notebook, log the commit hash yourself, or move training to a script in the repository.

prompt: A logistic-regression model logged with log_model builds into a 4 GB serving image. Its logged requirements.txt lists torch and transformers. Why?
optionA: Requirement inference saw them installed; pass exact pip_requirements
optionB: The image was built from the wrong Dockerfile, as MLflow lists no torch
optionC: MLflow always adds torch so that models can be converted for GPU use
optionD: Logistic regression in MLflow is implemented on top of torch internally
correctAnswerText: Requirement inference saw them installed; pass exact pip_requirements
explanation: Inference picks up packages present in the environment, not only those the model needs. Naming the exact requirements keeps the serving environment small and matching training.

prompt: The API always loads the highest version number of "telecom-churn". An intern registered an experimental model as version 7 and scores went wrong in production. What is the flaw?
optionA: The intern used the wrong flavour, which made the registry reorder versions
optionB: The tracking store was SQLite, which cannot hold more than six versions
optionC: Version numbers are random, so the API picked an old version by mistake
optionD: Registration alone changed serving; it should load an alias set on review
correctAnswerText: Registration alone changed serving; it should load an alias set on review
explanation: With "latest" any registration goes live. Loading @champion separates registering a model from approving it; moving the alias is the deliberate promotion step.

prompt: A script logs mlflow.log_metric("cv_auc", fold_auc) inside its loop over five folds (0.79, 0.81, 0.76, 0.80, 0.74). The runs table shows cv_auc = 0.74. Why?
optionA: The table is stale and will show the mean after a page refresh
optionB: The summary keeps the last logged value, not the mean of the folds
optionC: MLflow averages folds only when the run name ends in "_cv"
optionD: MLflow keeps the lowest value of a metric, to be conservative
correctAnswerText: The summary keeps the last logged value, not the mean of the folds
explanation: Repeated log_metric calls build a history and the summary shows the latest. Compute the mean and standard deviation yourself and log them as cv_auc_mean and cv_auc_std.

prompt: Run X logged val_auc 0.83 from one random 80/20 split; run Y logged cv_auc_mean 0.80 ± 0.02 from 5-fold CV on the same rows. A manager says X is better. What is the flaw?
optionA: One split is a noisy, different measurement, so 0.83 vs 0.80 is not like for like
optionB: Y is better, because 5-fold CV always scores lower than the true AUC
optionC: Nothing; a single split is always more accurate than any cross-validation run
optionD: X must have leaked, because no single split can beat a CV average
correctAnswerText: One split is a noisy, different measurement, so 0.83 vs 0.80 is not like for like
explanation: A single split's score swings with which rows land in it, and it is a different procedure. Re-run X under the same CV scheme before comparing.

prompt: With autolog on, a team sorts runs by training_roc_auc and picks a deep tree at 0.99. On new data it does badly. What did they misread?
optionA: Autolog logs the metrics of the previous run, so the values were shifted
optionB: Autolog's training metrics are on fitted rows, so they reward overfitting
optionC: Autolog rounds metrics, so 0.99 was in fact a much lower training score
optionD: Autolog computes AUC on the test set, which the deep tree had memorised
correctAnswerText: Autolog's training metrics are on fitted rows, so they reward overfitting
explanation: training_* metrics are measured on the data the model was fitted on. Selection needs cross-validated or validation metrics, logged explicitly.

prompt: Four teammates each log to sqlite:///mlflow.db on their own laptops. At review nobody can see the others' runs. What is the fix?
optionA: Point everyone's tracking URI at one shared MLflow server
optionB: Email each mlflow.db to the lead so the UI can open them all
optionC: Use one experiment name, since that merges the four stores
optionD: Give every run a unique name so the UI can find the others
correctAnswerText: Point everyone's tracking URI at one shared MLflow server
explanation: Each local SQLite file is its own store. A shared server with a database backend and an artefact store gives one place to search; the logging code is unchanged.

prompt: Two comparable runs: gradient boosting, R² 0.86 ± 0.03, 240 MB, 60 ms per call; ridge regression, 0.85 ± 0.02, 50 KB, 2 ms. Errors by region are logged as figures. How should you choose?
optionA: Re-run both until one has a standard deviation below one thousandth
optionB: Treat it as a tie and decide on cost and the error in key regions
optionC: Ship ridge, because simpler models are always better in production
optionD: Ship gradient boosting, because a higher mean R² always settles it
correctAnswerText: Treat it as a tie and decide on cost and the error in key regions
explanation: A 0.01 gap against spreads of 0.02–0.03 is noise. The logged size, latency and per-region errors are the evidence that should break the tie.

prompt: Forty runs from three people cannot be compared. Which change prevents this next quarter?
optionA: One training script for all that logs data hash, commit, seed and fixed metrics
optionB: Autolog switched on in every notebook, which records all that is needed
optionC: A weekly meeting where each person reads their best numbers aloud to the team
optionD: A rule that only the senior data scientist may log runs to the server
correctAnswerText: One training script for all that logs data hash, commit, seed and fixed metrics
explanation: Comparable runs come from one procedure: same data version, splits and metric names, with code and seed recorded. Autolog does not know the evaluation design.

prompt: An NBFC's auditor will ask how its credit model was chosen. A colleague says "autolog is on, so we're covered". Is that a sound judgement?
optionA: Yes, provided the run names describe what each run did in plain words
optionB: Yes; autolog records everything an auditor could ever ask about runs
optionC: No; also log data version, CV design, test-once score and why it won
optionD: No; auditors accept only spreadsheets, so tracking is beside the point
correctAnswerText: No; also log data version, CV design, test-once score and why it won
