explanation: Autolog captures params, training metrics and the model. An audit needs the data used, the evaluation design, the honest test result and the reason for the choice.

prompt: A team moving to MLflow 3 copied a tutorial that loads models:/churn/Production. What should they do?
optionA: Load the newest version, which matches what Production meant
optionB: Switch to an alias such as @champion, as stages are deprecated
optionC: Keep stages, since aliases are an experimental MLflow 3 feature
optionD: Load by run ID in the code, so the registry is no longer used
correctAnswerText: Switch to an alias such as @champion, as stages are deprecated
explanation: MLflow 3 deprecates stages in favour of aliases, which do the same job more flexibly. Loading by run ID or "newest" would lose the deliberate promotion step.

prompt: A hyperparameter search will try 200 settings. How should it be tracked?
optionA: Only the best trial is logged, so the experiment stays clean for review
optionB: A parent run for the search, a nested child per trial, same metric names
optionC: One run that logs all 200 settings as params C_1, C_2 and so on up to 200
optionD: A separate experiment per trial, so each one has its own clean page
correctAnswerText: A parent run for the search, a nested child per trial, same metric names
explanation: Child runs keep each trial's settings and scores searchable while the parent groups the search. Logging only the winner hides how many tries were made.

prompt: The training table is 40 GB and is rebuilt weekly. How should each run record the data it used?
optionA: Log only the table name, since the name always means the same data
optionB: Log a hash or snapshot ID pointing at immutable, versioned storage
optionC: Log the whole 40 GB table as an artefact of every single run made
optionD: Log nothing, since the git commit already identifies the data used
correctAnswerText: Log a hash or snapshot ID pointing at immutable, versioned storage
explanation: A table name means different data each week, and copying 40 GB per run is waste. An ID or hash of a retained snapshot identifies the data and lets you fetch it again.

prompt: After the team adopts one standard training script, what should happen to 30 old runs with mixed metric names and splits?
optionA: Delete the experiment, since old runs can never hold useful evidence
optionB: Rename their metrics to cv_auc_mean so they sort with the new runs
optionC: Keep comparing them, since every number is still an AUC of some kind
optionD: Archive them; re-run any promising one under the standard script
correctAnswerText: Archive them; re-run any promising one under the standard script
explanation: Renaming a metric does not change how it was measured. Old runs stay as history; anything worth pursuing is re-run under the comparable procedure.

prompt: A colleague proposes logging test AUC on every run "for completeness, without using it to choose". Is that wise?
optionA: Yes; more metrics always make the record more complete and more trustworthy
optionB: No; test AUC cannot be logged at all until the model has been registered
optionC: Yes; test scores are only biased when the test set is smaller than CV folds
optionD: No; a visible test score invites selection, so log it for the chosen run only
correctAnswerText: No; a visible test score invites selection, so log it for the chosen run only
explanation: Once test scores sit beside CV scores, choices drift towards them and the test set stops being held out. Score it once, on the chosen model.

prompt: A team of six is choosing where to keep MLflow runs. Which option is soundest?
optionA: A shared server with a database backend and a shared artefact store
optionB: The mlruns folder committed to git, so the history is versioned too
optionC: A spreadsheet of final metrics, which is simpler than a server
optionD: Each person's laptop store, merged by hand before every review
correctAnswerText: A shared server with a database backend and a shared artefact store
explanation: One shared store makes every run searchable by everyone, with models and plots in durable storage. Committing mlruns bloats git and conflicts; laptops and spreadsheets lose provenance.

prompt: When moving the champion alias to a new version, what is most worth writing in that version's description?
optionA: Why it was chosen, what it was tested on, its test result and owner
optionB: A copy of the training data, so the version is fully self-contained
optionC: Nothing, since the source run already holds every needed detail
optionD: The full list of rejected runs, copied in with all their parameters
correctAnswerText: Why it was chosen, what it was tested on, its test result and owner
explanation: The run holds the mechanics; the version note holds the decision — why this one, on what evidence, and who answers for it. That is what a later reader needs.

prompt: What is data drift (covariate shift) in a deployed model?
optionA: The same feature is computed differently at serving time
optionB: The relationship between the inputs and the target changes
optionC: The distribution of the inputs changes from what training saw
optionD: The model's saved weights slowly change while it is serving
correctAnswerText: The distribution of the inputs changes from what training saw
explanation: Covariate shift is a change in P(x) — a 5G pack raises data use, a campaign brings in new customers. A changed input–target link is concept drift; different feature code is skew.

prompt: What is concept drift?
optionA: P(y) changes while each class still looks the same as before
optionB: The labels arrive later than they did when the model was trained
optionC: P(y | x) changes: the same inputs now lead to different outcomes
optionD: P(x) changes: the customers now look different from training
correctAnswerText: P(y | x) changes: the same inputs now lead to different outcomes
explanation: In concept drift the input–outcome relationship itself moves, so the model is wrong even on familiar inputs — like dual-SIM customers churning more after a rival's offer.

prompt: What are the usual rule-of-thumb bands for the Population Stability Index (PSI)?
optionA: Below 0.05 major, 0.05 to 0.25 investigate, above 0.25 stable
optionB: Below 0.5 stable, 0.5 to 1.0 investigate, above 1.0 major
optionC: Below 0.01 stable, 0.01 to 0.05 investigate, above 0.05 major
optionD: Below 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 investigate, above 0.25 major
correctAnswerText: Below 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 investigate, above 0.25 major
explanation: These credit-scoring conventions are widely used. They are rules of thumb for the size of a shift, not statistical tests.

prompt: What does "prediction drift" monitoring watch?
optionA: The time each prediction request takes from arrival to response
optionB: The distribution of each raw input feature, compared with training
optionC: The distribution of the model's scores and the share above the threshold
optionD: The training loss of the model, recomputed each day on the training set
correctAnswerText: The distribution of the model's scores and the share above the threshold
explanation: The score distribution and decision rate are available immediately, need no labels, and show whether the business decision is changing.

prompt: What is label (prior) shift?
optionA: Labels are recorded with a delay compared with training time
optionB: The label column is renamed in the data that reaches the model
optionC: P(y | x) changes, so familiar inputs now lead to new outcomes
optionD: P(y) changes while P(x | y), how each class looks, stays the same
correctAnswerText: P(y) changes while P(x | y), how each class looks, stays the same
explanation: Under label shift the class balance moves — more defaulters, say — but each class looks as it did. Ranking can survive while the predicted rates go wrong.

prompt: Once labels arrive, which simple check shows whether a churn model's probabilities are still calibrated?
optionA: The number of features whose PSI went above the 0.25 line
optionB: Mean predicted churn compared with the actual churn rate
optionC: The share of requests that returned an HTTP 422 response
optionD: AUC on the month compared with the AUC from training time
correctAnswerText: Mean predicted churn compared with the actual churn rate
explanation: Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities match observed rates. AUC measures ranking only, which can hold while calibration breaks.

prompt: Against what is a live feature's distribution usually compared when computing drift?
optionA: Yesterday's data, whatever model was serving at the time
optionB: A uniform distribution across the feature's full range
optionC: The test set of a different model that uses the feature
optionD: A reference: the data the current model was trained on
correctAnswerText: A reference: the data the current model was trained on
explanation: Drift is measured against what the model learned from. The reference is reset when the model is retrained on newer data.

prompt: A loan default label takes 12 months. What is a proxy label in this setting?
optionA: A random label used to keep the monitoring dashboard filled in
optionB: The model's own predicted probability, used in place of the label
optionC: An early signal linked to default, such as a bounced first EMI
optionD: A label copied from a similar applicant who was scored last year
correctAnswerText: An early signal linked to default, such as a bounced first EMI
explanation: Proxies such as first-EMI bounces or 30+ days past due at three months arrive early and correlate with the true outcome, bridging the wait.

prompt: In a champion–challenger setup, what is the challenger?
optionA: A second copy of the live model used to share the request load
optionB: A rule-based model kept as a fallback in case the API goes down
optionC: A newly trained candidate compared with the live model before switching
optionD: The live model that currently serves every prediction in production
correctAnswerText: A newly trained candidate compared with the live model before switching
explanation: The champion serves; a challenger, typically retrained on recent data, must beat it on the same evaluation data before the alias moves.

prompt: Which checks make up input data-quality monitoring for a model service?
optionA: The PSI of the model's score against its training reference
optionB: Latency percentiles and the HTTP error rate of the endpoint
optionC: Null rates, out-of-range values and unknown categories per batch
optionD: AUC and calibration per month once the delayed labels arrive
correctAnswerText: Null rates, out-of-range values and unknown categories per batch
explanation: Quality checks catch broken pipelines — nulls, unit changes, renamed categories — which are the most common real failure and must be ruled out before drift.

prompt: How can a model's AUC stay steady while its probabilities become badly wrong?
optionA: AUC is fixed at deployment and is never recomputed after that point
optionB: AUC depends only on ranking, which can survive a shift in overall rates
optionC: AUC averages calibration across classes, which hides any single error
optionD: AUC is computed on training data, so it cannot see live changes at all
correctAnswerText: AUC depends only on ranking, which can survive a shift in overall rates
explanation: If everyone's risk rises together, the order stays right (same AUC) but predicted rates fall short of actual ones, which breaks threshold economics.

prompt: Why is a Kolmogorov–Smirnov p-value a poor drift alarm on a feature measured for 2 lakh customers?
optionA: With samples that large, trivial shifts give tiny p-values
optionB: The KS test works only when samples are under one thousand
optionC: KS p-values are always above 0.05 for any numeric feature
optionD: The KS test needs labels, which arrive late for drift checks
correctAnswerText: With samples that large, trivial shifts give tiny p-values
explanation: A p-value answers "exactly the same distribution?", and at large n the answer is nearly always no. Size measures such as PSI say whether a shift matters.

prompt: Why can a large shift in one input barely move a model's score distribution?
optionA: PSI on inputs is always larger than PSI on outputs by definition
optionB: The model may give that feature little weight in its predictions
optionC: Scores are averaged over the month, which hides any input change
optionD: Scores are clipped to the training range, which cancels any shift
correctAnswerText: The model may give that feature little weight in its predictions
explanation: A shift matters to predictions in proportion to how much the model uses the feature. That is why output drift, not input drift alone, says whether decisions are changing.

prompt: Why can input drift checks never detect pure concept drift?
optionA: The inputs can look exactly as before while their outcomes change
optionB: Concept drift always shows first as a rise in null or missing values
optionC: Input checks run weekly, while concept drift lasts for only a day
optionD: Concept drift happens only in categorical features, which PSI skips
correctAnswerText: The inputs can look exactly as before while their outcomes change
explanation: Concept drift is a change in P(y | x). If P(x) is unchanged, nothing in the inputs moves; only outcomes — labels or proxies — reveal it.

prompt: Why are data-quality checks done before investigating drift?
optionA: Drift statistics cannot be computed at all on data that contains no nulls
optionB: Data-quality checks need labels, so they must be run before labels arrive
optionC: A pipeline fault such as a unit change looks just like drift but needs a fix
optionD: Drift is rare in practice, so it is not worth checking until quality fails
correctAnswerText: A pipeline fault such as a unit change looks just like drift but needs a fix
explanation: Broken inputs are the commonest failure and are fixed in the pipeline, not by retraining. Retraining on broken data bakes the bug into the next model.

prompt: Why are the PSI bin edges taken from the reference data's deciles rather than recomputed from each new batch?
optionA: Deciles of new data are always empty, so PSI would then be undefined
optionB: Fixed edges make each week's shares comparable with the same bins
optionC: Recomputing edges is too slow for batches larger than a few thousand
optionD: PSI is defined only for exactly ten bins taken from the newest batch
correctAnswerText: Fixed edges make each week's shares comparable with the same bins
explanation: Each batch is placed into the reference's bins, where each bin holds about 10% of reference rows. New edges per batch would make the current shares uniform and hide the shift.

prompt: A known, investigated change keeps one drift alert firing every week. Why is that harmful?
optionA: Each alert retrains the model, which wastes compute every week
optionB: PSI grows each week the alert fires, until it overflows its range
optionC: People learn to ignore alerts and miss the one that matters
optionD: The alert blocks the API, so predictions stop while it is firing
correctAnswerText: People learn to ignore alerts and miss the one that matters
explanation: An alert that never stops teaches the team to tune it out. Investigate once, record the change, and reset the reference after the next retrain.

prompt: Why is "retrain automatically whenever any PSI exceeds 0.25" a poor rule?
optionA: PSI above 0.25 can be reached only once in the life of any model
optionB: Automatic retraining always makes a model worse than its champion
optionC: Retraining is impossible until every drifted feature is dropped
optionD: A shift may not hurt the model, and the new data may be broken
correctAnswerText: A shift may not hurt the model, and the new data may be broken
explanation: Drift is a reason to look. Retrain when performance shows harm, with a challenger that beats the champion; never retrain blindly on data that may be faulty.

prompt: Why monitor the share of customers above the offer threshold, not just the mean score?
optionA: It never changes unless the model is broken, which makes alerts very clear
optionB: It replaces the need for labels, since it measures accuracy directly each day
optionC: It is the only figure that can be computed before the model has been trained
optionD: It is the decision the business acts on, and it can move when the mean barely does
correctAnswerText: It is the decision the business acts on, and it can move when the mean barely does
explanation: Offers, approvals and referrals depend on how many cross the threshold. A small change in the mean can still move many customers across it.

prompt: Churn labels arrive a month after each score. Why does the monitoring plan split into "now" checks and "when labels land" checks?
optionA: Regulators require two dashboards, one for each calendar fortnight
optionB: Labels make the input checks wrong, so they must stop when labels land
optionC: The two sets of checks use different models, one per time period
optionD: Inputs and scores are visible now; AUC and calibration need outcomes
correctAnswerText: Inputs and scores are visible now; AUC and calibration need outcomes
explanation: Quality, input drift and score drift can be seen daily. Performance needs the true outcomes, so it is checked per labelled month, with proxies in between.

prompt: A feature's three reference bins hold 30%, 40% and 30% of rows. This month they hold 10%, 40% and 50%. Using PSI = Σ (c − r)·ln(c / r), what is the PSI and its reading?
optionA: About 0.32, a major shift
optionB: About 0.22, worth a look
optionC: About 0.04, stable as is
optionD: About 0.12, worth a look
correctAnswerText: About 0.32, a major shift

prompt:
Weekly PSI against training:

tenure_months   0.04
monthly_income  0.18
region          0.31
score           0.06

Which reading follows the usual bands?
optionA: Only the score matters, so all three inputs are ignored
optionB: Income is a major shift, region worth a look, score major
optionC: All four are stable, since every value is below 0.5
optionD: Region is a major shift, income worth a look, tenure stable
correctAnswerText: Region is a major shift, income worth a look, tenure stable
explanation: Below 0.1 stable (tenure, score), 0.1–0.25 investigate (income), above 0.25 major (region). The modest score PSI suggests the model's output has moved less than its inputs.

prompt: In a labelled month the model's mean predicted default is 0.12; the actual default rate is 0.16. What is the calibration gap relative to the actual rate?
explanation: |0.12 − 0.16| / 0.16 = 0.25. Divided by the predicted rate it would be 33%, which is why a retraining rule must say which rate it divides by.

prompt:
Rule: retrain if AUC < 0.70 or |predicted − actual| / actual > 20%.

month  AUC   mean predicted  actual
Jan    0.74  0.10            0.11
Feb    0.72  0.10            0.12
Mar    0.69  0.11            0.12

Which months trigger the rule?
optionA: None, because every gap is under 20 percent
optionB: February only, because its gap is about 17%
optionC: February and March, on calibration and AUC
optionD: March only, because its AUC fell below 0.70
correctAnswerText: March only, because its AUC fell below 0.70
explanation: Gaps: Jan 9.1%, Feb 16.7%, Mar 8.3% — none above 20%. Only March's AUC of 0.69 breaks the rule.

prompt: A model was trained when 10% defaulted; under pure label shift the rate is now 20%. Adjusting by the prior odds ratio, odds′ = odds × (0.20/0.80) / (0.10/0.90), what does a score of 0.10 become?
A churn model scores customers daily; whether each one churned is known 30 days later. Which monitoring schedule fits?
optionA: Daily: retrain on today's data, so that no further monitoring is needed
optionB: Daily: quality and score drift; weekly: input PSI; monthly: AUC and calibration
optionC: Daily: AUC on today's scores; weekly: calibration; monthly: quality checks
optionD: Monthly only: every check waits until the labels for the month arrive
correctAnswerText: Daily: quality and score drift; weekly: input PSI; monthly: AUC and calibration
explanation: What needs no labels is checked often; performance waits for outcomes. AUC on today's scores is impossible without today's outcomes.

prompt: A rival launches a cheap dual-SIM plan. Customers' recorded features look as before, but dual-SIM users now churn far more often. Which kind of change is it?
optionA: Covariate shift, a new mix of customers in the inputs
optionB: Concept drift, a new link between the inputs and churn
optionC: A data-quality fault, a broken field in the pipeline
optionD: Training–serving skew, a feature computed two ways
correctAnswerText: Concept drift, a new link between the inputs and churn
explanation: The inputs did not move; the outcome for the same inputs did. That is P(y | x) changing — concept drift — visible only once labels arrive.

prompt: A campaign brings in many new customers, so 30% now have tenure of 1–3 months. Short-tenure customers churn at the same rate as before. Which kind of change is it?
optionA: Label shift: the churn rate moved while the inputs stayed put
optionB: No change: a campaign cannot affect a churn model's inputs
optionC: Concept drift: the link between tenure and churn has changed
optionD: Covariate shift: the inputs moved, the input–churn link did not
correctAnswerText: Covariate shift: the inputs moved, the input–churn link did not
explanation: P(x) moved (tenure PSI will be high) while P(y | x) held. The model may still be right for each customer; check whether its performance holds on the new mix.

prompt: A feature rose 1% on average across 2 lakh customers. The KS test gives p below 1e-12; the PSI is 0.001. What should the monitor conclude?
optionA: A real but negligible shift; no action beyond noting it
optionB: A retraining trigger, since any significant shift qualifies
optionC: A broken test, since KS and PSI must agree with each other
optionD: A major shift, since the p-value is astronomically small
correctAnswerText: A real but negligible shift; no action beyond noting it
explanation: At this sample size even a 1% change is "significant". A PSI of 0.001 is far inside the stable band; size, not the p-value, decides.

prompt: Overnight the mean churn score jumps from 0.18 to 0.31 and the share above the offer threshold from 22% to 51%. What is the first step?
optionA: Retrain the model at once on the data from the last day of scores
optionB: Raise the threshold until the share returns to about 22 percent
optionC: Send offers to the 51%, since the model has found more churners
optionD: Check the inputs and any upstream release for a pipeline change
correctAnswerText: Check the inputs and any upstream release for a pipeline change
explanation: A sudden jump overnight is far more often a pipeline change (units, nulls, a renamed category) than real behaviour. Rule that out before acting on the scores or the model.

prompt: A default model trained at a 10% rate is now scored where 20% default. Each class looks as it did. AUC is 0.798 before and after; mean predicted is 0.115 against 0.20 actual. What is the diagnosis and cheapest fix?
optionA: Covariate shift; drop the drifted features and retrain without them
optionB: Data-quality fault; fix the pipeline, since AUC cannot stay put here
optionC: Concept drift; retrain from scratch, since the model ranks badly now
optionD: Label shift; recalibrate to the new base rate, as ranking is intact
correctAnswerText: Label shift; recalibrate to the new base rate, as ranking is intact
explanation: The class balance moved while P(x | y) held, so ranking (AUC) is unchanged but probabilities are too low. A prior or recalibration adjustment fixes the rates.

prompt: A home-made PSI function returns inf for a categorical feature after a new category appears. It computes np.sum((c - r) * np.log(c / r)) on the shares. What is wrong?
optionA: PSI cannot be used on categorical features, only on numeric features
optionB: A share of zero in r makes c / r infinite; floor shares at a small value
optionC: np.log cannot take arrays, so it must be applied to each bin in a loop
optionD: The shares should be counts, and counts never produce infinite values
correctAnswerText: A share of zero in r makes c / r infinite; floor shares at a small value
explanation: A new category has a reference share of 0, so the log ratio blows up. Clipping shares to a small floor (for example 1e-4) keeps PSI finite, and the new category deserves its own alert.

prompt: A monitor compares each week only with the week before. Data use has crept up 5% a week for ten weeks, but PSI never passes 0.05. Why did it miss the drift?
optionA: Week-on-week comparison hides slow drift; compare with the training data
optionB: PSI cannot detect increases, only decreases in a feature's distribution
optionC: Data use is a ratio feature, and PSI is only valid for count features
optionD: Ten weeks is too short a period for PSI to accumulate a measurable value
correctAnswerText: Week-on-week comparison hides slow drift; compare with the training data
explanation: Each small step looks stable against its neighbour, yet the total move against what the model learned from is large. The reference should be the current model's training data.

prompt: Overnight, data_gb's PSI jumps to 8.3 and its median goes from 3.3 to 3,400. Everything else is stable. A teammate proposes retraining on this week's data. What is the right reading?
optionA: Real concept drift from heavy users; retrain at once on this week's data
optionB: A PSI bug, since PSI values above 1 are mathematically impossible
optionC: A unit fault upstream (MB as GB); fix the pipeline, do not retrain on it
optionD: Normal seasonal growth; raise data_gb's PSI alert threshold to 10
correctAnswerText: A unit fault upstream (MB as GB); fix the pipeline, do not retrain on it
explanation: A sudden ~1000× jump in one field is a data-quality fault, not drift. Retraining would bake the broken unit into the model; fix the feed and add a range check.

prompt: App-version PSI is 0.40 after a release. The score PSI is 0.01, the share above threshold is unchanged and last month's AUC and calibration held. What does this show?
optionA: A hidden failure: the model must be broken if its scores did not move
optionB: A reason to retrain now, before the scores start to follow the input
optionC: A real input shift the model barely uses; record it, no retrain needed
optionD: A PSI miscount, since a 0.40 input shift must always move the scores
correctAnswerText: A real input shift the model barely uses; record it, no retrain needed
explanation: Input drift matters through the model. With output, decisions and labelled performance all steady, the evidence says the change is harmless for now; keep watching.

prompt: A scheduled weekly retrain auto-promoted a model trained during a feed outage, when income arrived as 0 for 40% of rows. Approvals then fell sharply. What failed?
optionA: The model was too simple; a deeper model would ignore the zeros
optionB: The schedule was too slow; daily retraining would have avoided it
optionC: No quality check or champion–challenger gate stood before promotion
optionD: The alias was wrong; MLflow should have refused zeros in income
correctAnswerText: No quality check or champion–challenger gate stood before promotion
explanation: Scheduled retraining is fine with gates: data-quality checks on the training batch and a comparison with the champion on recent labelled data before the alias moves.

prompt: A lender retrains each year only on approved applicants, the only ones with repayment outcomes. Over years the model grows unreliable on borderline applicants. Why?
optionA: Approved applicants are a random sample, so this cannot be the cause
optionB: It never sees outcomes for those it rejected, so it is blind there
optionC: Annual retraining is too frequent and overfits to the latest year
optionD: Rejected applicants are counted as repaid, so risk is understated
correctAnswerText: It never sees outcomes for those it rejected, so it is blind there
explanation: This is the selective-labels problem: the training data cover only the region the old model approved, so the new model has no evidence about the rest.

prompt: A fraud model's monthly monitor tracks accuracy, steady at 97%. Fraud is 3% of transactions. Losses doubled last month. What is wrong with the monitor?
optionA: Accuracy of 97% proves the model is fine, so losses must be unrelated
optionB: The monitor should track latency, since fraud losses come from timeouts
optionC: Accuracy stays near 97% even if recall on fraud collapses to zero
optionD: Accuracy is only valid for balanced classes, so it reads 97% wrongly
correctAnswerText: Accuracy stays near 97% even if recall on fraud collapses to zero
explanation: Predicting "not fraud" for everything scores 97%. Monitor recall and precision at the operating threshold, and PR-AUC, which show the minority class.

prompt: Overall AUC and calibration look fine. Yet a new dealer network, 6% of loans, shows 21% actual defaults against 9% predicted. Why did the dashboard miss it?
optionA: Calibration is defined only for the whole portfolio, not for subsets
optionB: The dealer loans must be mislabelled, since overall figures were fine
optionC: Aggregates are dominated by the large segments and hide a small one
optionD: AUC cannot be computed for any segment below a tenth of the volume
correctAnswerText: Aggregates are dominated by the large segments and hide a small one
explanation: A 6% segment barely moves portfolio-wide numbers. Monitor calibration and AUC by segment — new channels, regions, products — where shifts start.

prompt: A challenger trained on January–September beats the champion on September's labels, 0.81 against 0.74 AUC. It is promoted, then performs like the champion in October. What went wrong?
optionA: October was an unusual month, so its result says nothing about the model
optionB: The champion was scored with the wrong metric, so the gap was reversed
optionC: AUC cannot compare two models, so the result was always meaningless
optionD: It was scored on September, which it trained on, so its score was inflated
correctAnswerText: It was scored on September, which it trained on, so its score was inflated
explanation: A fair comparison scores both on recent labelled data neither was trained on. Evaluating the challenger on its own training month measures fit, not generalisation.

prompt: A team is choosing a drift alarm for a model scoring 5 lakh customers a week. Which design is soundest?
optionA: Alert whenever any feature's KS p-value is below 0.05 in the week
optionB: Alert only when the API error rate rises, since drift shows as errors
optionC: PSI thresholds on key features and scores, then a check on performance
optionD: No alarm; retrain every week so that drift never has time to build
correctAnswerText: PSI thresholds on key features and scores, then a check on performance
explanation: Size-based thresholds avoid alarms on trivial but "significant" shifts at this volume, and confirming with performance avoids acting on harmless drift. Drift does not raise API errors.

prompt: A new online portal makes patients book appointments further ahead; a no-show model's booking-gap PSI is 0.38. What is the best response?
optionA: Remove booking gap from the model, since a drifting feature is useless
optionB: Clip the booking gap to its training range so the alert stops firing
optionC: Confirm the cause, check performance on long gaps, retrain if hurt
optionD: Ignore it, since a cause that is known can never hurt a model's score
correctAnswerText: Confirm the cause, check performance on long gaps, retrain if hurt
explanation: A known cause still may hurt the model where training data were thin. Labelled performance on the shifted segment decides; then reset the reference after retraining.

prompt: Which retraining policy is soundest for a churn model with monthly labels?
optionA: Never retrain, since a model that worked at launch keeps working while it runs
optionB: Retrain every night and promote automatically, since newer data is always better
optionC: Retrain on a schedule or trigger, promote only past a quality and challenger gate
optionD: Retrain only when a customer complains about receiving an unwanted offer
correctAnswerText: Retrain on a schedule or trigger, promote only past a quality and challenger gate
explanation: Retraining cadence should match how fast data move, but promotion needs gates: clean training data and a win over the champion on recent labelled data.

prompt: A two-wheeler loan model's default label matures in 12 months. Which monitoring plan is strongest?
optionA: Inputs and scores from day one, early proxies, then cohort AUC and calibration
optionB: Nothing for a year, then a full review once every loan has a mature label
optionC: Daily AUC computed with the model's own scores standing in for the labels
optionD: Approval rate alone, since it is the only number visible from the first day
correctAnswerText: Inputs and scores from day one, early proxies, then cohort AUC and calibration
explanation: Quality, drift and score distribution show change at once; proxies such as first-EMI bounces give early outcome signal; mature labels confirm ranking and calibration by cohort.

prompt: A churn model still ranks well (AUC 0.74) but predicts 20% churn where 29% happen, so the break-even threshold targets too few. A retrain takes a month. What is best now?
optionA: Recalibrate or adjust the threshold as a stopgap, and tell the team
optionB: Swap in a random model, since this one's probabilities are wrong
optionC: Leave it as is, since the AUC shows nothing important has changed
optionD: Switch the model off until the retrain is done, sending no offers
correctAnswerText: Recalibrate or adjust the threshold as a stopgap, and tell the team
explanation: Ranking is intact, so the cheapest fix is to correct the probabilities or the cut-off. Switching off throws away a useful ranking; ignoring it keeps the offer economics wrong.

prompt: A lender sees outcomes only for applicants it approves. Which response to this selective-labels problem is most defensible?
optionA: Treat every rejected applicant as a defaulter and add them to training
optionB: Approve everyone for one month so that labels exist for every applicant
optionC: Ignore it, since approved applicants represent everyone well enough
optionD: A small, governed band of approvals just below the cut-off to learn there
correctAnswerText: A small, governed band of approvals just below the cut-off to learn there
explanation: Limited, controlled exploration buys outcome data where the model is blind at bounded cost. Assuming rejects defaulted bakes in the old model's view; approving everyone is reckless.

prompt: Which monthly performance metrics best monitor a fraud model where 2% of transactions are fraud?
optionA: Accuracy and overall error rate, since they summarise both classes
optionB: The mean score and its standard deviation, computed without labels
optionC: Recall and precision at the threshold, plus PR-AUC and losses caught
optionD: Training loss on the original data, recomputed on the same rows
correctAnswerText: Recall and precision at the threshold, plus PR-AUC and losses caught
explanation: With a 2% positive class, accuracy is dominated by the majority. Metrics about the fraud class at the operating point, and the money caught, show what matters.

prompt: For a credit model sold through branches, dealers and an app, which segmentation of the monthly performance report is most useful?
optionA: By the hour each loan was scored, since time of day drives default
optionB: No segmentation, since the overall AUC already covers every channel
optionC: By channel and new-versus-existing segment, with volumes shown
optionD: By applicant name, so every single loan is reviewed every month
correctAnswerText: By channel and new-versus-existing segment, with volumes shown
explanation: Shifts start in channels, regions and new segments. Reporting those, with volumes so small segments are read with care, catches problems the aggregate hides.

prompt: What should a challenger have to show before the champion alias moves to it?
optionA: A higher cross-validated AUC on its own training data than the champion
optionB: A newer training date than the champion, whatever its evaluation scores
optionC: Better AUC and calibration on the same recent month neither trained on
optionD: The same AUC as the champion, measured on the champion's old test set
correctAnswerText: Better AUC and calibration on the same recent month neither trained on
explanation: Only the same unseen, recent evaluation data makes the comparison fair; reviewing which decisions flip guards the business. Recency alone proves nothing.

prompt: A model uses 200 features. Alerting at PSI > 0.25 on all of them produces several alerts a week, mostly harmless. What is the better design?
optionA: Raise every feature's threshold to 1.0 so that alerts stop firing
optionB: Drop monitoring entirely and retrain the model every single month
optionC: Keep all 200 alerts, since one alert per feature is the safest way
optionD: Alert on the score and decision rate, plus PSI on the top features
correctAnswerText: Alert on the score and decision rate, plus PSI on the top features
explanation: Output and decision drift show whether anything that matters changed; the most important features explain why. Hundreds of feature alerts create noise and alert fatigue.

prompt: A byte-level BPE tokeniser starts training from which basic symbols before it learns any merges?
optionA: Every word in an English dictionary
optionB: The 256 possible UTF-8 byte values
optionC: The 26 letters of the Latin alphabet
optionD: Whole sentences split at full stops
correctAnswerText: The 256 possible UTF-8 byte values
explanation: Byte-level BPE begins from raw bytes, so no text is ever "unknown", and then repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pairs into new tokens. Starting from letters or words would leave Telugu or emoji with no representation.

prompt: In a decoder-only transformer, what does the causal mask do inside attention?
optionA: Stops each token attending to any later position
optionB: Hides the system prompt from the user's tokens
optionC: Removes rare tokens from the model vocabulary
optionD: Blocks tokens that repeat an earlier token id
correctAnswerText: Stops each token attending to any later position
explanation: The mask sets scores for future positions to minus infinity, so after softmax their weights are zero. That is what lets the model be trained on next-token prediction and generate left to right.

prompt: What does the KV cache hold while a model generates a reply?
optionA: Keys and values of earlier tokens, reused each step
optionB: Previous replies to the same prompt, for re-serving
optionC: The vocabulary table that maps ids back into text
optionD: Copies of the weights kept in a faster memory tier
correctAnswerText: Keys and values of earlier tokens, reused each step
explanation: Each new token attends to every earlier token, so their keys and values are stored instead of being recomputed. It is not a response cache: it lives only for the current sequence and grows with its length.

prompt: What are the two phases a model goes through when it answers one prompt?
optionA: Decode all tokens at once, then sort them into an order
optionB: Prefill of the whole prompt, then decode token by token
optionC: Retrieve passages first, then fine-tune on those passages
optionD: Tokenise the reply first, then embed the user's prompt
correctAnswerText: Prefill of the whole prompt, then decode token by token
explanation: Prefill runs every prompt token through the layers in parallel and fills the KV cache; decode then produces one token per step. Retrieval and fine-tuning are not part of a single forward generation.

prompt: Mechanically, what does the temperature setting do to the model's next-token scores?
optionA: Removes every token whose probability is below T
optionB: Divides the logits by T before softmax is applied
optionC: Adds T to every logit so that all tokens rise equally
optionD: Multiplies the length of the reply by the value T
correctAnswerText: Divides the logits by T before softmax is applied
explanation: probabilities = softmax(logits / T). A small T widens the gaps and sharpens the distribution; a large T flattens it. Cutting tokens below a threshold is what top-p or top-k do, not temperature.

prompt: Which tokens does top-p (nucleus) sampling allow the model to draw from?
optionA: Every token whose own probability is greater than p
optionB: All tokens, after each probability is multiplied by p
optionC: The smallest set whose probabilities sum to at least p
optionD: Exactly p tokens, taken from the top of the ranking
correctAnswerText: The smallest set whose probabilities sum to at least p
explanation: Top-p keeps the most probable tokens until their cumulative probability reaches p, renormalises them, and samples from that set. A fixed count of tokens is top-k; a per-token cut-off is neither.

prompt: A chat response comes back with finish_reason set to "length". What does that mean?
optionA: The model chose to end its turn on its own
optionB: The reply reached max_tokens and was cut off
optionC: A stop sequence appeared in the output text
optionD: The prompt was too long and was rejected
correctAnswerText: The reply reached max_tokens and was cut off
explanation: "length" means the output cap was hit, so the text may end mid-sentence. The model ending its own turn gives "stop"; a rejected over-long prompt returns an error, not a finish reason.

prompt: Which training stage gives a model its broad knowledge by next-token prediction on a huge corpus?
optionA: Prompt engineering
optionB: Preference tuning
optionC: Pre-training
optionD: Instruction tuning
correctAnswerText: Pre-training
explanation: Pre-training teaches next-token prediction on web pages, books and code, and that is where facts and fluency come from. Instruction and preference tuning mostly shape how the model uses that knowledge in conversation.

prompt: When a local model is described as "quantised to 4 bits", what has been done to it?
optionA: Its context window has been limited to 4,000 tokens
optionB: Only 4 of its layers are kept and the rest removed
optionC: Its vocabulary has been cut to a quarter of its size
optionD: Its weights are stored in 4 bits with per-block scales
correctAnswerText: Its weights are stored in 4 bits with per-block scales
explanation: Quantisation stores each weight in fewer bits (8 or 4 instead of 16) with a scale factor per small block, cutting memory roughly in proportion. Vocabulary, layer count and context length are unchanged.

prompt: What does it usually mean when a model is called "open-weight"?
optionA: It is served free of charge through every provider's API
optionB: It may be used for any purpose with no licence terms at all
optionC: Its weights can be downloaded; data and code often cannot
optionD: Its training data and code are public; weights are not
correctAnswerText: Its weights can be downloaded; data and code often cannot
explanation: Open weight means the trained parameters are downloadable so you can run them yourself. It is not the same as open source, and the licence may still restrict commercial use or cap users.

prompt: Why is a model unreliable at reversing a string or comparing 9.11 with 9.9?
optionA: Its softmax layer cannot represent any numeric value exactly
optionB: Its context window is too short to hold more than a few digits
optionC: Its temperature makes every digit a random choice by design
optionD: It works on subword tokens, so digits and letters are hidden
correctAnswerText: It works on subword tokens, so digits and letters are hidden
explanation: "9.11 vs 9.9" becomes tokens such as "9", ".", "11", and the model reasons over those ids, not characters or place values. That is why exact character and digit work is done in code, whatever the temperature.

prompt: Why can the same refund question need several times more tokens in Telugu than in English on an older tokeniser?
optionA: Few merges were learnt for the script, so it falls back to bytes
optionB: Providers add a fixed surcharge token for non-English messages
optionC: Telugu sentences always contain more words than English ones
optionD: Telugu is converted to English inside the tokeniser before use
correctAnswerText: Few merges were learnt for the script, so it falls back to bytes
explanation: BPE merges are learnt from the tokeniser's training corpus; a script that was rare there gets few merged pieces and splits towards single bytes. A larger multilingual vocabulary narrows the gap, which is why token budgets must be measured per language.

prompt: Why does a longer prompt raise time to first token while the tokens-per-second rate afterwards stays about the same?
optionA: Each output token re-reads the entire prompt from the start
optionB: Prefill must process the whole prompt; decode reuses the cache
optionC: Long prompts wait in a separate queue before any work starts
optionD: Tokenising a long prompt is repeated for every output token
correctAnswerText: Prefill must process the whole prompt; decode reuses the cache
explanation: All prompt tokens pass through the layers before the first output token, so prefill time grows with prompt length. Decode then reuses cached keys and values; recomputing the whole prompt each step is exactly what the KV cache avoids.

prompt: Why is it advised to send fewer passages and place the best ones close to the question in a long prompt?
optionA: Passages in the middle are removed by the tokeniser to save space
optionB: Attention can only reach a fixed number of tokens nearest the end
optionC: Models use the middle of a long context less reliably than its ends
optionD: The causal mask hides any passage placed before the user's question
correctAnswerText: Models use the middle of a long context less reliably than its ends
explanation: Measured across many models, facts at the start and end of a long context are used more reliably than those buried in the middle. The causal mask hides later tokens, not earlier ones, so the question can still attend to them — just less reliably.

prompt: Why should the fixed system instructions and examples come before the per-request text when prefix caching is used?
optionA: Prefix caches store only the final part of each prompt they see
optionB: The model ignores any instruction that is placed after user text
optionC: Cached keys and values are reused only for an identical start
optionD: Instructions placed first are billed at a lower per-token rate
correctAnswerText: Cached keys and values are reused only for an identical start
explanation: A prefix cache can skip prefill only for a beginning that is exactly the same as an earlier request. Varying text at the start means no two prompts share a prefix, so nothing is reused.

prompt: Why does a base model given a quiz question often answer it and then write more questions of its own?
optionA: Its KV cache overflows, so it forgets where the answer stopped
optionB: Its tokeniser does not contain an end-of-text token to emit
optionC: It completes documents; answering and stopping come from tuning
optionD: Its temperature is too high, so it keeps sampling extra content
correctAnswerText: It completes documents; answering and stopping come from tuning
explanation: Pre-training teaches continuation of documents, and quiz pages contain question after question. Instruction tuning is what teaches a model to answer one request and end its turn.

prompt: Why do chat models tend to abandon a correct answer when a user insists it is wrong?
optionA: Pre-training removed all examples of people disagreeing online
optionB: The chat template marks every user turn as more trusted than facts
optionC: The KV cache keeps only the most recent user message in memory
optionD: Preference tuning rewarded answers that people found agreeable
correctAnswerText: Preference tuning rewarded answers that people found agreeable
explanation: Raters tended to prefer agreeable answers, so preference tuning pushed models towards agreeing under pressure. The engineering fix is to verify in code rather than ask the model to re-judge a result.

prompt: Greedy decoding is deterministic, so why can two identical temperature-0 calls to a hosted model differ?
optionA: Batching changes floating-point order and near-tied tokens flip
optionB: Servers quietly replace temperature 0 with a small random value
optionC: Each call re-tokenises the prompt with a randomly chosen tokeniser
optionD: Greedy decoding picks randomly among the top five tokens each step
correctAnswerText: Batching changes floating-point order and near-tied tokens flip
explanation: Floating-point addition is not associative, and the batch your request shares changes the summation order, so logits differ in the last digits. When two tokens are almost tied the winner flips and the rest of the text follows.

prompt: Why is a system prompt a strong influence on behaviour but not a security boundary?
optionA: It is tokenised apart and never reaches the attention layers
optionB: System prompts apply only when temperature is set to 0
optionC: Providers delete the system prompt after the first turn
optionD: Tuning taught the model to weight it; no code enforces it
correctAnswerText: Tuning taught the model to weight it; no code enforces it
explanation: Following the system turn is a learnt habit from instruction and preference tuning, not a rule the runtime enforces. Real limits on data and actions must live in code and permissions.

prompt: Why does a mixture-of-experts model run faster than its total parameter count suggests, yet still need a lot of memory?
optionA: Its weights are always stored at 4 bits, unlike dense models
optionB: Each token uses only some experts, but all must stay loaded
optionC: Its experts are loaded from disk only when they are needed
optionD: It skips the attention step for most of the tokens it reads
correctAnswerText: Each token uses only some experts, but all must stay loaded
explanation: Routing sends each token through a few experts, so compute follows the active parameter count. Every expert must still be resident in memory, so memory follows the total count.

prompt: A 32,000-token window must hold a 2,000-token system prompt, 4,000 tokens of history, a 1,000-token answer cap and 100 tokens of message markers. How many tokens are left for retrieved passages?
optionA: 26,000 tokens
optionB: 24,800 tokens
optionC: 25,900 tokens
optionD: 24,900 tokens
correctAnswerText: 24,900 tokens
explanation: Input and output share the window: 32,000 − 2,000 − 4,000 − 1,000 − 100 = 24,900. Forgetting the answer cap gives 25,900, the usual mistake.

prompt: A model has 24 layers, 8 KV heads and head size 128, with a 16-bit cache. Roughly how much KV cache does one 10,000-token conversation need?
optionA: About 0.9 GiB, at 96 KiB per token
optionB: About 9 GiB, at 960 KiB per token
optionC: About 94 MiB, at 9.6 KiB per token
optionD: About 1.8 GiB, at 192 KiB per token
correctAnswerText: About 0.9 GiB, at 96 KiB per token
explanation: Per token: 2 (K and V) × 24 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 98,304 bytes = 96 KiB. Times 10,000 tokens is about 983 million bytes, roughly 0.92 GiB, per concurrent conversation.

prompt: Three candidate tokens have logits 3, 1 and 0. At temperature 1, what does softmax give them (e ≈ 2.718, e³ ≈ 20.09)?
explanation: Exponentiate first: 20.09, 2.718 and 1, summing to 23.80; dividing gives 0.844, 0.114 and 0.042. Dividing the raw logits by their sum (3/4, 1/4, 0) is the tempting mistake.

prompt: Sorted next-token probabilities are 0.40, 0.25, 0.20, 0.10 and 0.05. With top-p = 0.7, how many tokens can be drawn?
optionA: Two, as 0.65 is the total closest to 0.7
optionB: One, as only 0.40 is above 0.7 times 0.5
optionC: Four, as top-p keeps tokens until 0.95
optionD: Three, as the total first reaches 0.7 at 0.85
correctAnswerText: Three, as the total first reaches 0.7 at 0.85
explanation: Cumulative totals are 0.40, 0.65, 0.85: the third token is the first to take the total to at least 0.7, so three tokens are kept and renormalised. "Closest to p" is not the rule.

prompt: An 8-billion-parameter model must run on a 12 GB GPU with room left for the KV cache. Which is the highest weight precision that fits?
optionA: 32-bit, about 12 GB, with no cache at all
optionB: 8-bit, about 8 GB, leaving about 4 GB
optionC: 16-bit, about 16 GB, with the cache offloaded
optionD: 16-bit, about 8 GB, leaving about 4 GB
correctAnswerText: 8-bit, about 8 GB, leaving about 4 GB
explanation: Weights need about parameters × bytes per parameter: 8B × 2 bytes = 16 GB at 16-bit, too much; 8B × 1 byte = 8 GB at 8-bit fits with space for the cache. 32-bit would need 32 GB.

prompt: A feature extracts the GSTIN and invoice total from scanned bills into a database. Which decoding set-up fits?
optionA: Temperature 0–0.2, schema output, and checks in code
optionB: High temperature, retrying until two replies match
optionC: Temperature 0.7 with top-p 0.5, tuned both together
optionD: Temperature 1.0, so that every field gets a fresh look
correctAnswerText: Temperature 0–0.2, schema output, and checks in code
explanation: Extraction wants the most likely token every time, a fixed output shape and validation of the identifiers and totals in code. High temperature lets unlikely digits be drawn, and tuning temperature and top-p together hides which change did what.

prompt: A CRM assistant must copy a customer's 10-character PAN from a chat transcript into a form field, exactly. How should it be built?
optionA: Put the PAN in quotes so that it becomes a single token
optionB: Use a larger model, as larger models never alter characters
optionC: Ask the model to spell the PAN twice and keep the first copy
optionD: Extract it with a regex in code and check the model against it
correctAnswerText: Extract it with a regex in code and check the model against it
explanation: Identifiers are split into several tokens and copying them is a generation step that can slip. A fixed format such as a PAN is extracted and validated in code; quoting does not change tokenisation and bigger models only reduce the error rate.

prompt: A summariser makes 50,000 calls a day with 1,200 input and 150 output tokens each. What are its daily token volumes?
optionA: 60M input and 7.5M output tokens
optionB: 600M input and 7.5M output tokens
optionC: 6M input and 0.75M output tokens
optionD: 60M input and 75M output tokens
correctAnswerText: 60M input and 7.5M output tokens
explanation: 50,000 × 1,200 = 60,000,000 input and 50,000 × 150 = 7,500,000 output tokens. Daily cost is then 60 × P_in + 7.5 × P_out, with prices per million tokens.

prompt: You load open instruct weights with transformers and call model.generate yourself. How should the system and user messages be turned into the input?
optionA: Join the two messages with a newline as plain text
optionB: Put the system text after the user text in one line
optionC: apply_chat_template with add_generation_prompt=True
optionD: Tokenise each message on its own and add the ids
correctAnswerText: apply_chat_template with add_generation_prompt=True
explanation: Instruct models were tuned on turns wrapped in their own special tokens. apply_chat_template builds exactly that layout and opens the assistant turn; plain text does not look like a turn, and the model may answer with end-of-turn at once.

prompt: Prompts to a local Ollama model will be up to 10,000 tokens, plus a 1,000-token answer. What should the set-up include?
optionA: Temperature 0, so that long prompts are read in full
optionB: num_ctx of at least 11,000, and a token count before sending
optionC: The default num_ctx, since Ollama grows it when it is needed
optionD: A longer keep_alive, so the whole prompt stays in memory
correctAnswerText: num_ctx of at least 11,000, and a token count before sending
explanation: Ollama loads a model with a fixed context length and silently drops what does not fit. Set num_ctx in the request options or a Modelfile, and count tokens in code so overflow becomes a logged error.

prompt: A self-hosted model server streams Telugu replies that show "�" in mid-word, yet the saved final reply is correct. What is the cause?
optionA: The model emitted invalid tokens that the save step repaired
optionB: A letter spans two tokens and each token is decoded on its own
optionC: The tokeniser drops vowel signs during the streaming phase
optionD: The browser font lacks Telugu glyphs for some of the letters
correctAnswerText: A letter spans two tokens and each token is decoded on its own
explanation: A token is a run of bytes, and a multi-byte UTF-8 character can be split across two tokens. Decoding token by token prints half-characters; an incremental UTF-8 decoder, or re-decoding the accumulated ids, fixes it.

prompt: A cost forecast for a Hindi-first app came in far below the provider's bill. The forecast used "1 token ≈ 4 characters". What went wrong?
optionA: Hindi words are long, so each became one cheaper token
optionB: Providers bill Hindi messages by character instead of token
optionC: The rule holds; output tokens must have been undercounted
optionD: Hindi needs more tokens per character than that English rule
correctAnswerText: Hindi needs more tokens per character than that English rule
explanation: The 4-characters rule is for English prose. On the course's measurement a Hindi sentence ran 2.4 characters per token on a newer tokeniser and under 1 on an older one, so both cost and context use were underestimated.

prompt: A locally loaded instruct model returns an empty string for every question. With special tokens shown, the output is a single end-of-turn token. Diagnosis?
optionA: max_new_tokens is too small for the model to begin a reply
optionB: The prompt was sent as plain text without the chat template
optionC: Greedy decoding always selects the end-of-turn token first
optionD: The model was quantised and lost its trained vocabulary
correctAnswerText: The prompt was sent as plain text without the chat template
explanation: Plain text does not look like a conversation turn the model was tuned on, so it predicts "end of turn" at once. More tokens or sampling do not fix a malformed input; apply_chat_template does.

prompt: A CI test asserts a temperature-0 hosted reply equals a stored string; it fails about weekly with a reworded but correct reply. What is happening?
optionA: Hosted inference is not bit-for-bit repeatable; test behaviour
optionB: The provider has a bug, since temperature 0 must never vary
optionC: The prompt is too short to pin the reply down to one wording
optionD: The stored string is stale and must be refreshed every week
correctAnswerText: Hosted inference is not bit-for-bit repeatable; test behaviour
explanation: Batching changes floating-point order and near-ties flip, so exact strings drift occasionally. Tests should assert fields, categories or citations, and log the model version to tell a real change from noise.

prompt: A self-hosted model whose weights fit comfortably runs out of GPU memory once 16 users hold 8,000-token chats at the same time. Why?
optionA: KV cache grows with context length times concurrent chats
optionB: The vocabulary table is reloaded once for every user turn
optionC: Each user is given a private copy of the model's weights
optionD: Attention weights are saved to GPU memory after each reply
correctAnswerText: KV cache grows with context length times concurrent chats
explanation: Each conversation keeps keys and values for every token: at about 128 KiB per token, 8,000 tokens is about 1 GiB per chat, so 16 chats need about 16 GiB on top of the shared weights.

prompt: After moving a local model from 8-bit to 4-bit, chat looks unchanged but an EMI-calculation test set falls from 90% to 74%. What is the best reading?
optionA: The test set must be faulty, as quantisation keeps answers
optionB: 4-bit models need temperature 1.0 to regain lost precision
optionC: Quantisation error shows first on exact arithmetic tasks
optionD: The context window halved, so the questions were truncated
correctAnswerText: Quantisation error shows first on exact arithmetic tasks
explanation: Quantisation adds a small error to every weight. Casual chat hides it; exact arithmetic and multi-step reasoning reveal it first. Measure on your own task and step back to 8-bit or a larger model if needed.

prompt: A tax assistant confidently quotes last year's income-tax slabs after this year's budget changed them. Which cause and fix match?
optionA: Tokenisation; write the slab amounts out in words
optionB: Sycophancy; tell the model to disagree with users more
optionC: Pre-training cut-off; put the current slabs in the prompt
optionD: Sampling noise; lower the temperature to get new slabs
correctAnswerText: Pre-training cut-off; put the current slabs in the prompt
explanation: The model learnt facts only up to its corpus date and cannot know a later budget. Fresh facts arrive through retrieval or tools. Decoding settings and wording cannot add knowledge the model does not have.

prompt: Every prompt starts with "Current time: <hh:mm:ss>", then a fixed 3,000-token instruction block, then the question. Prefix-cache hits are near zero. Why?
optionA: Caching needs temperature 0, and the calls use sampling
optionB: Prefix caches work only for prompts under 1,000 tokens long
optionC: The first line changes every call, so no prefix is ever shared
optionD: The instruction block is too long to be stored in the cache
correctAnswerText: The first line changes every call, so no prefix is ever shared
explanation: A prefix cache matches from the first token. A timestamp at the top makes every prompt unique from the start; moving it after the fixed block lets the 3,000 instruction tokens be reused.

prompt: At temperature 1.2, a reconciliation step occasionally reports an amount one digit off from the statement; at temperature 0 it does not. Diagnosis?
optionA: High temperature lets low-probability digit tokens be drawn
optionB: The tokeniser splits numbers differently at each temperature
optionC: Temperature 0 turns on a hidden arithmetic checker inside
optionD: High temperature shortens the context, so digits are lost
correctAnswerText: High temperature lets low-probability digit tokens be drawn
explanation: Temperature flattens the distribution, so a wrong but plausible digit gets real probability and is sometimes sampled. Temperature does not change context or tokenisation; the amount should also be checked in code.

prompt: A hospital's patient-safety team finds the model refuses to summarise medication-error incident reports for its review meeting. Which stage most likely caused it?
optionA: Pre-training, which left out all medical text from its corpus
optionB: Preference tuning, which rewards declining risky-looking asks
optionC: Decoding, since greedy search always ends with a refusal
optionD: Tokenisation, which splits drug names into unknown tokens
correctAnswerText: Preference tuning, which rewards declining risky-looking asks
explanation: Refusals and over-refusals of harmless requests are shaped by preference tuning. Clear system context about who the users are and why they need it often helps; the medical knowledge itself comes from pre-training.

prompt: Model A leads a public leaderboard by 4 points. Model B scores 2 points higher on your 250 labelled real support tickets and costs less. Which choice is best justified?
optionA: A, since a 4-point lead outweighs a 2-point gap on tickets
optionB: Neither, until both are tested on a second leaderboard
optionC: B, since your own data at your settings is the real test
optionD: A, since leaderboard leads transfer to every kind of task
correctAnswerText: B, since your own data at your settings is the real test
explanation: Leaderboards can be contaminated, saturated or unrelated to your task. A labelled set of real inputs is the evidence that matters; with B also cheaper, it is the sound pick — re-checked as the set grows.

prompt: A start-up will ship an open-weight model inside a paid product. Its page says "free to download" under a custom licence. What is the sound judgement?
optionA: Avoid all open weights, since none allow commercial use
optionB: Ship it, since downloadable weights are always open source
optionC: Read the licence on commercial use and caps before shipping
optionD: Ship it, provided the weights fit on the target hardware
correctAnswerText: Read the licence on commercial use and caps before shipping
explanation: Open weights are not automatically free for any use. Custom licences can restrict commercial use, cap users or require attribution; permissive licences such as Apache 2.0 and MIT do not. Many open-weight models are fine commercially.

prompt: A two-person team has low, spiky traffic, no data-location rule, and a task only strong models pass. Hosted API or self-hosted open weights?
optionA: Either, since model choice has no effect on running costs
optionB: A hosted API: no idle GPUs, no ops load, strongest models
optionC: Self-hosting, since owning GPUs is always cheaper per token
optionD: Self-hosting, since hosted APIs cannot handle spiky traffic
correctAnswerText: A hosted API: no idle GPUs, no ops load, strongest models
explanation: Self-hosting pays when GPUs stay busy, when data rules demand it and when someone can run the infrastructure. None holds here, and the task needs a strong model, so a per-token API is cheaper and simpler.

prompt: A team classifies 5 million short Hinglish messages a day; a few per cent are genuinely hard. Which model strategy is best justified?
optionA: A small model that passes your set, escalating hard cases
optionB: Any model, since volume does not change the cost picture
optionC: The leaderboard leader, since rank predicts Hinglish quality
optionD: The largest hosted model for every message, to be safe
correctAnswerText: A small model that passes your set, escalating hard cases
explanation: At this volume cost per call dominates, so the smallest model that passes your own labelled set is the base, with a larger model only for uncertain cases. Leaderboard rank and size are weak proxies for Hinglish classification.

prompt: A developer wants to raise a local model's num_ctx from 8,000 to 64,000 on a 16 GB laptop "to be safe", though prompts stay under 6,000 tokens. How do you judge it?
optionA: Unwise: the KV cache grows with it; size it to real prompts
optionB: Sound: a larger context always makes local answers better
optionC: Unwise: num_ctx must always equal the model's training size
optionD: Sound: num_ctx has no effect on memory, only on latency
correctAnswerText: Unwise: the KV cache grows with it; size it to real prompts
explanation: The cache needed grows with the loaded context length, so a 64,000-token context can exhaust laptop memory for no benefit. Size num_ctx to the prompts you send plus the answer, and count tokens before sending.

prompt: For the same GPU memory, a team can run a 14B model at 4-bit or a 7B model at 8-bit for a Hinglish support bot. How should they decide?
optionA: Always take the 7B model, as 8-bit loses nothing at all
optionB: Always take the 14B model, as size beats precision always
optionC: Score both on their own set, checking arithmetic cases too
optionD: Pick by download size, since quality is the same for both
correctAnswerText: Score both on their own set, checking arithmetic cases too
explanation: A larger model at 4 bits often beats a smaller one at higher precision for the same memory, but 4-bit loss shows on exact arithmetic and smaller languages. Only the team's own evaluation set settles it.

prompt: To get more varied marketing lines, an engineer changes temperature to 0.9 and top-p to 0.5 in the same release. What is the soundest critique?
optionA: Top-p must always equal the temperature for valid sampling
optionB: Tune one at a time, or you cannot tell which change did what
optionC: Both should be 0, since variety is never wanted in marketing
optionD: Neither setting affects variety; only max_tokens does that
correctAnswerText: Tune one at a time, or you cannot tell which change did what
explanation: The common advice is to adjust temperature or top-p, not both, so the effect can be attributed. Here top-p 0.5 also narrows choices while temperature widens them, partly cancelling each other.

prompt: Which test plan for a model-backed ticket classifier is most defensible, given that hosted outputs vary slightly?
optionA: Retry each failing case until it passes, then mark it green
optionB: A labelled set scored on category, with model version logged
optionC: One manual check per release, signed off by the developer
optionD: Exact-string checks on ten replies captured on launch day
correctAnswerText: A labelled set scored on category, with model version logged
explanation: Behaviour such as the chosen category is what matters and survives harmless rewording. Logging the model version separates a provider change from noise; retry-until-green hides real regressions.

prompt: A model sometimes ignores the required JSON shape. A teammate proposes fine-tuning straight away. What is the sound order of attack?
optionA: Fine-tune first, as prompting cannot influence output format
optionB: Switch to a base model, which follows formats more strictly
optionC: Raise temperature, so the model tries different output shapes
optionD: Schema output and examples first; tune if an eval shows a gap
correctAnswerText: Schema output and examples first; tune if an eval shows a gap
explanation: Format following comes from instruction tuning and is usually fixed by schema-constrained output and examples. Fine-tune only when an evaluation set shows a gap those cannot close; a base model follows instructions less, not more.

prompt: A codebase names one provider's model directly in 40 call sites. New models appear every few months. Which design is best?
optionA: Keep it hard-coded, since switching models is never needed
optionB: Swap models whenever a new one tops a public leaderboard
optionC: Call every available model and keep the longest answer
optionD: Model, base URL and key as config, switched after an eval run
correctAnswerText: Model, base URL and key as config, switched after an eval run
explanation: With the model as configuration, a switch is a settings change plus an evaluation run, not a rewrite. Switching on leaderboard news skips the evidence, and longer answers are not better answers.

prompt: What must happen to a scanned PDF page before its contents can be chunked?
optionA: Encryption, because scans may hold personal details
optionB: Compression, because scans exceed chunk size limits
optionC: Nothing, because pypdf reads scanned images as text
optionD: OCR, because the scan has no text layer to extract
correctAnswerText: OCR, because the scan has no text layer to extract
explanation: A scanned page is an image; text extraction reads only a text layer, which a scan lacks, so it returns empty strings. Detect near-empty pages and send them to OCR first.

prompt: In BM25 scoring, how is each matching query word weighted?
optionA: By how close its embedding is to the query vector
optionB: By the position of the word inside the user query
optionC: By how many letters the matching word happens to have
optionD: By how rare the word is across the whole corpus
correctAnswerText: By how rare the word is across the whole corpus
explanation: BM25 weights each matching term by its inverse document frequency, with diminishing returns for repeats and a correction for chunk length. It uses no embeddings, which is why it catches exact codes but not paraphrases.

prompt: In reciprocal rank fusion, what does each ranked list add to a chunk's fused score?
optionA: 1 / (k + rank), where k is a constant such as 60
optionB: The chunk's raw score from that list, unchanged
optionC: k × rank, where k is the number of lists fused
optionD: The rank itself, so that lower totals rank higher
correctAnswerText: 1 / (k + rank), where k is a constant such as 60
explanation: RRF sums 1/(k + rank) over the lists a chunk appears in, ignoring raw scores entirely. k = 60, from the original paper, damps the gap between ranks 1 and 2 so agreement between lists counts most.

prompt: How does a cross-encoder re-ranker score a question against a candidate chunk?
optionA: It counts the words that the two texts have in common
optionB: It compares two vectors that were computed separately
optionC: It looks up the chunk's stored score from ingestion
optionD: It reads both together in one pass and outputs a score
correctAnswerText: It reads both together in one pass and outputs a score
explanation: A cross-encoder sees question and chunk side by side, which makes it more accurate than comparing separately computed embeddings — and much slower, because nothing can be precomputed.

prompt: What makes an ordinary embedding model a "bi-encoder" in retrieval terms?
optionA: It always outputs exactly two vectors for every chunk
optionB: It encodes question and chunk apart, then compares them
optionC: It needs two GPUs, one for queries and one for chunks
optionD: It encodes each text twice, once forwards and once back
correctAnswerText: It encodes question and chunk apart, then compares them
explanation: A bi-encoder embeds each side independently, so chunk vectors can be computed once at ingestion and searched fast. The cost is that neither side ever sees the other, which a cross-encoder fixes on a short list.

prompt: How is mean reciprocal rank (MRR) computed over a golden set?
optionA: Average rank of the first relevant hit, ignoring misses
optionB: Share of the top k results that are relevant passages
optionC: Average of 1/rank of the first relevant hit, 0 if none
optionD: Share of questions with any relevant hit in the top k
correctAnswerText: Average of 1/rank of the first relevant hit, 0 if none
explanation: Each question scores 1 at rank 1, 0.5 at rank 2, 0.33 at rank 3, and 0 if no relevant chunk is found; MRR averages these. The other options describe average rank, hit rate and precision@k.

prompt: In retrieval evaluation, what is a golden set?
optionA: Questions each labelled with the passages that answer them
optionB: The best-scoring chunks, cached to answer repeated queries
optionC: The documents whose embeddings were checked by hand
optionD: A set of model answers that reviewers rated as excellent
correctAnswerText: Questions each labelled with the passages that answer them
explanation: A golden set pairs real questions with their answering passages, so any retrieval design can be scored on recall@k and MRR without calling a model. Rated answers measure generation, not retrieval.

prompt: What does the HyDE technique search with instead of the user's question?
optionA: The embeddings of the chunks retrieved on the last turn
optionB: The embedding of the question translated into English
optionC: A keyword list extracted from the user's question by BM25
optionD: The embedding of a short model-written hypothetical answer
correctAnswerText: The embedding of a short model-written hypothetical answer
explanation: HyDE asks a model to draft a plausible answer and searches with its embedding, because answers resemble chunks more than questions do. A wrong draft can pull wrong chunks, so it must be measured.

prompt: In a chat assistant, what does a "condense" step before retrieval do?
optionA: Rewrites a follow-up into a standalone search question
optionB: Compresses the vectors so the search runs more quickly
optionC: Shortens each retrieved chunk to fit the context budget
optionD: Summarises the whole conversation into the final answer
correctAnswerText: Rewrites a follow-up into a standalone search question
explanation: A message like "And for L5?" embeds to nothing useful. The condense step resolves it with the history into a question that stands alone, which is used for search only.

prompt: How does a recursive character splitter decide where to cut a document?
optionA: Wherever the embedding of the text changes direction
optionB: Largest natural separator first, then finer ones if needed
optionC: At random offsets, so chunks differ between each run
optionD: Every N characters exactly, whatever the text contains
correctAnswerText: Largest natural separator first, then finer ones if needed
explanation: It tries blank lines first and falls back to lines, sentences and spaces only for a piece still too long, so cuts land on natural boundaries. Cutting every N characters is fixed-size chunking.

prompt: Why are allowance-table rows rewritten as "Grade: L4-L6; Hotel per night (metro): Rs 6,000" before embedding?
optionA: Embedding models refuse any text containing numbers
optionB: Vector stores cannot store characters like "|" or tabs
optionC: It turns the table into one chunk, saving index space
optionD: A row cut off from its headers means nothing on its own
correctAnswerText: A row cut off from its headers means nothing on its own
explanation: Extracted tables often leave rows far from their header line, so "L4-L6 Rs 6,000" carries no meaning for search or for the model. Pairing each value with its header makes every row self-contained.

prompt: Why should a header line repeated on every PDF page be stripped before chunking?
optionA: It stops the PDF parser from reading the following lines
optionB: It changes the vector dimension of the affected chunks
optionC: It is copyrighted, so it may never be stored in a database
optionD: It makes chunks look alike and wastes tokens in each one
correctAnswerText: It makes chunks look alike and wastes tokens in each one
explanation: Boilerplate on every page pulls all chunk vectors towards the same text and spends tokens on nothing. Counting line frequency across pages and dropping the frequent lines is the standard clean-up.

prompt: Why does reciprocal rank fusion use ranks rather than adding BM25 and cosine scores?
optionA: Ranks are stored more precisely than floating-point scores
optionB: The scores are on different scales, so a sum would skew
optionC: Adding scores is too slow for more than a few chunks
optionD: Cosine scores can be negative, which breaks a sorted list
correctAnswerText: The scores are on different scales, so a sum would skew
explanation: BM25 runs from 0 to about 10 while cosine runs from −1 to 1, so a plain sum is dominated by BM25. Ranks put both lists on one scale with no tuning beyond k.

prompt: Why is a cross-encoder applied to roughly the top 20 candidates instead of the whole corpus?
optionA: Its token limit stops it reading more than twenty chunks
optionB: It runs once per pair at query time, too slow for all chunks
optionC: Its scores only make sense inside a list of fixed length
optionD: It needs the bi-encoder's vectors as one of its own inputs
correctAnswerText: It runs once per pair at query time, too slow for all chunks
explanation: Nothing can be precomputed for a cross-encoder, so scoring a million chunks means a million model runs per question. A fast first stage narrows the pool; the cross-encoder orders the shortlist.

prompt: In multi-query retrieval, why is the user's own question kept as one of the queries?
optionA: A poor rewrite then cannot lose what the user really typed
optionB: The vector store must receive at least one English query
optionC: Generated queries cannot share the same embedding model
